args.summary: This is a PNAS research article (published June 7, 2010) investigating how Escherichia coli strains harboring the pks genomic island cause DNA damage in mammalian cells. The study demonstrates that these E. coli strains, which produce a genotoxin called Colibactin, induce DNA double-strand breaks in vivo in mouse enterocytes and trigger genomic instability in cultured mammalian cells even at low infectious doses. Key findings include: (1) pks+ E. coli induced γH2AX foci (a DNA damage marker) in mouse colon cells in vivo, comparable to 0.5 Gy gamma irradiation; (2) low-dose infection caused a transient DNA damage response followed by cell division with incomplete repair, leading to anaphase bridges, chromosome aberrations, micronuclei, and aneuploidy; (3) chromosomal instability persisted for up to 21 days after infection, including breakage-fusion-bridge cycles; (4) infected cells showed significantly increased gene mutation frequency at the hprt and tk loci; and (5) cells exhibited anchorage-independent colony formation (a transformed phenotype). The authors conclude that colonization with pks+ E. coli strains, which are found in up to 34% of commensal E. coli from healthy individuals, could contribute to the development of sporadic colorectal cancer by repeatedly provoking low-grade DNA damage at the enterocyte level.

# Helicobacter pylori and colorectal cancer risk

[View Results from this Project](/learn/plco/lab-results/browse/2013-0192/)

## Principal Investigator

Name  
 Meira Epplein

Degrees  
 PhD, MS, MA

Institution

Position Title

Email  
 [meira.epplein@duke.edu](mailto:meira.epplein@duke.edu)

## About this CDAS Project

Study

Project ID   
 2013-0192

Initial CDAS Request Approval   
 Nov 11, 2013

Title   
 Helicobacter pylori and colorectal cancer risk

Summary   
 Recent studies suggest that infection with Helicobacter pylori, a known carcinogen for its association with gastric cancer, may also increase the risk of colorectal cancer, although these findings have been inconsistent. Two recent meta-analyses found significant 40% to 50% increased odds for colorectal cancer among those individuals with evidence of a current or past H. pylori infection. However, the majority of the studies surveyed did not take into account the H. pylori strain type. It is known that as H. pylori has evolved over 50,000 years to live in the stomach, the bacteria have become highly diverse genetically. The proposed project builds on our pilot work exploring H. pylori subtype-specific prevalence and colorectal cancer incidence in the Southern Community Cohort Study, a US population with high prevalence of H. pylori, in which we found a significant 60-80% increase in the odds of colorectal cancer for individuals sero-positive to one of five specific H. pylori proteins. When limiting the outcome to colon cancer, these associations were strengthened, so that sero-positivity to any of these five proteins was associated with a significant, approximate two-fold increased risk for colon cancer, most prominently for the known virulence factor vacuolating cytotoxin (VacA) (OR for VacA sero-positivity, 2.24). The association of VacA sero-positivity was particularly strong for distant colorectal cancer (OR, 5.93), among younger (less than 55 y) individuals (OR, 3.48), and for cancer of the right colon (OR, 3.13). Furthermore, a strong positive dose-response association by increasing quartile of VacA antibody level was also observed. The current project seeks to further our understanding of the H. pylori colorectal cancer association through replication and validation of our initial findings, assessment of the change in the association as disease nears, and examination of potential mechanisms.

Aims

The main aim of this study is to further our understanding of the H. pylori colorectal cancer association. To do this, we propose to first attempt to replicate our pilot findings of an H. pylori subtype-specific association with colorectal cancer risk in a consortium of prospective studies, including the Multiethnic Cohort Study, the Cancer Prevention Studies, the Health Professionals Follow-up and Nurses Health Study, and the NYU Womens Study, and to assess variation in the association by histologic site, stage, and age at onset. Secondly, we will seek to validate the H. pylori subtype-specific association with colorectal cancer risk among the screened participants of the Prostate, Lung, Colorectal, and Ovarian Screening Trial, and to investigate the association among those individuals with two or three blood draws at different time points prior to cancer diagnosis to assess changes in the association over time. Our third and final aim is to examine the potential mechanistic pathway between H. pylori strain-specific infection and colorectal cancer by analyzing the associations with gastric atrophy, measured using pepsinogen levels (among all participants in Aims 1 and 2), gastrin, measured as serum gastrin levels (for those participants with fasting blood draws), and the end product of the COX-2 pathway, urinary prostaglandin E2 (among the members of the cohorts with available urine samples). We will assess whether these measures of potential intermediate variables add predictive value to the H. pylori strain-specific model. We hypothesize that infection with a VacA-positive strain of H. pylori is associated with an increased risk of colon cancer in the general US population, and that this association is strongest for early-onset, advanced-stage disease. We also hypothesize that high gastrin levels will add predictive capability to the model of H. pylori antibodies and colorectal cancer risk, and will suggest that only VacA-positive H. pylori-infected individuals who also have high gastrin levels are at specifically increased risk of colon cancer. We expect to also see a similar association between a low pepsinogen I:II ratio and for high PGE-M levels. Finally, we believe that the association of VacA antibody levels and colorectal cancer risk could strengthen as onset of disease nears (possibly as a marker of increased host inflammation) or the association could weaken as onset of disease nears, as the H. pylori bacterial load could decrease as simultaneously gastrin levels increase. The understanding of this association, through the use of the PLCOs unique resource of serial samples prior to diagnosis, will help to put the pieces together that will then provide the opportunity for the development of an H. pylori biomarker for colorectal cancer risk.

This webpage from the National Cancer Institute's Cancer Data Access System (CDAS) describes research Project ID 2013-0192, "Helicobacter pylori and colorectal cancer risk," led by Principal Investigator Meira Epplein, PhD, of Duke Cancer Institute and Duke University. The project is part of the PLCO (Prostate, Lung, Colorectal, and Ovarian) Screening Trial study.

The research investigates whether infection with specific strains of Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) increases colorectal cancer risk. Prior pilot work found that sero-positivity to certain H. pylori proteins (particularly VacA) was associated with a significant 60-80% increase in colorectal cancer odds, with a two-fold increased risk for colon cancer specifically. 1. Replicate pilot findings of H. pylori subtype-specific association with colorectal cancer risk in a consortium of prospective studies (Multiethnic Cohort Study, Cancer Prevention Studies, Health Professionals Follow-up and Nurses Health Study, NYU Womens Study).
2. Validate the association among PLCO screening trial participants using serial blood draws at different time points prior to cancer diagnosis.
3. Examine potential mechanistic pathways involving gastric atrophy (pepsinogen levels), gastrin levels, and COX-2 pathway products (urinary prostaglandin E2).

# More Evidence Linking H. Pylori Infection to Colorectal Cancer

— Increased CRC incidence and mortality, significantly reduced by infection treatment

March 5, 2024
• 3 min read

![](//assets.medpagetoday.net/assets/images/MPT_logo.svg)
![ A computer rendering of Helicobacter pylori bacterium.](data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAABAAAAAJCAQAAACRI2S5AAAAEklEQVR42mP8/4cBL2AcVQAGAGnrEd24fu28AAAAAElFTkSuQmCC)
![ A computer rendering of Helicobacter pylori bacterium.](data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAABAAAAAJCAQAAACRI2S5AAAAEklEQVR42mP8/4cBL2AcVQAGAGnrEd24fu28AAAAAElFTkSuQmCC)

A history of *Helicobacter* *pylori* infection had a modest but statistically significant association with an increased risk of colorectal cancer (CRC), including fatal CRC, a large retrospective analysis showed.

Already a causative factor in gastric cancer, infection with *H. pylori* increased the likelihood of developing CRC by 18% and the risk of dying of CRC by 12% versus no history of the infection. Patients with infection confirmed by serologic testing had the highest risk.

Treatment of *H. pylori* infection reduced the risk of CRC and CRC mortality by a magnitude similar to that afforded by colonoscopy, reported Shailja C. Shah, MD, MPH, of the University of California San Diego and VA San Diego Healthcare System, and co-authors in the [*Journal of Clinical Oncology*](https://ascopubs.org/doi/pdf/10.1200/JCO.23.00703).

"While our data, supported by mechanistic studies, are compelling, more studies are needed to confirm the strength and consistency of these associations," the authors wrote in conclusion. "In the interim, on the basis of the data presented herein, we posit that testing and treating for *H. pylori* may reduce the risk not only for gastric cancer but also for CRC."

The findings added to evidence from observational studies implicating *H. pylori* in the development of CRC and showing a potentially beneficial effect of treatment for the infection, according to the authors of an [accompanying editorial](https://ascopubs.org/doi/10.1200/JCO.24.00019).

"They found a small but significant reduction in both colorectal cancer incidence and mortality among *H. pylori*-positive individuals who received eradication therapy, compared with *H. pylori*-positive individuals who did not," wrote Julia Butt, PhD, of the German Cancer Research Center in Heidelberg, and Meira Epplein, PhD, of the Duke University Cancer Institute in Durham, North Carolina. "This specific benefit of *H. pylori* eradication has not been clearly demonstrated previously but is consistent with the general findings from observational studies of an increased risk of colorectal cancer among individuals with *H. pylori*."

"Although the statistically significant absolute risk reduction was small, the potential impact of a feasible, noninvasive interception strategy that could reduce both gastric and colorectal cancers is incredibly potent and should be considered in clinical care for individuals at high risk for GI [gastrointestinal] cancers," they added.

The [most common chronic bacterial infection worldwide](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31862245/), *H. pylori* has a group I carcinogen designation because of its causal association with gastric cancer. Treatment of the infection has been shown to [reduce the risk of gastric cancer](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35315732/).

Meta-analyses have suggested that *H. pylori* also increases the risk of CRC, but the consistency and strength of the association has varied, the authors noted in their introduction. No randomized clinical trials or observational studies have evaluated the impact of treatment on CRC incidence or mortality.

To address the gaps in evidence, Shah and colleagues conducted a retrospective cohort study among U.S. military veterans who completed *H. pylori* testing from 1999 through 2018 and received care through the Veterans Health Administration (VHA). Investigators excluded patients with a history of total colectomy, inflammatory bowel disease-associated colitis, or CRC.

The primary exposures were *H. pylori* infection status and, among *H. pylori*-positive individuals, receipt of guideline-recommended treatment for the infection. The primary outcome was incident CRC, as identified by the VHA Central Cancer Registry and Oncology Domain or the National Death Index (NDI). Secondary outcomes included fatal CRC as defined by NDI code.

Data analysis included 812,736 individuals, 205,178 of whom tested positive for *H. pylori*. The analysis showed that *H. pylori*-positive status was associated with an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.18 for CRC versus *H. pylori*-negative status (95% CI 1.12-1.24) and an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.12 for CRC mortality (95% CI 1.03-1.21). Untreated patients had a 23% higher risk of developing CRC and a 40% higher risk of CRC death.

Stratification by race and ethnicity did not significantly alter the results for CRC incidence and mortality. The impact of untreated *H. pylori* infection was greater among non-Hispanic Black patients (aHR 1.61, 95% CI 1.23-2.10) and Hispanic patients (aHR 1.95, 95% CI 1.21-3.14) as compared with non-Hispanic white patients (aHR 1.19, 95% CI 0.99-1.43).

Treatment for *H. pylori* infection led to absolute risk reductions of CRC incidence and mortality of 0.23% to 0.35%.

"To put this into context, colonoscopy is associated with a 0.84%-1.22% absolute risk reduction in incident CRC (31% relative risk reduction) and 0.15%-0.30% absolute risk reduction in fatal CRC (50% relative risk reduction) among persons completing colonoscopy for CRC screening," the authors wrote. "*H. pylori* treatment is a noninvasive intervention that additionally reduces the risk of other complications, namely gastric cancer and peptic ulcer disease, further underscoring the clinical relevance of the findings presented herein."

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108)Abstract

Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a complex and widespread disease, currently ranked as the third most frequent cancer worldwide. It is well known that the gut microbiota has an essential role in the initiation and promotion of different cancer types, particularly gastrointestinal tumors. In fact, bacteria can trigger chronic inflammation of the gastric mucosal, which can induce irreversible changes to intestinal epithelial cells, thus predisposing individuals to cancer. Some bacterial strains, such as _Helicobacter pylori, Streptococcus bovis, Bacteroides fragilis, Clostridium septicum_ and _Fusobacterium_ spp. have a well established role in CRC development. However, the role of _Enterococcus faecalis_ still remains controversial. While part of the literature suggests a harmful role, other papers reported _E. faecalis_ as an important probiotic microorganism, with great applicability in food products. In this review we have examined the vast majority of published data about _E. faecalis_ either in CRC development or concerning its protective role. Our analysis should provide some answers regarding the controversial role of _E. faecalis_ in CRC.

**Keywords:**chronic inflammation, colorectal cancer, _Enterococcus faecalis_, gastrointestinal cancer, gut microbiota

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108)Introduction

Colorectal cancer (CRC) is one of the most commonly diagnosed cancers among both men and women worldwide, being the third most frequent in many developed countries, with an estimated 135,430 new cases expected in 2017 in the United States.[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr1-1756284818783606) The increasing incidence in developing countries seems to be closely related to changes in lifestyle.[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr2-1756284818783606),[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr3-1756284818783606) In fact, only 15% of patients with this disease present a genetic background of familiarity, whereas 85% of cases are represented by sporadic forms.[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr4-1756284818783606) Known environmental factors involved in CRC development include smoking, alcoholism, obesity, sedentary lifestyle, diabetes mellitus, consumption of red meat, a high-fat diet and inadequate intake of fibers.[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr5-1756284818783606) The gut microbial composition has also been reported as another important factor associated with CRC progress.

Recent findings show that gut microorganisms could modulate the mucosal immune system and change the expression of some host genes associated with important functions, such as nutrient uptake, metabolism, angiogenesis and mucosal barrier function.[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr6-1756284818783606),[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr7-1756284818783606) Accordingly, the imbalance of the symbiotic relationship that exists between the gut and its microbiota[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr8-1756284818783606) may disturb the intestinal epithelial integrity, resulting in multiple downstream consequences, including inflammation, oncogenesis and the progression of primary tumors into metastasis.[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr9-1756284818783606),[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr10-1756284818783606) However, even if some microorganisms constitute a fundamental part of natural gut composition, playing protective roles against cancer,[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr11-1756284818783606) the role of other strains, such as _Enterococcus faecalis_, still remains unclear.

_E. faecalis_ is a _Firmicutes_ member, sometimes used as a probiotic product.[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr12-1756284818783606),[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr13-1756284818783606) However, in some specific situations, _E. faecalis_ can result in pathogenic and, as reported by some authors, a harmful microorganism on CRC development, due to its ability to damage colonic epithelial cell DNA.[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr14-1756284818783606) Because of these conflicting roles, in this review we examine the most relevant published data that correlate _E. faecalis_ with CRC either in a harmful or a protective way.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108)Features of CRC

CRC is a multifactorial disease that occurs in a multistep process involving accumulating mutations in tumor suppressor genes and oncogenes. This means that the colorectal tumorigenesis includes several genetic and epigenetic changes required for tumor initiation and progression.[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr15-1756284818783606) CRC is one of the most genetically complex cancers that have been investigated, and its underlying genetic basis is described by the ‘adenoma–carcinoma sequence’ model ([Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#fig1-1756284818783606)), which posits that the genomic instability drives epithelial dysplasia and hyperplasia in the colon, resulting, eventually, in CRC.[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr16-1756284818783606)

Differently from the CRC molecular phenotype originating from genetic familiarity, that is characterized by high-frequency microsatellite instability phenotypes, and by germline mutations in the mismatch repair genes[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr17-1756284818783606) or the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) gene,[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr18-1756284818783606) the sporadic cases of CRC phenotypes present chromosomal instability and allelic imbalance at several chromosomal _loci_ (reviewed by Cunningham and colleagues).[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr19-1756284818783606) Besides the occurrence of genetic and epigenetic abnormalities, many aspects of CRC malignancy are affected by cancer-associated inflammation, such as proliferation and survival of malignant cells, angiogenesis and tumor metastasis. Finally, the presence of an inflammatory microenvironment also plays a crucial role in CRC development.[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr20-1756284818783606),[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr21-1756284818783606) In this scenario, cancer could be described not just as a concentration of malignant cells, but it is also composed of the stromal and infiltrating immunological or inflammatory cells.

It is well known that the diet is definitely the most important (and previously identified) exogenous factor in CRC etiology,[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr22-1756284818783606) since components, ingested through the diet, are the major source of mutagenic compounds that may promote both cancer initiation and progression.[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr23-1756284818783606) In addition, epidemiological studies show that diet–gene interactions are one of the leading causes explaining the wide variation in CRC developing risk among different individuals.[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr24-1756284818783606) For example, the excessive consumption of fats, animal proteins, processed meat, and heterocyclic amines (HCAs) has shown strong correlations with CRC incidence.[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr25-1756284818783606),[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr26-1756284818783606) However, a vegetarian diet helps to prevent CRC, since fruits and vegetables invariably contain antioxidants, which scavenge free radicals, inhibiting the DNA damage responsible for mutations and eventually cancer.[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr27-1756284818783606),[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr28-1756284818783606) The diet also influences the features of gut microbiota, as well as other factors, such as the host’s age, sex, geography and ethnicity.[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr29-1756284818783606)

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108)General aspects of gut microbiota

The gut microbiota, now fully recognized as a natural defensive barrier against infections, is involved in several physiological functions and plays a large role in maintaining the gut homeostasis.[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr30-1756284818783606) Almost immediately after birth, the human gastrointestinal tract (GI) is colonized by a large and diverse community of microorganisms which will compose the GI microbiota.[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr31-1756284818783606) The colonization pattern is influenced by the type of delivery (vaginal delivery or caesarean section)[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr32-1756284818783606) and the type of baby diet (breast or formula feeding).[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr33-1756284818783606) These pioneer microorganisms modulate the expression of some genes from host epithelial cells, creating a flattering habitat for themselves, and also preventing the growth of other microorganisms.[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr34-1756284818783606)

The adult phylogenetic composition of gut microbiota could be influenced by a lot of factors like diet, antibiotic consumption, external environmental microorganisms, geographic/cultural traditions and age.[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr35-1756284818783606),[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr36-1756284818783606) Gut microbiota is normally compounded by autochthonous members, which occupy specific niches constituting the most stable populations over long periods, and by allochthonous members that may be found in any given habitat in significant numbers, but do not influence the gut ecosystem balance in the same way.[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr37-1756284818783606) Humans have a close relationship with these microorganisms, given that their health and wellbeing are closely interconnected with this complex mutualism.[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr38-1756284818783606) The microbiota plays a fundamental role in displaying some essential organismal functions such as helping food digestion, contributing to nutrition,[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr39-1756284818783606) modulating the immune system[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr40-1756284818783606),[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr41-1756284818783606) and defending against a lot of diseases caused by other pathological microbes.[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr42-1756284818783606)

Over the gastric tract, there are variations in the concentration of microorganisms, species and specific functions. For example, in the proximal GI tract, the relatively low (10 8 cells/ml) microbial biomass is associated with the host amino acid requirements,[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr43-1756284818783606) and is composed of _Bacteroidetes_, members of the _Clostridiales_ clusters (clusters XIV and I), and specifically in lumen by _Enterobacteriaceae_ V. This restricted bacterial composition is determined by several factors such as acid pH, rapid lumen ﬂow tendency, bile salts and the presence of immunoglobulin A (IgA). In contrast, the large intestine, which is associated, for example, with the production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) by fermentation of dietary compounds (that escape from the digestion in the small intestine), is colonized by higher concentrations (10 11 cells/g) of microorganisms, mainly by _Firmicutes_ (clusters IX, XIV, and XVI), _Bacteroidetes, Actinobacteria, Verrucomicrobia, Proteobacteria_ and _Fusobacteria_ (reviewed by Walter and Ley).[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr44-1756284818783606)

Even if these data are well known, there is no consensus about what is a ‘healthy’ or ‘average’ intestinal microbiota. For example, studies with rodents have demonstrated that a given bacterial species can have opposite effects in disease induction in one susceptible host, but can protect another rodent strain. Furthermore, different bacterial species can induce variable clinical phenotypes in a single genetically susceptible host.[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr45-1756284818783606) Nevertheless, it seems that beyond the organization of this complex and diverse bacterial ecosystem, the two most common phyla present in the gut, are the _Firmicutes_ and the _Bacteroidetes_,[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr46-1756284818783606) with a documented hierarchy of dominant anaerobic bacteria, like _Bacteroides, Eubacterium, Bifidobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, Ruminococcus, Clostridium_ and _Propionibacterium_, and a subdominant bacteria represented by the _Enterobacteriaceae_ family, especially _Escherichia coli_ and the genera _Streptococcus, Enterococcus, Lactobacillus, Fusobacterium, Desulfovibrio_ and _Methanobrevibacter._[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr47-1756284818783606) In fact, one of the most studied parameters regarding the ‘normal composition’ of gut microbiota is the _Firmicutes_/_Bacteroidetes_ ratio, as well as its variations between individuals,[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr42-1756284818783606) and it seems to be closely linked to health problems such as obesity and metabolic disorders.[48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr48-1756284818783606),[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr49-1756284818783606)

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108)Gut microbiota and CRC

As well as in different types of tumors such as skin, liver, lungs and breast cancers, CRC can be associated with host microbiome dysbiosis.[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr50-1756284818783606),[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr51-1756284818783606) In fact, microorganisms are suspected to be involved in approximately 20% of cancers,[52](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr52-1756284818783606) especially CRC,[53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr53-1756284818783606) since the dynamic crosstalk between intestinal epithelial cells (IECs), the microbes that colonize their apical surface and the surrounding local immune cells, is necessary to maintain intestinal homeostasis.[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr54-1756284818783606) Changes in the _Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes_ ratio[55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr55-1756284818783606) as well as other microbiota imbalances[56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr56-1756284818783606),[57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr57-1756284818783606) are associated with the beginning, maintenance, and determination of the phenotype of human inflammatory bowel diseases (IBDs), especially Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis. These diseases, characterized by chronic inflammation of the GI tract (as a result of inappropriate activation of intestinal mucosal immunity), affect more than 0.4% of Europeans and North Americans,[58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr58-1756284818783606) and are associated with an increased risk of CRC development.[59](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr59-1756284818783606),[60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr60-1756284818783606)

The relationship between the commensal microbiota and IBD could occur in different forms (reviewed by Sartor and Mazmanian),[61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr61-1756284818783606) but all of them seem to be related to the increase in bacterial antigens’ exposure to effector T cells and innate immune cells (resident in the intestinal mucosa) or alteration of the host immune response to commensal bacteria.[62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr62-1756284818783606) Nevertheless, different studies have also demonstrated that patients with IBD present a reduction of _Firmicutes_ members, specifically _Faecalibacterium_ and _Roseburia_, which play a role in protecting the intestine by producing SCFAs.[63](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr63-1756284818783606)

However, an interesting way to explain the role of microorganisms in CRC development was proposed by Tjalsma and colleagues in the ‘bacterial driver-passenger’ model.[64](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr64-1756284818783606) According to this model, the DNA damage caused by distinct indigenous intestinal bacteria (_driver bacteria_) can drive genome instability, which starts the first phase of cancer progression. These microorganisms may be able to induce alterations in mucosal permeability, which favors the translocation of bacteria and bacterial toxins, causing a gut inflammatory response that contributes to the development and progression of cancer. The intestinal inflammation can result from an aberrant ratio of protective (tolerogenic) to aggressive (proinflammatory, damage-inducing, protumorigenic) microbiota, since GI bacteria are able to trigger production of both interleukin (IL)-10 (tolerogenic) and IL-17 (proinflammatory) cytokines.[65](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr65-1756284818783606) This CRC microenvironment could impact the microbial regulation, alter microbiota composition by selective pressure on the microbial community, and thus could support the outgrowth of specific opportunistic bacteria (_passengers bacteria_) that potentially have carcinogenic effects[63](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr63-1756284818783606),[66](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr66-1756284818783606) ([Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#fig1-1756284818783606)).

Furthermore, this inflammatory scenario has an important role in tumor development and maintenance. Once activated, inflammatory cells produce reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive nitrogen that can promote the accumulation of additional mutations and epigenetic changes. These mutations can activate oncogenes or inactive tumor suppressor genes, thus increasing the risk of cancer development.[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr23-1756284818783606),[67](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr67-1756284818783606),[68](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr68-1756284818783606) One of the important bacteria cited as an ‘inducer’ of genetic instability in colonic epithelial cells’ DNA, through the oxidative process, is _E. faecalis._[61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr61-1756284818783606),[69](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr69-1756284818783606)

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108)Properties of _E. faecalis_

Among the enterococci that colonize the GI tract, the most prevalent cultured strain found in human feces is _E. faecalis_ (10 5–10 7 colony-forming units (CFU)/g) followed by _E. faecium_ (10 4–10 5 CFU/g). However these numbers can change with the host’s geographical location, and especially, diet. For instance, Hill and colleagues demonstrated that feces samples of individuals from England, Scotland and the USA (who have a Western diet) present lower concentrations of _Enterococcus_ spp. compared with subjects from India, Japan and Uganda, who adopt a mainly vegetarian diet.[70](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr70-1756284818783606) This Gram-positive commensal bacterium belongs to the lactic acid bacteria (LAB), it is a facultative anaerobic, resistant to extreme environmental challenges and is usually found in the human oral cavity, GI and vagina mucosa.[71](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr71-1756284818783606) However, it can emerge as a human pathogen of significant concern[72](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr72-1756284818783606) and so can be associated with various pathologies including urinary tract infections,[73](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr73-1756284818783606) endocarditis,[74](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr74-1756284818783606) persistent endodontic diseases,[75](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr75-1756284818783606) blood stream infections[76](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr76-1756284818783606) and chronic periodontitis.[77](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr77-1756284818783606)

_E. faecalis_ is the first colonizer of the human GI tract and has a major impact on intestinal immune development in the very early stages of life.[78](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr78-1756284818783606) In newborn babies, it plays a protective role regulating the colonic homeostasis during development by suppressing pathogen-mediated inflammatory responses in human IECs, inducing IL-10 expression,[79](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr79-1756284818783606) and attenuating the secretion of proinflammatory cytokines, especially IL-8.[80](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr80-1756284818783606) Moreover, because of this anti-inflammatory potential, _E. faecalis_ is commonly adopted as a probiotic in the treatment of some diseases such as recurrent chronic sinusitis, bronchitis or infant acute diarrhea.[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr13-1756284818783606),[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr14-1756284818783606) In fact, it has been demonstrated that, compared with 70 different LABs isolated from healthy adults, _E. faecalis_ showed the highest probiotic activity.[81](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr81-1756284818783606) Furthermore, due to its thermophilic fermentation potential (it can ferment different types of sugars, grows at 10°C, and survives at 60°C for 30 min), _E. faecalis_ is commonly used in the production of some cheeses and fermented sausages.[82](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr82-1756284818783606),[83](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr83-1756284818783606)

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108)The ‘Gianus’ role of _E. faecalis_ in cancer development

Data about the role of _E. faecalis_ in CRC are discordant: some authors suggest a protective role or no role at all in CRC while others demonstrated harmful activity. For example, Viljoen and colleagues did not find any significant clinical association between this bacterium and colon adenocarcinoma.[84](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr84-1756284818783606) In another study, when cocultivated with HCT-116 (an aggressive CRC linage), _E. faecalis_ was able to downregulate the expression of the FIAF gene (angiopoietin-like protein 4), normally associated with the development of some cancer types.[85](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr85-1756284818783606) In a mouse model of ulcerative colitis, the increase in _E. faecalis_ colonization after a treatment with vinegar was associated with the inhibition of inflammation by suppressing T helper (Th)-1 and Th17 responses.[86](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr86-1756284818783606) On human peripheral blood mononuclear cells, the heat-killed _E. faecalis_ YM-73 strain shows immunomodulatory ability, increasing Th1- and reducing Th2-associated cytokines.[87](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr87-1756284818783606)

In a recent study, when murine primary colon epithelial cells were cocultured with M1 macrophages polarized by _E. faecalis_, their Wnt/β-catenin signaling was activated and pluripotent transcription factors associated with dedifferentiation were induced. Consequently, these cells were reprogrammed and transformed the primary colon epithelial cells, thus suggesting a role of the microbiome in inducing CRC.[88](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr88-1756284818783606) In contrast, Miyamoto and colleagues demonstrated that in Min mice (APC-mutant mice) which develop many intestinal polyps through activation of β-catenin signaling, administration of the heat-killed _E. faecalis_ EC-12 strain tends to reduce polyp development in the proximal to middle portion of the small intestine, by suppressing β-catenin signaling.[89](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr89-1756284818783606) Nevertheless, the same probiotic strain EC-12 has been demonstrated to protect the host against pathogens by inducing B-cell activation in the gut.[90](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr90-1756284818783606) The other probiotic strain, CECT7121, can protect animals from lymphoma challenge and rechallenge by downregulating LBC cell – a poorly immunogenic cell line derived from a spontaneous murine T-cell lymphoma – proliferation, inducing apoptosis in these cells and enhancing the immune response.[91](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr91-1756284818783606) This strain is also able to enhance and skew the cytokine profile to the Th1 phenotype in different conditions such as vaccination, antitumor immunity, and allergic reactions.[92](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr92-1756284818783606),[93](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr93-1756284818783606) Furthermore, Hassan and colleagues suggested that _E. faecalis_ strains, isolated from human breast milk, could be candidates for breast cancer prevention and treatment once they are able to inhibit the proliferative activity of breast cancer cells.[94](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr94-1756284818783606)

The anticarcinogenic role of some LABs has already been described and related to their immunomodulatory activities, inducing changes in the cytokine profile.[95](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr95-1756284818783606) These changes are orchestrated by the activation of dendritic cells (DCs), which recognize and respond to microbial structures _via_ PRRs (pattern-recognition receptors) such as toll-like receptors (TLRs).[96](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr96-1756284818783606) In addition, different stimuli can induce the production of specific cytokines that are responsible for the fine tuning of an adequate immune response in each pathogen.[97](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr97-1756284818783606) For example, in the case of the CECT7121 strain, it has been demonstrated that, whereas cell wall and soluble lysates are capable of activating DCs and induce dose-dependent secretion of IL-6 and IL-12, only the cell wall, but not the soluble lysates, can induce tumor necrosis factor α and IL-10 secretion.[93](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr93-1756284818783606)

Despite the fact that commensal and clinical strains share the same evolutionary origin, behavioral differences may occur when harmless ones acquire antibiotic resistant or putative virulent genes from other bacteria, _via_ horizontal gene transfer (HGT). HGT favors rapid changes occurring in bacterial structure, generating resistance and pathogenicity island (a dynamic component of their genome), which can affect or influence their virulence.[98](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr98-1756284818783606),[99](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr99-1756284818783606) Many putative virulence factors of _E. faecalis_ have been described. Most of them are associated with aggregation substance, surface adhesins, sex pheromones, lipoteichoic acid, extracellular superoxide, gelatinase, hyaluronidase and cytolysin (hemolysin) (reviewed by Kayaoglu and Ørstavik).[100](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr100-1756284818783606)

The harmful role of _E. faecalis_ has been suggested to be mainly associated with its ability to generate ROS and extracellular superoxide that can cause genomic instability, damaging colonic DNA, and because of that, predisposing the host to mutations and thus cancer.[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr16-1756284818783606) Moreover, _E. faecalis_ has been demonstrated to produce metalloprotease that can directly compromise the intestinal epithelial barrier and induce inflammation.[101](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr101-1756284818783606) It can also activate the macrophage matrix metalloprotease MMP-9[102](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr102-1756284818783606) and lead to disruption of monolayer integrity, which could be responsible for morphological transformation of progenitor cells that get a migrating phenotype, contributing to epithelial mesenchymal transition.[103](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr103-1756284818783606) Furthermore, some authors have observed that, compared with healthy controls, the fecal _E. faecalis_ population was increased in Indian patients with CRC,[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr11-1756284818783606),[104](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr104-1756284818783606) which is also noted in oral cancerous lesions.[105](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr105-1756284818783606),[106](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr106-1756284818783606)

These contrasting data suggest that the origin of the isolated strain is an important variable that should be considered when its role is analysed.[107](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr107-1756284818783606) This is also motivated by the rapid and continuous changes in the DNA of _E. faecalis_ that could modify genes associated with important features of enterococcal virulence, including hemolytic, gelatinase activities,[108](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr108-1756284818783606) antibiotic resistance and biofilm production.[109](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr109-1756284818783606) Different dysbiotic scenarios, such as those promoted by the use of antibiotics, which perturb the normal commensal microbiota and set the stage for intestinal domination, could favor these gene changes between the strains, thus suggesting possible explanations for the different roles of this bacterium in IBD, dysplasia and carcinoma.[110](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr110-1756284818783606)

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108)Discussion

In recent years, crucial discoveries and findings about gut microbiota and its impact on host functions have increased the interest evaluating the microbiome role in human health. Finding microorganisms that can be used as probiotics, either to contrast the infections, or for antitumor treatments, has become a fundamental area of investigation in translational research, generating high expectations for science and medicine.

In this review, we report that _E. faecalis_ has been associated with human IEC injury by ROS production. However, it has also been described as showing a protective role in the same cells by inducing IL-10 expression, attenuating the secretion of the proinflammatory cytokines (e.g. IL-8).

In order to provide an explanation for this scenario, we suggest that this conflicting role could be attributed to the different isolated and investigated strains of _E. faecalis._ In fact, this bacterium could come up against various mutations due to gene transfer. These mutations have shown the potential to make it more or less virulent,[111](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr111-1756284818783606) especially by changing the cytokine/functional profile of the respondents of APCs, like DCs and macrophages.

Furthermore, when we analyzed the studies associating _E. faecalis_ with cancer development, we noted that data demonstrated only an increase in its concentration, but not the functional roles of its bacterium on CRC development. In the case of documented cell or tissue injuries, the conditions were extreme, such as immunosuppressed animals. Therefore, we propose that in CRC, _E. faecalis_ could act as a ‘passenger’ bacterium, rather than a ‘driver’, as suggested by Tjalsma and colleagues. We also suggest that, due to its intrinsic resistance and ability to acquire it (by mutations or HGT), _E. faecalis_ can emerge as pathogenic only when the major environment undergoes alterations, such as during the appearance of cytokines and mucins or during changes in oxygen tension (typically observed on CRC onset and progression conditions).[112](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108#bibr112-1756284818783606) By considering all environmental changes caused by tumorigenesis, _E. faecalis_ can grow uncontrolled, thus increasing the possibility of new mutations that can modify its virulence and also change the final product of its metabolism, becoming potentially harmful to the epithelial tissue. This could be an explanation for the increased concentrations of _E. faecalis_ that were found in some studies on CRC patients’ feces, as well as its harmful role in immunodeficient mice.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108)Conclusion

By considering all these contrasting data, we suggest that the role of _E. faecalis_ should be investigated in more detail and under different experimental conditions since its adoption not only as a fermentative bacterium in food manufacturing, but also as a probiotic product. Our group is currently studying the role of this bacterium in Italian patients with CRC. Our recent data are showing interesting results about the presence and incidence of _E. faecalis_ in patients with CRC, as well as the effects of different strains on tumor cells and inflammatory response (data forthcoming).

args.key_excerpts: "Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a complex and widespread disease, currently ranked as the third most frequent cancer worldwide.", "While part of the literature suggests a harmful role, other papers reported E. faecalis as an important probiotic microorganism, with great applicability in food products.", "The harmful role of E. faecalis has been suggested to be mainly associated with its ability to generate ROS and extracellular superoxide that can cause genomic instability, damaging colonic DNA, and because of that, predisposing the host to mutations and thus cancer.", "We propose that in CRC, E. faecalis could act as a 'passenger' bacterium, rather than a 'driver', as suggested by Tjalsma and colleagues.", "By considering all these contrasting data, we suggest that the role of E. faecalis should be investigated in more detail and under different experimental conditions since its adoption not only as a fermentative bacterium in food manufacturing, but also as a probiotic product."
args.summary:
This is a scientific review article published in Therapeutic Advances in Gastroenterology (2018) examining the controversial role of Enterococcus faecalis in colorectal cancer (CRC). CRC is the third most frequent cancer worldwide, with only 15% of cases having a genetic background, while 85% are sporadic and linked to environmental factors including diet, lifestyle, and gut microbiota composition.

The gut microbiota plays a crucial role in maintaining intestinal homeostasis, but dysbiosis can contribute to CRC development through chronic inflammation, DNA damage, and immune system modulation. The "bacterial driver-passenger" model proposes that certain bacteria (drivers) cause DNA damage initiating cancer, while tumor microenvironment changes favor opportunistic bacteria (passengers).

E. faecalis is a Gram-positive, facultative anaerobic commensal bacterium that is a member of lactic acid bacteria. It colonizes the human GI tract early in life and is commonly used as a probiotic and in food fermentation. However, its role in CRC is controversial:

**Harmful effects:** E. faecalis can generate ROS and extracellular superoxide that damage colonic epithelial cell DNA, produce metalloprotease that compromises the intestinal epithelial barrier, and activate macrophage MMP-9. Some studies found increased fecal E. faecalis in CRC patients compared to healthy controls.

**Protective effects:** E. faecalis can induce IL-10 expression, attenuate proinflammatory cytokines like IL-8, suppress Th1 and Th17 responses, and some strains (e.g., EC-12, CECT7121) show antitumor properties by suppressing β-catenin signaling, inducing apoptosis in cancer cells, and enhancing immune responses.

The authors suggest that the conflicting roles may be attributed to different strains of E. faecalis, as horizontal gene transfer can lead to mutations that alter virulence. They propose that E. faecalis likely acts as a "passenger" bacterium in CRC rather than a "driver" — it may become pathogenic only when the intestinal environment undergoes alterations (such as those caused by tumorigenesis), allowing uncontrolled growth and potential acquisition of virulence factors. The authors call for more detailed investigation of E. faecalis under different experimental conditions given its widespread use in food manufacturing and as a probiotic.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267)Abstract

### Background

Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most common cancer with a significant impact on loss of life. In 2020, nearly 1.9 million new cases and over 9,35,000 deaths were reported. Numerous microbes that are abundant in the human gut benefit host physiology in many ways. Although the underlying mechanism is still unknown, their association appears to be crucial in the beginning and progression of CRC.

### Summary

Diet has a significant impact on the microbial composition and may increase the chance of getting CRC. Increasing evidence points to the gut microbiota as the primary initiator of colonic inflammation, which is connected to the development of colonic tumors. However, it is unclear how the microbiota contributes to the development of CRCs. Patients with CRC have been found to have dysbiosis of the gut microbiota, which can be identified by a decline in commensal bacterial species, such as those that produce butyrate, and a concurrent increase in harmful bacterial populations, such as opportunistic pathogens that produce pro-inflammatory cytokines. We believe that using probiotics or altering the gut microbiota will likely be effective tools in the fight against CRC treatment.

### Purpose

In this review, we revisited the association between gut microbiota and colorectal cancer whether cause or effect. The various factors which influence gut microbiome in patients with CRC and possible mechanism in relation with development of CRC.

### Conclusion

The clinical significance of the intestinal microbiota may aid in the prevention and management of CRC.

### Graphical abstract

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267)Introduction

Cancer is a multifactorial disease that involves the uncontrolled proliferation of cells, arising from genetic and epigenetic changes in the vital genes leading to deviation from normal signaling pathways, consequently causing dynamic changes in the genome (Hanahan and Weinberg [2000](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR74)).

Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the world’s third most prevalent form of cancer after breast and lung cancer. It accounts for 10% of new cases of cancers and causes 9.4% of death of total inflicted CRC patients, as reported in 2020 (900-world-fact-sheets.pdf [2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR1)). It was revealed that age and gender were associated with the prevalence of CRCs. Incidence rates per sex were found to be 23.4 and 16.2 per 1000 people worldwide for males and females, respectively. In contrast, the age-standardized incidence and death rates for CRC were estimated to be 19.5 and 9.0 per 100,000 people (900-world-fact-sheets.pdf [2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR1)). In India, CRC is the 4th most common cancer in males after oral, lung and stomach cancers. In contrast, it was found to be the 5th most common cancer in females after breast, cervix uteri, ovary, and oral cancers (356-india-fact-sheets.pdf [2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR2)). Global studies indicate that developed countries experience 3–4 times higher prevalence of CRC than developing countries (Rawla et al. [2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR147)). Diet and lifestyle habits have been associated with a higher prevalence of CRC in developed countries (Rawla et al. [2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR147)). The rise in CRC cases over the past decade suggests that, in addition to genetic and epigenetic factors, unhealthy dietary habits, such as those involving a diet high in red meat, processed meat, refined grains, sugar-sweetened beverages, desserts, and potatoes (Tabung et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR179)), a lack of fiber intake, a high-fat diet etc., are also important contributors to CRC (Jeon et al. [2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR87)). The other contributing factors, such as physical inactivity, alcohol consumption, obesity and cigarette smoking, have been identified as the main etiological factors in CRC (Fig.[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#Fig1)). The mortality and morbidity rates of CRC have significantly increased in low and middle-income countries. It is expected to increase by 60% with more than 2.2 million new cases and 1.1 million deaths by 2030 (Arnold et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR9)). Furthermore, the occurrence of CRC in younger people, especially those < 50 years of age, is being observed. Such trends in CRC occurrence indicate a necessity to review the association of environmental factors, especially dietary habits and gut microbiome in CRC (Keum and Giovannucci [2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR91)).

### Fig. 1.

[![Image 25: Fig. 1](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/d37a/11798267/d719ec24ab87/432_2022_4422_Fig1_HTML.jpg)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/core/lw/2.0/html/tileshop_pmc/tileshop_pmc_inline.html?title=Click%20on%20image%20to%20zoom&p=PMC3&id=11798267_432_2022_4422_Fig1_HTML.jpg)

[Open in a new tab](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/figure/Fig1/)

Representation of dietary, lifestyle and host’s genetic factors affects the gut microbiome that leads to dysbiosis of gut bacteria, consequently leading to the development of colorectal cancers via producing oncometabolite, inflammation, oxidative stress, genotoxins, virulence factors and biofilm

Intestinal microflora maintains homeostasis and its imbalance contributes to disease development. Studies show that changes in the intestinal microflora permit environmental hazard factors to initiate and lead to the progression of CRC (Scott et al. [2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR162)). It could be an essential factor in regulating the metabolism and immune function of the gut. Advances in understanding the composition and metabolism of the human microbiota have shown that the microbiome significantly effects human health. Through the pro-carcinogenic activity of a specific pathogen that affects inflammation, DNA damage, and apoptosis as well as through influence on the microbial community, primarily its metabolites, the microbiota plays a role in the development of numerous types of cancer (Louis et al. [2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR114)). Studies using animal models have shown that the release of genotoxic virulence factors is stimulated by the synthesis of microbial metabolites, which disrupt the host immune system. Since the exposure to microorganisms is maximum in the gut, particularly the large intestine, therefore the role of the gut microbiota in colorectal cancer has been an active area of research (Louis et al. [2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR114); Belkaid and Harrison [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR16)). Some studies have shed light on the potential action of malignant bacteria on the initiation and progression of CRC through pro-inflammatory interplay with host cells (Schwabe and Jobin [2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR161); Kostic et al. [2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR99); Mármol et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR118)). At the same time, the inhabitant intestinal bacteria, especially their metabolites, had a substantial impact on CRC resistance and susceptibility (Schwabe and Jobin [2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR161)). Unlike human _Papillomavirus_ and _Helicobacter pylori,_ which are associated with cervical cancer and gastric cancer, respectively, no specific microorganism has been reported as the causative agent in CRC.

In this review, we revisited the association between gut microbiota and colorectal cancer whether cause or effect. The various factors which influence gut microbiome in patients with CRC and possible mechanism in relation with development of CRC. Further, we have discussed the clinical importance of intestinal microbiota and possible strategies that could help in the prevention and treatment of CRC.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267)Dysbiosis of gut microbiota and CRC

The gut consists of an abundant and diverse community of microorganisms (bacteria, fungi, archaea, protozoa, bacteriophage and viruses), which are collectively referred to as the gut microbiome. Bacteria are the most abundant among all microorganisms. There are a hundred trillion bacterial cells from over several hundred different species that reside on an adults’s gut mucosa. The human intestinal microbial population is ten times greater than the total number of cells in the human body and carries 150 times more microbial genes than the human genome (Zou et al. [2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR229)). This complex ecosystem does not passively colonize our gut, rather actively participates in nutritional absorption, digestion of complex plant matter, metabolism, immune homeostasis, defenses against pathogenic bacterial species through competition and mucosa maintenance. Now alteration in its balance is being associated various diseases including cancer (Bosch and McFall-Ngai [2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR22); Guarner and Malagelada [2003](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR66); Rowland [2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR153); Kamada et al. [2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR90)). Gut microbiota participates in the maintenance of mucosal homeostasis and epithelial barrier function. Specific perturbations in the mucosal barrier function leads to an increase in the number and species of opportunistic pathogenic bacteria causing alteration in gut microbiota which is defined as dysbiosis. The composition of gut microbiota varies from person to person (Rajoka et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR145)). In healthy conditions, the intestinal barrier keeps bacteria in the lumen which is mainly populated by a core microbiota. These bacteria can be subdivided into various types, with 60% belonging to phyla Firmicutes, especially _Clostridium_ spp. and > 20% belonging to Bacteroidetes and a lesser range to Actinobacteria, Proteobacteria and Verrucomicribia (Arrieta et al. [2006](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR10); Saus et al. [2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR158)). Among these, only specific members of gut microbiota may contribute in the event of pro-inflammatory response, tumor microenvironment formation, immune cells inhibition which provide favorable conditions for progression of CRC (Konstantinov et al. [2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR96); Brennan and Garrett [2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR24)). Studies have shown that fecal samples from patients with CRC have reduced bacterial diversity with predominance in intestinal mucosa samples compared to healthy individuals (Chen et al. [2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR31); Saffarian et al. [2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR157)). In addition, CRC patients show a significant alteration in a specific bacterial group between the right side colon (ascending, proximal, transverse colon) and left side colon (descending, sigmoid, distal colon) with a possible impact on mucosal immune response in comparison to healthy control (Saffarian et al. [2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR157)). CRC patients display a significant increase in opportunistic pathogens such as _Bacteroides fragilis_, _Fusobacterium nucleatum_, _Enterococcaceae, Peptostreptococcus, Enterococus faecalis, Escherichia coli, Shigella_ and _Streptococcus gallolyticus_. While others belong to the genus _Roseburia, Alistipe, Eubacterium, Parasutterella,_ butyrate-producing bacteria belonging to the family Lachnospiraceae, including _Blautia_ and _Clostridium,_ were considerably less abundant in CRC than healthy individuals. Authors suggest that these changes may lead to an imbalance in intestinal homeostasis, ultimately leading to tumor progression (Wang et al. [2012a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR201); Shen et al. [2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR165); Gao et al. [2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR59)). It is still unclear whether dysbiosis occurs due to aggravating factors involved in pro-inflammatory processes or other factors prominent to neoplasms such as host genetics, diet, and lifestyle are responsible for the alteration of microbial composition. Although metabolites produced by gut microorganisms have been recognized to mediate the host interaction, the mechanism by which the gut microbiome influence the host is not fully understood. We, in further sections have tried to elucidate the facts related to the role of dysbiotic gut in CRC.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267)Gut microbiota in CRC pathogenesis

Colorectal malignancy is a complex, multifaceted process affected by environmental and genetic factors, with several triggering mechanisms including inflammation, oxidative stress, immune regulation, biofilm and genotoxins production. These mechanisms have been found to be closely associated with the gut microbiota (Tilg et al. [2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR183)). The association of gut microbiota has been evident from numerous in an animal studies. Germ-free animal studies are associated with lower tumor load than those with elevated germ load. Likewise, reducing gut microbiota burden through antibiotic usage has been suggested to decrease CRC development. Evidence indicates that microbial dysbiosis in the human gut may be essential environmental factor in CRC. Early evidence for gut microbial involvement to CRC pathogenesis came from C57BL/6 _Apc_ _min/_+mice, a genetic mouse model of CRC, where mice housed in germ-free conditions had a lower incidence of tumor formation in the intestine compared with mice housed in specific pathogen-free conditions (Tomkovich et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR186)).

### Pathogenic bacteria in the development of CRC

Despite the differences in intestinal microbiota, several individual bacterial species have been associated with CRC. Although there are hundreds of trillion bacteria reside in the human gut, but some of them have been described to promote intestinal carcinogenesis via attenuating immune response and formation of tumor microenvironment as well as activating oncogenic signaling pathways. Recently, studies have elucidated the functional role and molecular mechanism of several specific bacterial species such as enterotoxigenic _Bacteroides fragilis_ (ETBF),_Fusobacterium nucleatum, Parvimonas micra, Prevotella_ spp._Streptococcus gallolyticus,_ strain of _Escherichia coli_ and _Peptostreptococcus_ spp. may stimulate colorectal carcinogenesis. The pathogenic bacteria in the human gut-associated with colorectal cancer have been summarized in Table [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#Tab2).
