#### Fusobacterium nucleatum

_Fusobacterium nucleatum_ (_F. nucleatum_) was observed to accelerate colon cancer development and provide the growing tumor with defense against attacking immune cells(Gholizadeh et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR62); Bolstad et al. [1996](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR20)). _F. nucleatum_ may assist in disease development and is mainly linked with microsatellite instability (MSI) and CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP). Ito and colleagues observed that _F. nucleatum_ was significantly higher in CRC lesions (56%) than in premalignant lesions suggesting its contribution to the progression of CRC (Ito et al. [2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR85)). Studies have also validated a potential link between the _F. nucleatum_ and colorectal carcinogenesis in the different ethnic groups (McCoy et al. [2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR122); Li et al. [2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR105)). It has been shown that _F. nucleatum_ found enriched in colorectal adenomas and carcinomas compared with adjacent normal tissue (Kostic et al. [2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR99); Abed et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR3)). Yang et al. demonstrated that CRC cell line infected with _F. nucleatum_ leads to increased expression of miR21 by activating TLR4 signaling to MYD88, resulting in activation of NF-kB and consequently the development of CRC compared to control cells. Furthermore, in situ hybridization analysis revealed the level of _F. nucleatum_ DNA and miR21 were elevated in colon tumor tissue compared with normal tissue from Chinese patients (Yang et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR214)). Fap2 protein of _F. nucleatum_ can link with TIGIT (T cell immune receptor with Ig and ITIM domains), an inhibitory immune receptor on a natural killer cell and T cells, and inhibit NK cell cytotoxicity (Rubinstein et al. [2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR155)). Moreover, _F. nucleatum_ has been found to be associated with oxaliplatin, and 5 FU-related chemoresistance in CRC patients by inducing autophagy through Toll-like receptor 4 (Yu et al. [2017b](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR220)). Therefore, further investigation would be help to further understand the interactive role and mechanism of _F. nucleatum_ on host immunity.

#### Bacteroides fragilis

_Bacteroides fragilis_ is a gram-negative, non-spore forming, rod-shaped, obligate anaerobic, common human symbionts that colonize the whole length of the colon and characterize only a small proportion of fecal microbiota (approximately 0.5–1%) (Huang et al. [2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR80); Macfarlane et al. [2005](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR116)). There are two molecular subtypes of B. fragilis, one is enterotoxigenic _B. fragilis_ (ETBF) and another is nontoxigenic _B. fragilis_ (NTBF). Over the past 25 years, ETBF has been emerged as a global etiology of diarrheal disease in animals and humans by causing colitis (Zhang et al. [1999](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR225); Housseau and Sears [2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR79)). The main difference between ETBF and NTBF is the existence of B. fragilis toxin encoded _btf_ gene and its capability to produce biofilm. BFT product is a 20 kDa zinc-dependent metalloprotease toxin with three isotypes (BFT-1, BFT-2 and BFT-3), also known as fragilysin or BFT (Boleij et al. [2015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR19); Sears et al. [2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR163); Rhee et al. [2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR149)). BFT triggers the expression of cyclooxygenase (COX-2) and releases PGE 2, which can disrupt the intestinal environment inducing inflammation and activating signal transducers and activators of the transcription 3 (STAT3) pathway by interacting with epithelial cells. Thus, T-regulatory (T-regs) cells get activated and diminish interleukin (IL-2) quantity (Cheng et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR32)). Toprak et.al. performed a cohort study using fecal samples from 73 CRC patients and 59 healthy subjects and found that the enterotoxin gene _bft_ was exhibited by 38% of the CRC patients compared to 12% in the healthy group. It was the first study indicating a possible correlation between the presence of _bft_ genes and colon cancer carcinogenesis (Ulger Toprak et al. [2006](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR191)). Haghi et al. further studied role of ETBF in CRC and found that the incidence of _bft_ gene was significantly higher in stage III patients compared to stage I and II patients (Haghi et al. [2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR70)). Moreover, the frequency of B. fragilis with isotype _bft-2_ is significantly higher in fecal sample of CRC patients than healthy individuals. A relation between ETBF and inflammatory bowel disease and CRC has also been recognized (Prindiville et al. [2000](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR142)). Clinical studies have shown that ETBF is significantly enriched in stool and mucosa samples of patients with CRC compared to the healthy subject (Ulger Toprak et al. [2006](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR191); Legakis et al. [1981](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR103)). Emerging animal model studies have revealed that in vivo ETBF but not NTBF induce BFT-dependent chronic and acute colitis in specific pathogen-free (SPF) mice C57BL/6J, whereas rapidly persistent colitis in wild-type germ-free mice 129S6/SvEv (Rhee et al. [2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR149); Wick et al. [2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR206)). A study was performed in a mouse model by injecting ETBF treated or untreated CRC cells and compared its results in human CRC patients tissue samples. They suggested that ETBF might have a role in CRC tumorigenesis via upregulating toll-like receptor (TLR) 4 that increases expression of JmjC-domain containing histone demethylase 2B (JMJD2B) via the nuclear factor of activated T cell 5 (NFAT5) dependent signaling. Furthermore, JMJD2B epigenetically elevate NANOG gene expression by specifically demethylating promoter repressive Histone H3 Lysine9trimethylation (H3K9me3), consequently promoting the CRC cell stemness in humans (Liu et al. [2020a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR109)).

#### Escherichia coli

_Escherichia coli_ is a gram-negative, facultative anaerobic, rod-shaped, a coliform bacterium that belonging to the Enterobacteriaceae family and inhabitants in the intestine. It can be distributed into five phylogenic groups viz A, B1, B2, D, and E. Out of these, E coliform phylogroup A and B1 are generally non-pathogenic. Studies on gut microbiota have proposed that pathogenic strains of _E. coli_ can play a crucial role in colorectal cancer progression (Arthur et al. [2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR12), [2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR13); Arthur and Jobin [2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR11); Bonnet et al. [2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR21)). Subsequent studies showed that mucosa internalized and mucosa-associated _E. coli_ were detected more frequently in tumor tissue of patients with CRC compared to controls and cyclomodulin positive _E. coli_ more common in stage III/IV compared to stage I. These findings suggest that _E. coli_ may play a crucial role in the pathogenesis of CRC (Swidsinski et al. [1998](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR178); Martin et al. [2004](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR119)). The pathogenic _E. coli_ can synthesize toxins such as cytolethal distending toxins (CDT), cycle preventing factors and cytotoxic narcotizing factors (CNF), which are genotoxic or restrict the cell cycle (Buc et al. [2013](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR27); Taieb et al. [2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR180)). CDT might influence DNA damage via DNase activity (Ge et al. [2008](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR60)). In a recent in vitro study, B2 phylogenic group of _E. coli_ was shown to produce genotoxic colibactin, that caused ds DNA damage, cell cycle arrest, chromosomal instability, and mutations in CRC tissue as compared to healthy ones (Yan et al. [2016](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR213)). These isolated strains are involved in the onset and progression of CRC, for example, colibactin-producing enterogenic _E. coli_ was shown to be capable of inducing colon tumorigenesis in a CRC mouse model (Arthur et al. [2012](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR12)). A study performed in the healthy Japanese population by Watanabe and colleagues on the association between dietary fibers and pathogenic gut microbiota revealed a negative association between the prevalence of polyketide synthase (_pks_+) producing _E. coli_ in those having a higher intake of green tea and manganese compared to (_pks_−) _E. coli_ while there is a higher prevalence of _pks_+_E. coli_ in the male gender. They supported the hypothesis that reduction of pks+_E. coli_ may be the reason for a lower risk of developing CRC in people with high dietary fiber intake which needs further validation (Watanabe et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR204)).

#### _Peptostreptococcus_ spp.

_Peptostreptococcus anaerobius_ is an anaerobic bacterium enriched in CRC stool and tissue samples. A retrospective study performed by Kwong et al. observed that patients with _Peptostreptococcus_ bacteremia, particularly _Peptostreptococcus anaerobius,_ and _Peptostreptococcus stomatis_ have an elevated risk of CRC development (Kwong et al. [2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR102)). A combined in vitro and in vivo study by Tsoi et al. revealed a pro-tumorigenic effect of _P. anaerobius_ through TLR 2 and TLR4 leading to the accumulation of ROS, which stimulates the biosynthesis of cholesterol and proliferation of the intestinal epithelial cell. Thus _P. anaerobius_ is a critical oncogenic bacteria that promote CRC (Tsoi et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR188); Purcell et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR144)). Compared with other bacteria, _P. anaerobius_ adhere to the intestinal mucosa and encode a virulence factor to stimulate the host immune response. _P. anaerobius_ surface protein, putative cell wall repeats 2 (PCWBR2) interacts with cell surface receptors integrin α2/β1. Consequently, experimental data from CRC cells and _APC_ _Min_/+mice showed that _P. anaerobius_ activated the PI3K/AKT and NF-κB signaling pathways via phosphorylation of the AKT and p65 NF-κB subunits. As a result, _P. anaerobius_ restrains the tumor immune environment, including enlargement of tumor-associated macrophages, myeloid-derived suppressor cells and granulocytic tumor-associated neutrophils. Thus, cell proliferation and pro-inflammatory responses such as cytokines (IL-10 and INF- γ) were significantly increased by _P. anaerobius_ infection which accelerated colorectal tumorigenesis (Long et al. [2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR111)).

_P. stomatis_ species are shown to be increased in consensus molecular subtypes 1 (CMS1) CRC. These findings have been confirmed by targeted qRT-PCR on CRC tumor tissue (Purcell et al. [2017](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR144)). Further, studies have proposed that _P. stomatis_ may provide an acidic and hypoxic tumor microenvironment, which stimulates bacterial settlement. However, no functional analysis on _P. stomatis_ in CRC development exists till date. Hence, the role of _P. stomatis_ in CRC initiation and progression needs to be investigated.

#### Parvimonas micra

_Parvimonas micra_ may be an opportunistic pathogen that may promote CRC development. _P. micra_ has been found to be more significant in patients with CRC than in control (Shah et al. [2018](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR164)). Xu et al. performed a cohort study that revealed a significantly increased abundance of _P. micra_ in patients with CRC compared to colorectal adenoma (CRA) and healthy control. These results were validated by qRT-PCR (Xu et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR211)). Moreover, Lowe mark and colleagues found significantly elevated levels of _P. micra_ in patients with CRC than in healthy controls. Findings suggested that _P. micra_ could be used as a potential non-invasive biomarker associated with an another microbial biomarker for early detection of CRC (Löwenmark et al. [2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11798267#CR115)). The role of _P. micra_ in colorectal tumorigenesis can be studied more so that it could be used as CRC screening tools.

#### Prevotella intermedia

_Prevotella intermedia_ is a gram-negative and obligate anaerobic pathogenic bacterium that has been associated with a high risk of developing CRC. Although, the mechanistic role of _P. intermedia_ has not been appropriately investigated in association with colorectal development. This is a scientific review article published in the Journal of Cancer Research and Clinical Oncology (2022) titled "Implication of gut microbes and its metabolites in colorectal cancer" by Kumar et al. from GIPMER and TERI, New Delhi, India.

**Background:** Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most common cancer worldwide, with nearly 1.9 million new cases and over 935,000 deaths reported in 2020. The gut microbiome appears to play a crucial role in CRC initiation and progression, though the underlying mechanisms remain unclear.

**Key Findings:**
- CRC patients exhibit dysbiosis characterized by reduced beneficial bacteria (e.g., butyrate-producing species like Lachnospiraceae, Blautia, Clostridium) and increased opportunistic pathogens (e.g., Bacteroides fragilis, Fusobacterium nucleatum, Enterococcus faecalis, Escherichia coli, Streptococcus gallolyticus).
- Diet significantly impacts microbial composition and CRC risk. High red meat, processed foods, and low fiber intake are risk factors.
- The article reviews 17 human studies on gut microbiome in CRC across multiple countries (USA, China, India, Europe, South Korea, Japan, Malaysia).

**Specific Pathogenic Bacteria Discussed:**
1. **Fusobacterium nucleatum** - Enriched in adenomas and carcinomas; activates TLR4/MYD88/NF-κB signaling; associated with chemoresistance to oxaliplatin and 5-FU.
2. **Enterotoxigenic Bacteroides fragilis (ETBF)** - Produces BFT toxin (fragilysin); triggers COX-2 expression, STAT3 pathway activation; found in 38% of CRC patients vs 12% of healthy controls.
3. **Escherichia coli** - Pathogenic strains produce colibactin (genotoxin causing DNA damage), CDT, and CNF; associated with advanced stages.
4. **Peptostreptococcus anaerobius** - Promotes tumorigenesis via TLR2/TLR4, ROS accumulation, and PI3K/AKT/NF-κB signaling.
5. **Parvimonas micra** - Potential non-invasive biomarker for early CRC detection.
6. **Prevotella intermedia** - Oral pathogen associated with high CRC risk.

**Conclusion:** The review emphasizes that gut microbiota modulation through probiotics may be an effective tool for CRC prevention and treatment. The clinical significance of intestinal microbiota could aid in CRC management.

# Video Upload Options

Colorectal cancer (CRC) is one of the leading cancers that cause cancer-related deaths worldwide. The gut microbiota has been proved to show relevance with colorectal tumorigenesis through microbial metabolites. By decomposing various dietary residues in the intestinal tract, gut microbiota harvest energy and produce a variety of metabolites to affect the host physiology. However, some of these metabolites are oncogenic factors for CRC.

## 1. Function of Microbial Metabolites in CRC

Microbiota-derived metabolites have a profound effect on host physiology, and it has been estimated that approximately 50% of all metabolites in the plasma have a bacterial origin [[1](#ref_1)]. With an estimated number of 1014 bacteria [[2](#ref_2)], the human colon harbors the densest and metabolically active microbial community in the body. Over the past decades, several catogries of gut microbial specific metabolites have been identified, including SCFAs, secondary bile acids, polyamines, indoles, methylamines, polyphenolics, vitamines and others [[3](#ref_3)]. Accumulating evidence indicates microbiota-derived metabolites exert an important influence on host physiology and diseases development. In the following parts, we will mainly summarize SCFAs, secondary bile acids, polyamine metabolism and their underlying molecular functions in colorectal carcinogenesis [[4](#ref_4)] ([Figure 1](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-1989/11/3/159/htm#fig_body_display_metabolites-11-00159-f001)).

![Metabolites 11 00159 g001 550](/media/item_content/202104/6084e988c2552metabolites-11-00159-g001-550.jpg)

**Figure 1.** Typical microbial metabolites in CRC pathogenesis.

### 1.1. Short-Chain Fatty Acids (SCFAs)

SCFAs are fatty acids with fewer than six carbon atoms, and they consist principally of acetate (C2), propionate (C3) and butyrate (C4). They are mostly produced from bacterial anaerobic fermentation of undigested dietary carbohydrates and endogenous epithelial-derived mucus [[5](#ref_5)] ([Figure 2](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-1989/11/3/159/htm#fig_body_display_metabolites-11-00159-f002)) in the colon. The most abundant acetate is produced by many gut commensal bacteria primarily through the fermentation of organic substrates, some acetogenic bacteria also generate acetate through the Wood-Ljundahl pathway [[6](#ref_6)][[7](#ref_7)]. Propionate is mainly produced by Bacteroidetes and some Firmicutes through the succinate pathway, while the other two pathways including the acrylate pathway and propanediol pathway also contribute to the formation of relatively smaller amounts of propionate [[8](#ref_8)]. Butyrate is formed by the most SCFA-productive microbial species in Clostridium and Bifidobacterium, dominantly using acetate as substate via butyryl-CoA:acetyl-CoA transferase activity [[9](#ref_9)][[10](#ref_10)]. The less commonly employed metabolic pathway is the butyrate kinase pathway [[11](#ref_11)]. Some bacterial species also undergo fermentation of protein and amino acids to generate butyrate through the lysine degradation pathway [[12](#ref_12)].

![Metabolites 11 00159 g002 550](/media/item_content/202104/6084e988cf257metabolites-11-00159-g002-550.jpg)

**Figure 2.** The biosynthesis and metabolism pathways of acetate, propionate and butyrate.

Acetate, propionate and butyrate typically have a combined concentration of 10–130 mM in the colon with a 3:1:1 ratio, which can be influenced by the gut microbiota composition, diet and other environmental factors. The concentration of SCFAs varies along the intestinal tract, with the highest levels in the cecum and proximal colon, and its levels decrease in the distal colon due to absorption by colonic epithelial cells. SCFAs are rapidly absorbed by colonocytes. In fact, butyrate is one of the chief energy sources for local colonic epithelial cells, while the majority of acetate and propionate enter the circulation to exert systemic effects, which influence various pathological conditions including obesity, fatty liver disease and metabolic syndrome [[13](#ref_13)][[14](#ref_14)]. Due to extensive absorption, only a small amount of unabsorbed SCFAs (about 5–10% of the total) are detected in fecal samples [[15](#ref_15)]. Hence, SCFAs could come directly into contact with the colon epithelium, and such interaction has received increasing attention due to the putative roles of SCFAs in colorectal tumorigenesis.

Butyrate is the most widely studied SCFA and it has been suggested that it plays a protective role in CRC [[16](#ref_16)]. Several clinical studies have reported the depletion of butyrate-producing bacteria species and diminished fecal butyrate levels are associated with colon tumorigenesis, suggesting that SCFAs may confer protective effects against carcinogenesis [[17](#ref_17)][[18](#ref_18)]. In homeostasis, butyrate helps to control the gut barrier function by providing colonocytes with energy, decreasing activity of type IV collagen to stimulate epithelial cell attachment and deterring the colonization of pathogens [[9](#ref_9)]. In CRC, butyrate inhibits tumorigenesis via directly inhibition of histone deacetylases (HDACs) activity to modulate translation of tumor suppressor genes. It also mediates its effect via alternative pathways such as metabolic rewiring of cancer cells, activation of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) signaling pathways, which culminates in cancer cells apoptosis and anti-inflammatory responses [[19](#ref_19)].

Butyrate has a major impact on the epigenetic landscape in cancer cells, by virtue of its inhibitory effect on HDACs. In CRC, the dysregulation of HDACs creates a non-permissive chromatin conformation that prevents the transcription of tumor suppressive genes. HDACs inhibitors have shown great potential in anticancer therapy by reversing this process [[20](#ref_20)]. A growing body of work reported butyrate stimulates apoptosis of cancer cells through HDACs inhibition. In a gnotobiotic mice model treated with a butyrate-producing bacterium and high-fiber diet, the increased level of butyrate was associated with a lower tumor burden when compared with normal controls [[21](#ref_21)]. Furthermore, in CRC cell lines, butyrate was shown to induced expression of cell-cycle regulators such as p21 and p27 and pro-apoptotic genes such as FAS through inducing histone acetylation, thus to inhibit proliferation and promote apoptosis [[22](#ref_22)]. Butyrate also promotes an anti-inflammatory microenvironment, which is crucial for preventing tumorigenesis. By enhancing histone H3 acetylation and inhibiting the NF-κB signaling pathway, butyrate attenuated the production of inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-6 and IL-12 to relieve colitis in mice model [[23](#ref_23)]. In addition, butyrate promotes regulatory Treg cell differentiation [[24](#ref_24)] and inhibits macrophage pro-inflammatory function [[25](#ref_25)] through enhancing histone acetylation, thereby contributing to an anti-inflammatory microenvironment.

Apart from epigenetic modifications, butyrate also suppresses CRC development by modulating tumor metabolism. It has been well documented that butyrate serves as an energy source for normal colonic epithelial cells to sustain cell proliferation [[26](#ref_26)]. In contrast, butyrate induces metabolic rewiring in cancer cells to inhibit proliferation and induce apoptosis. For example, a study reported that butyrate could directly bind to PKM2, the M2 isoform of a pyruvate kinase, to inhibit aerobic glycolysis and reverse Warburg effects, thereby compromising the growth of cancer cells which are frequently dependent on glycolysis while normal cells are spared [[27](#ref_27)].

Butyrate is also an agonist of several GPCRs and regulates downstream signaling pathways. GPR109A is a typical receptor of butyrate. Activation of GPR109A induced down-regulation of Bcl-2, Bcl-xL, and cyclin D1, and up-regulation of death receptor pathway to promote apoptosis in colon cancer cells, together with the inhibition of NK-κB signaling [[28](#ref_28)]. In addition, GPR109A signaling induced by butyrate promotes the anti-inflammatory properties of macrophages and dendritic cells in colonic milieu to facilitate the differentiation of Treg cells and IL-10-producing T cells [[29](#ref_29)]. Butyrate is also recognized by GPR43. By interacting with GPR43, microbial-derived butyrate suppresses the Wnt/β-catenin signaling to inhibit intestinal tumor development [[30](#ref_30)].

Although the majority of propionate is absorbed to enter the circulation and is metabolized in liver, it has also shown to have protective effects on colonic cells [[31](#ref_31)]. Propionate inhibits colonic inflammation [[32](#ref_32)][[33](#ref_33)]. Much less is known with regards to the molecular mechanism of propionate in colon cancer; however, it may share a similar mechanism with butyrate through inhibition of HDACs [[34](#ref_34)]. Acetate is also a potential chemopreventive agent against CRC by inhibiting cell proliferation and inducing apoptosis [[35](#ref_35)]. However, others reported that acetate promoted plasma membrane relocalization of MCT-1 and triggered increased glucose consumption and lactate production, thus increasing the glycolytic phenotype in cancer cells [[36](#ref_36)].

Based on current evidence, SCFAs are considered to exert preventive effects on CRC. More in-depth investigations will be required to understand its role in mediating colon epithelium and gut microbiota interactions in the context of tumorigenesis.

### 1.2. Bile Acids

Bile acids, which are primarily produced in the liver, are metabolized to secondary bile acids by the gut microbiota in the intestinal tract [[37](#ref_37)]. Primary bile acids, including cholic acid (CA) and chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA), are produced from cholesterol in hepatocytes and are excreted through the bile duct after conjugation with glycine or taurine. The primary function of bile acid secretion is to emulsify lipids and to facilitate their absorption after meal ingestion. In the gastrointestinal tract, primary bile acids are mostly re-absorbed via enterohepatic circulation in the ileum. However, ~5% of bile acids are deconjugated and biotransformed to secondary bile acids via the action of gut microbiota in colon [[38](#ref_38)]. CA and CDCA are dehydroxylated to generate deoxycholic acid (DCA) and lithocholic acid (LCA) respectively. CDCA can also be metabolized by bacterial hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (HSDH) to generate ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA). The main bacterial genera involved in secondary bile acids biosynthesis are Bacteroides, Clostridium, Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium and Eubacterium, they also serve key roles in regulating host fat metabolism [[39](#ref_39)]. The most abundant bile acids in humans include the primary bile acid CA and CDCA and the secondary bile acid DCA ([Figure 3](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-1989/11/3/159/htm#fig_body_display_metabolites-11-00159-f003)).

![Metabolites 11 00159 g003 550](/media/item_content/202104/6084e988d920dmetabolites-11-00159-g003-550.jpg)

**Figure 3.** The biosynthesis and metabolism of bile acids in human. CA: cholic acid, CDCA: chenodeoxycholic acid, TCA: taurocholic acid, GCA: glycocholic acid, TCDCA: taurochenodeoxycholic acid, GCDCA: glycochenodeoxycholic acid, DCA: deoxycholic acid, LCA: lithicholic acid, UDCA: ursodeoxycholic acid.

Metabolomics studies suggested a correlation between bile acid dysfunction and CRC in multiple cohorts. A multi-omics study combining metabolomics and microbiome analyses fecal/urinary metabolites and fecal microbiota revealed that the higher fecal concentrations of tumor-promoting DCA and increased levels of 7α-dehydroxylating bacteria were observed in CRC high risk population [[40](#ref_40)]. Another study also showed bile acids such as DCA were increased in multiple polypoid adenomas and intramucosal carcinomas patients, and were positively associated with the abundance of Bilophila wadsworthia, whose growth is stimulated by bile acids [[41](#ref_41)]. These studies indicate an extensive crosstalk between bile acids production and gut microbiota, which may form a positive feedback loop to drive CRC pathogenesis.

Secondary bile acids, especially DCA, are considered significant contributors to the development of CRC. DCA was first shown to be a carcinogen that promotes CRC development in mice in 1940 [[42](#ref_42)]. In a recent study, administration of DCA induced colonic tumor formation particularly in the context of obesity [[43](#ref_43)], as high-fat diet induced alterations in the gut microbiota contributed to increased intestinal DCA levels. Hydrophobic DCA exerts multiple pathogenic effects on the colon epithelium including the disruption of cell membrane, induction of oxidative damage to DNA, and activation of NF-κB to provoke inflammation. A study reports that DCA disrupted cell monolayer integrity and increased pro-inflammatory cytokine production in the intestine, leading to low grade inflammation and aggravation of intestinal tumorigenesis in ApcMin/+ mice [[44](#ref_44)]. In vitro experiments showed that DCA exposure induced single-strand breaks of DNA in CRC cells [[45](#ref_45)]. DCA-induced mitochondrial oxidative stress can activate NF-κB signaling in CRC cells, leading to decreased apoptosis and tumor progression [[46](#ref_46)]. Furthermore, bile acids could interact with bile acid receptors to promote CRC. DCA antagonizes intestinal farnesoid X receptor (FXR) function, which in turn, induces cell proliferation and Lgr5+ cancer stem cell expansion [[47](#ref_47)]. Collectively, DCA is a key secondary bile acid implicated in the promotion of colorectal tumorigenesis.

In contrast to DCA, UDCA and tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA) have been associated with suppression of colon tumor development. UDCA regulated intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, suppressed cell cycle progression in colon cancer cells, and reduced the formation of colon cancer stem-like cells [[48](#ref_48)]. On the other hand, TUDCA suppressed NF-κB signaling in CRC cells and ameliorated colitis-associated tumorigenesis in AOM/DSS-treated mice [[49](#ref_49)]. The different biological and pathological effects of DCA and UDCA present are not been fully elucidated, one possible explanation for their different effects on cancer is the diverging effects on the same oncogenic signaling pathway [[50](#ref_50)]. These results suggest that the mechanisms by which secondary bile acids affect the progression of CRC are complex and more research is needed to fully understand their roles in colorectal tumorigenesis.

### 1.3. Polyamines

Polyamines are polycationic molecules that have more than two amino groups, and they are biosynthesized from the amino acids arginine and ornithine [[51](#ref_51)]. The intestinal tract contains high levels of polyamines, mainly including putrescine, spermidine and spermine, which are obtained from diet or biosynthesized by host and bacteria. Polyamine biosynthesis in the host involves arginase 1 (converts l-arginine to l-ornithine), the rate-limiting enzyme ornithine decarboxylase (ODC), which synthesizes putrescine from ornithine, and sequential enzymes catalyzing the interconversion of putrescine, spermidine and spermine. In contrast to host polyamine metabolism, bacteria use constitutive or inducible forms of amino acid decarboxylases to produce polyamines [[52](#ref_52)][[53](#ref_53)]. Polyamines are involved in a range biological processes. For the host, polyamines are essential to cell proliferation, immune cell differentiation and activation [[54](#ref_54)]. Several pathogens, such as Escherichia coli, Helicobacter pylori, and Shigella flexneri [[55](#ref_55)], also depend on polyamines for their virulence.

Polyamines are essential for cell growth, and the constrained intracellular polyamine level is linked to cell growth defects. As expected, tumor cells require more polyamines than normal cells to meet the demands for sustaining rapid growth, which is reflected in the increased levels of polyamines in urine or blood sample in cancer patients when compared to healthy individuals [[56](#ref_56)]. Dysregulation of polyamine metabolism by either the host and gut microbiota may thus be a contributing factor for CRC. A metabolomics screen comparing paired colon cancer and normal tissue samples from patients revealed that the host and microbiota participate in a positive feedback loop, whereby host CRC cells-generated polyamines promote bacterial biofilms growth, and in return, bacteria in biofilms generate polyamines to potentiate cancer development. Following treatment with antibiotics, resected CRC tissues harboring no biofilms or culturable bacteria had decreased levels of a polyamine metabolite, N1,N12-diacetylspermine, as compared to biofilm-positive tissues. Thus, host- and bacteria-derived polyamines may act synergistically to promote tumorigenesis [[57](#ref_57)].

Molecular mechanisms that are involved in polyamines toxicity are diverse. Pathogens induced polyamines catabolism, which generated a number of reactive toxic metabolites that could damage DNA, protein, and other cellular components. In the mice model of CRC, enterotoxigenic Bacteroides fragilis induced spermine oxidase (SMO) could catalyze spermine to spermidine and produced H2O2 as by-product, thus promoted intracellular oxidative stress, leading to DNA damage and accelerated carcinogenesis [[58](#ref_58)]. Polyamines also activate oncogenic signaling, as depletion of spermidine/spermine N1-acetyltransferase (SSAT) in CRC cells resulted in increased level of spermidine and spermine and the expression of pAKT and β-catenin and promoted cell proliferation and tumor metastasis [[59](#ref_59)]. Apart from tumor cell intrinsic effects, preclinical studies in mice indicate that polyamines suppress antitumor immune responses. Polyamine depletion through the inhibition of ODC activity could abrogate tumor growth in a T cell-dependent manner, which provided evidence that reducing intratumoral availability of polyamines could reverse immune suppression in the tumor microenvironment [[60](#ref_60)].

### 1.4. Other Microbial Metabolites in CRC

In recent years, the microbial derived indole and its derivatives have acquired a high notoriety due to their regulation of gastrointestinal barrier function and immune response. The microbial tryptophanase converts dietary tryptophan into indole, which is subsequently converted to various derivatives such as indole-sulfonic acid, indole-3-acetic acid, indole-3-propionic acid, etc. [[61](#ref_61)]. Many of indole derivatives are ligands of AhR, which plays a critical role in controlling the generation of immune cells at gut barrier site [[61](#ref_61)]. In a preclinical colitis mice model, oral administration of indole-3-pyruvic acid regulated T cell and dendritic cell function to make the anti-inflammatory milieu and ameliorated colitis [[62](#ref_62)]. These studies implied that indole derivatives may play a role in colon tumorigenesis. Another important class of microbial metabolites in the colon are methylamines. Previous epidemiological studies had provided evidence for a correlation between colorectal cancer and trimethylamine-N-oxide (TMAO), which is produced by the combined action of gut microbiota and hepatocytes from dietary choline and carnitine [[63](#ref_63)]. Multi-cohorts analysis also indicated microbial genes associated with trimethylamine synthesis enriched in CRC cohorts [[64](#ref_64)]. However, it remains elusive whether the increase in TMAO levels is a cause or a consequence of cancer. Recent studies indicated that TMAO could exacerbate chronic inflammation to promote carcinogenesis, additional studies are still needed to further validate the molecular mechanisms [[65](#ref_65)].

In summary, many microbial-derived metabolites profoundly affect colon tumorigenesis. Metabolites such as butyrate and indole-3-propionic acid may impose positive effects on cancer risks, while some other metabolites including DCA, spermine and TMAO increase cancer risk. Further exploration of the molecular mechanisms of microbial metabolites associated carcinogenesis are needed to validate the causality of these metabolites in CRC.

## 2. Implication for Clinical Applications of Microbial Metabolites in CRC

As shown by our summary above, huge strides have been made in our understanding of the role of gut microbiota-derived metabolites in health and disease, particularly for CRC. The discovery of microbial metabolites involved in colorectal tumorigenesis has key implication for the discovery of potential biomarkers for disease screening as well as novel therapeutic targets. Furthermore, the profile of gut microbiota and that of microbial metabolites is rapidly renewable varying with the diet, making it more amenable for therapeutic intervention in CRC progression. Elucidation of the role of microbial metabolites will provide a new paradigm for cancer diagnosis, prevention and treatment.

### 2.1. Use of Microbial Metabolites as Biomarkers

There are already various biomarkers available for non-invasive diagnosis of CRC. Fecal occult blood test (FOBT), serum tumor marker carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) and methylated Septin9 are now commonly used biomarkers for CRC screening in the clinic [[66](#ref_66)][[67](#ref_67)]. Other molecular markers include microsatellite instability-high, BRAF and RAS mutations are predictive of patient prognosis and therapy response [[68](#ref_68)]. However, most of these biomarkers are significantly limited in clinical application due to their low sensitivity or specificity of detection. Hence, it is of great importance to develop accurate and non-invasive biomarkers for cancer screening and prognostication.

As mentioned above, some of the microbiota-derived metabolites are associated with CRC, and biomarker discovery from microbial metabolome is an area of active investigations. Several studies have found potential microbial metabolites as screening biomarkers in CRC cohorts. For instance, in a GC-MS based global stool metabolites profiling study, the higher level of acetate and the lower level of butyrate and UDCA were unveiled in CRC patients [[69](#ref_69)]. Another GC-MS metabolomic analysis using CRC tissue identified 19 differentiating metabolites, and pathway enrichment analysis revealed significant perturbation of short chain fatty acids metabolism, secondary bile acids metabolism and several carbohydrate metabolites pathways in CRC [[70](#ref_70)]. A paralleled investigation of tumor tissue and feces using NMR found the decreased level of butyrate in CRC patients, and the AUC for diagnosing CRC from normal samples in fecal and tissue sample were 0.692 and 0.717, respectively, and the level of fecal acetate demonstrated the highest diagnostic performance with an AUC of 0.843 [[71](#ref_71)]. A MS-based metabolomic analysis also discovered a panel of polyamine metabolites (N1-acetylspermidine, arginine, citrulline and ornithine) significantly upregulated in CRC cohort [[72](#ref_72)]. The integrated analysis of microbiome and metabolome revealed that the fecal abundance of microbial associated polyamines (putrescine and cadaverine) have high AUCs performance for CRC diagnosis [[73](#ref_73)]. These examples highlight the utility of metabolic markers for CRC screening.

Nevertheless, several metabolomics studies implied inconsistent findings. In a CRC cohort, the serum metabolomics analysis only detected serum glycochenodeoxycholate, a bile acid metabolite, that was positively associated with colorectal cancer among women, while no overall associations were observed between serum metabolites and CRC [[74](#ref_74)]. Meanwhile, in a fecal metabolomics study of SCFAs, the results demonstrated that SCFAs concentrations did not vary meaningfully between colonic adenoma, carcinoma and normal or after cancer treatment, indicating that fecal SCFAs are not predictive for colonic tumors [[75](#ref_75)]. These inconsistent results may due to the limited number of subjects in cohorts, different sample types and the use of different metabolomics analytic platforms and strategies. In summary, larger cohorts and standardized sample preparation and metabolomics analysis methods are needed to further evaluate the diagnostic value of microbial metabolites for CRC in clinical settings.

### 2.2. Modulation of Microbial Metabolites for CRC Prevention and Treatment

Cancer prevention represents an attractive strategy in reducing cancer burden. Epidemiological studies have indicated that dietary modulation is effective in reducing CRC risk [[76](#ref_76)]. The increased intake of red meat and processed meat is correlated with higher cancer risk, whereas dietary fiber may be protective. Diet profoundly affects the composition of microbial metabolites composition. In a cohort of advanced colorectal adenoma patients, a high-fiber diet subsequently increased microbial production of SCFAs, and was associated with a reduced cancer risk [[17](#ref_17)]. On the other hand, high-fat diet induced alterations in microbiota metabolite composition include increased secondary bile acids synthesis, decreased saccharolytic fermentation and butyrogenesis and colonic mucosa damage were also illustrated in another cohort with dietary exchanges experiment [[77](#ref_77)].

The direct supplementation of microbial metabolites has also shown promise in CRC prevention. Given the encouraging results in preclinical studies, butyrate supplementation could be a promising prevention strategy for CRC. In a short-term clinical trial (registered in the Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry as ACTRN12609000306213), the supplementation of butyryated high-amylose maize starch in diet could significantly increase the SCFAs level and prevent the red meat-induced deleterious adduct formation in the rectum [[78](#ref_78)]. Furthermore, in preclinical patient derived CRC organoid models, butyrate was shown to improve the efficacy of radiotherapy, which suggests the potential clinical application of butyrate in combination with other cancer therapies [[79](#ref_79)]. There are also preclinical studies of butyrate to improve CRC surgery outcomes. The mechanical bowel preparation prior to CRC resection results in diminishment of SCFAs producing bacterial species and butyrate levels, which could result in impairment of the intestinal barrier, thus leading to bacterial translocation and possible infectious complications [[80](#ref_80)]. Evidence from rat models supported that oral or rectal administration of butyrate enhanced the bursting wall tension of anastomosis after left or right colectomy. Moreover, SCFAs could hinder the growth of pathogens related to anastomotic leakage [[80](#ref_80)].

As for polyamines, the prospective studies of dietary polyamines supplementation indicate that intake of polyamines above the median amount in the general population was associated with 39% higher risk of colorectal adenoma [[81](#ref_81)]. However, in another cohort of average-risk, postmenopausal women, dietary polyamines were not associated with increased risk of CRC or CRC-specific mortality [[82](#ref_82)]. More studies are needed to confirm the effect of dietary polyamines on CRC risk.

UDCA is a promising chemopreventive agent for CRC in several clinical trials [[83](#ref_83)][[84](#ref_84)]. It is reported that the participants taking UDCA were associated with a reduction in colonic neoplasia incidence. Interestingly, the beneficial effects of UDCA appear to be gender-specific, as a randomized clinical trial (registered with the FDA under Investigational New Drug No.50236) revealed that men treated with UDCA have reduced risk for developing advanced lesions, whilst women showed a significantly higher risk [[85](#ref_85)][[86](#ref_86)].

While there are only a few clinical trials of microbial metabolites to comprehensively evaluate the safety and efficacy of microbial metabolites at present, it provides a new paradigm in CRC prevention and treatment. Supplement of beneficial metabolites could be a feasible strategy to improve cancer therapy and surgery in the future.

args.summary:
This webpage is a scientific encyclopedia article on the role of gut microbiota-derived metabolites in colorectal cancer (CRC). It provides a comprehensive review of how microbial metabolites influence colorectal tumorigenesis, focusing on three main categories: short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), secondary bile acids, and polyamines.

**Key Findings:**

1. **Short-Chain Fatty Acids (SCFAs):** Acetate, propionate, and butyrate are produced by bacterial fermentation of dietary fiber. Butyrate is the most studied and is considered protective against CRC. It inhibits tumorigenesis by inhibiting histone deacetylases (HDACs), modulating cancer cell metabolism, activating GPCR signaling pathways (GPR109A, GPR43), and promoting anti-inflammatory microenvironments. Butyrate induces apoptosis, suppresses proliferation, and promotes Treg cell differentiation.

2. **Secondary Bile Acids:** Primary bile acids (CA, CDCA) are converted to secondary bile acids (DCA, LCA, UDCA) by gut microbiota. DCA is a tumor promoter that disrupts cell membranes, induces oxidative DNA damage, activates NF-κB signaling, and antagonizes FXR function. In contrast, UDCA and TUDCA suppress colon tumor development.

3. **Polyamines:** Putrescine, spermidine, and spermine are essential for cell growth. Tumor cells require more polyamines. Host and bacteria-derived polyamines may act synergistically to promote tumorigenesis. Polyamines can generate reactive toxic metabolites, activate oncogenic signaling (pAKT, β-catenin), and suppress antitumor immune responses.

4. **Other Metabolites:** Indole derivatives (ligands of AhR) and trimethylamine-N-oxide (TMAO) are also implicated in CRC.

**Clinical Applications:**
- Potential biomarkers for CRC screening include altered levels of SCFAs, secondary bile acids, and polyamine metabolites in fecal/tissue samples.
- Dietary modulation (high-fiber, low-fat diets) can influence microbial metabolite profiles.
- Direct supplementation of beneficial metabolites (butyrate, UDCA) shows promise in CRC prevention and treatment.
- UDCA has shown gender-specific effects in clinical trials, reducing risk in men but increasing risk in women.

# Bacterial metabolites involved in risk of IBD and colorectal cancer

[Listen](https://app-eu.readspeaker.com/cgi-bin/rsent?customerid=12593&lang=nl_nl&readid=main&url=https://research.umcutrecht.nl/news/bacterial-metabolites-involved-in-risk-of-ibd-and-colorectal-cancer/ "Laat de tekst voorlezen met ReadSpeaker webReader")

![Host-microbe interaction]()

[Cancer](https://research.umcutrecht.nl/news/?filter-strategic-programs=cancer) [Infection & Immunity](https://research.umcutrecht.nl/news/?filter-strategic-programs=infection-immunity)

PhD research by Coco Duizer (UMC Utrecht) provides insights into the detrimental effects of bacterial-derived metabolites (in particular ADP-heptose and butyrate) on the intestinal epithelium. This was accomplished using *Fusobacterium nucleatum* and *Campylobacter jejuni*, which also provided insights into pathogenic effects of these bacterial species. The results expand existing knowledge on microbiota-derived metabolites in intestinal diseases such as IBD, colorectal cancer and acute gastroenteritis.

The human gastrointestinal tract is inhabited by trillions of microbial cells that mostly form a symbiotic relationship with the host. Out of these microbial cells, bacteria have been studied best with regard to their function and effects in the intestinal tract. To this end, several bacterial species have been identified to directly or indirectly contribute to intestinal pathologies, such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and colorectal cancer (CRC). Recent focus has shifted to the contribution of bacteria-derived metabolites, the intermediate or end products of metabolic reactions, on the intestinal tract. In this work, PhD candidate [Coco Duizer](https://www.linkedin.com/in/coco-duizer-989617135/) (Department of Medical Microbiology, UMC Utrecht) aimed to further delineate the contribution of microbiota-derived metabolites on IBD and CRC. For this, he investigated metabolites from the well-established oncobacterium [*F. nucleatum*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fusobacterium_nucleatum) in organoids, with additional exploration of [*C. jejuni*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campylobacter_jejuni).

## Role of bacterial-derived metabolites

Butyrate is a short-chain fatty acid that has been reported to be secreted by *Fusobacterium* species, which was confirmed to be released by these strains. Also, both *Fusobacterium*-released metabolites and butyrate induced autophagy in intestinal epithelial cells, indicating that this prolonged autophagy could result in toxicity. All in all, Duizer identified *Fusobacterium* species to secrete butyrate which promoted autophagy and organoid cytotoxicity.

*F. nucleatum* is not only associated with IBD, but also with CRC. Thus, Duizer wondered whether *Fusobacterium* species secrete metabolites that could promote development of colorectal cancer. A pro-inflammatory compound activating Alpha-kinase 1 (ALPK1) signaling was identified to be released from *Fusobacterium* species, which appeared to be the metabolite ADP-heptose. In addition, RNA-sequencing suggested that ADP-heptose released by *Fusobacterium* could promote immune evasion of tumor cells by upregulating the inhibitory receptor PD-L1. Thus, *Fusobacterium* species secrete ADP-heptose that could promote tumor development by evading the immune system via PD-L1 upregulation.

![Portrait picture of Coco Duizer]() 

Dr. Coco Duizer

Coco Duizer also identified another ADP-heptose secreting bacterium, *C. jejuni*, which is known to cause severe food-borne gastroenteritis. The pro-inflammatory effect of *C. jejuni* on epithelial cells was dependent on a functional ADP-heptose synthesis pathway in the bacterium, indicating that indeed specifically ADP-heptose or another upstream metabolite was responsible. Additionally, the ADP-heptose derived from *C. jejuni* activated a wide set of pro-inflammatory genes, indicating that this metabolite could contribute to the severe inflammation induced by *C. jejuni* infection.

Coco Duizer concludes: “These findings suggest that *Fusobacterium* and ADP-heptose might be important biomarkers for IBD and CRC, and that targeting *Fusobacterium* might be crucial in preventing the development of these diseases. Alternatively, the potential for therapeutic intervention targeting ADP-heptose or ALPK1 opens up new avenues for preventing inflammatory and carcinogenic processes initiated by bacteria secreting this metabolite.”

## PhD defense

Coco Duizer, MSc (1994, Rossum) defended his PhD thesis on June 13, 2024 at Utrecht University. The title of his thesis was “*Microbiota-derived metabolites in intestinal disease – Moving from association to molecular mechanism*”. Supervisors were Marcel de Zoete, PhD and prof. Rob Willems, PhD (both Department of Medical Microbiology, UMC Utrecht). Coco Duizer will continue his career as a postdoc at Ruaidhri Jackson’s lab at Harvard Medical School in Boston, MA (USA).
