## Introduction

Colorectal cancer (CRC) is not only a major global health burden but also a disease increasingly understood as the product of complex host–microbe interactions. It ranks as the third most common malignancy and the second leading cause of cancer-related mortality, with an increasing incidence in early-onset cases, particularly in industrialized nations and transitioning economies[1](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR1 "Bray, F. et al. Global cancer statistics 2022: GLOBOCAN estimates of incidence and mortality worldwide for 36 cancers in 185 countries. CA Cancer J. Clin. 74, 229–263 (2024)."). Early-life microbial colonization critically shapes immune development and long-term disease risk. Birth mode, breastfeeding, maternal microbiota, and early antibiotics influence microbial diversity during a sensitive period, where disruptions can lead to persistent dysbiosis, impaired tolerance, and higher susceptibility to inflammatory and neoplastic diseases later in life[2](#ref-CR2 "Arrieta, M.-C. et al. Early infancy microbial and metabolic alterations affect risk of childhood asthma. Sci. Transl. Med. 7, 307ra152 (2015)."),[3](#ref-CR3 "Tamburini, S., Shen, N., Wu, H. C. & Clemente, J. C. The microbiome in early life: implications for health outcomes. Nat. Med. 22, 713–722 (2016)."),[4](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR4 "Bautista, J. & López-Cortés, A. Microbial beginnings: determinants and disruptions of the neonatal microbiome. Front. Microbiol. 16, (2025).").

The human gastrointestinal tract harbors a complex microbial ecosystem exceeding 3.8 × 10¹³ microorganisms, predominantly belonging to the phyla *Bacteroidetes, Firmicutes, Actinobacteria, Proteobacteria, Fusobacteriota*, and *Verrucomicrobiota*, which collectively maintain intestinal homeostasis, nutrient metabolism, and immune regulation[5](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR5 "Senchukova, M. A. Microbiota of the gastrointestinal tract: friend or foe?. World J. Gastroenterol. 29, 19–42 (2023)."). Disruption of this balance, or dysbiosis, has been associated with shifts toward pathogenic or pro-inflammatory taxa, leading to chronic inflammation, epithelial barrier dysfunction, and exposure of host tissues to microbial toxins and metabolites with oncogenic potential[6](#ref-CR6 "Wu, S., Lim, K. C., Huang, J., Saidi, R. F. & Sears, C. L. Bacteroides fragilis enterotoxin cleaves the zonula adherens protein, E-cadherin. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA 95, 14979–14984 (1998)."),[7](#ref-CR7 "Rubinstein, M. R. et al. Fusobacterium nucleatum promotes colorectal carcinogenesis by modulating E-cadherin/β-catenin signaling via its FadA adhesin. Cell Host Microbe 14, 195–206 (2013)."),[8](#ref-CR8 "Pleguezuelos-Manzano, C. et al. Mutational signature in colorectal cancer caused by genotoxic pks+ E. coli. Nature 580, 269–273 (2020)."),[9](#ref-CR9 "Chung, L. et al. Bacteroides fragilis toxin coordinates a pro-carcinogenic inflammatory cascade via targeting of colonic epithelial cells. Cell Host Microbe 23, 203–214.e5 (2018)."),[10](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR10 "He, Z. et al. Campylobacter jejuni-derived cytolethal distending toxin promotes colorectal cancer metastasis. Cell Host Microbe 32, 2080–2091.e6 (2024)."). In line with emerging conceptual frameworks, the microbiome has been proposed as a hallmark of cancer, underscoring its central role in shaping key tumor-enabling processes such as inflammation, immune evasion, metabolic rewiring, and genomic instability[11](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR11 "Fulbright, L. E., Ellermann, M. & Arthur, J. C. The microbiome and the hallmarks of cancer. PLoS Pathog. 13, e1006480 (2017)."),[12](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR12 "Hanahan, D. Hallmarks of cancer: new dimensions. Cancer Discov. 12, 31–46 (2022)."). This conceptual shift repositions the microbiome from a peripheral risk factor to a core component of tumor biology, integrated within the evolving hallmarks of the cancer paradigm.

While strong associations between specific microbial taxa and CRC have been extensively documented, establishing a direct causal relationship remains a major challenge in microbiome-cancer research. Classic Koch’s postulates provide a conceptual foundation for defining causative pathogens; however, their direct application to the complex, polymicrobial structure of the gut microbiota is inherently limited[13](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR13 "Byrd, A. L. & Segre, J. A. Infectious disease. Adapting Koch’s postulates. Science 351, 224–226 (2016)."),[14](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR14 "Schmidt, T. S. B., Raes, J. & Bork, P. The human gut microbiome: from association to modulation. Cell 172, 1198–1215 (2018)."). To address this, modern adaptations of these criteria increasingly rely on integrating multi-omics datasets, microbial gene knockouts, and gnotobiotic or humanized murine models to move from correlation toward causality. A paradigmatic example is *pks⁺ Escherichia coli*, for which well-defined mutational signatures attributable to colibactin exposure have been identified in human CRC genomes and reproduced in preclinical models[8](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR8 "Pleguezuelos-Manzano, C. et al. Mutational signature in colorectal cancer caused by genotoxic pks+ E. coli. Nature 580, 269–273 (2020)."). Likewise, enterotoxigenic *Bacteroides fragilis* and polymicrobial biofilms have demonstrated tumor-promoting effects in longitudinal murine studies, providing functional evidence of microbe-driven oncogenesis[15](#ref-CR15 "Dejea, C. M. et al. Patients with familial adenomatous polyposis harbor colonic biofilms containing tumorigenic bacteria. Science 359, 592–597 (2018)."),[16](#ref-CR16 "Tomkovich, S. et al. Human colon mucosal biofilms from healthy or colon cancer hosts are carcinogenic. J. Clin. Invest. 129, 1699–1712 (2019)."),[17](#ref-CR17 "Dejea, C. M. et al. Microbiota organization is a distinct feature of proximal colorectal cancers. Proc Natl. Acad Sci USA 111, 18321–18326 (2014)."),[18](#ref-CR18 "Drewes, J. L. et al. High-resolution bacterial 16S rRNA gene profile meta-analysis and biofilm status reveal common colorectal cancer consortia. npj Biofilms Microbiomes 3, 34 (2017)."),[19](#ref-CR19 "Kvich, L. et al. Biofilms and core pathogens shape the tumor microenvironment and immune phenotype in colorectal cancer. Gut Microbes 16, 2350156 (2024)."),[20](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR20 "Johnson, C. H. et al. Metabolism links bacterial biofilms and colon carcinogenesis. Cell Metab. 21, 891–897 (2015)."). Collectively, these findings underscore that the mere presence or absence of a microorganism is insufficient to drive disease and highlight the need for rigorous mechanistic, longitudinal, and functional studies to establish robust causal inference in CRC.

CRC-associated microbiota alterations are consistently characterized by the enrichment of *Fusobacterium nucleatum*, *pks⁺ E. coli*, enterotoxigenic *Bacteroides fragilis* (ETBF), *Streptococcus gallolyticus, Enterococcus faecalis*, and specific *Porphyromonas* spp., alongside a decrease in beneficial butyrate-producing genera like *Faecalibacterium prausnitzii* and *Roseburia*[21](#ref-CR21 "Okumura, S. et al. Gut bacteria identified in colorectal cancer patients promote tumourigenesis via butyrate secretion. Nat. Commun. 12, 5674 (2021)."),[22](#ref-CR22 "Kostic, A. D. et al. Genomic analysis identifies association of Fusobacterium with colorectal carcinoma. Genome Res. 22, 292–298 (2012)."),[23](#ref-CR23 "Castellarin, M. et al. Fusobacterium nucleatum infection is prevalent in human colorectal carcinoma. Genome Res. 22, 299–306 (2012)."),[24](#ref-CR24 "Arthur, J. C. et al. Intestinal inflammation targets cancer-inducing activity of the microbiota. Science 338, 120–123 (2012)."),[25](#ref-CR25 "Wu, S. et al. A human colonic commensal promotes colon tumorigenesis via activation of T helper type 17 T cell responses. Nat. Med. 15, 1016–1022 (2009)."),[26](#ref-CR26 "Abdulamir, A. S., Hafidh, R. R. & Abu Bakar, F. The association of Streptococcus bovis/gallolyticus with colorectal tumors: the nature and the underlying mechanisms of its etiological role. J. Exp. Clin. Cancer Res. 30, 11 (2011)."),[27](#ref-CR27 "Wirbel, J. et al. Meta-analysis of fecal metagenomes reveals global microbial signatures that are specific for colorectal cancer. Nat. Med. 25, 679–689 (2019)."),[28](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR28 "Wang, T. et al. Structural segregation of gut microbiota between colorectal cancer patients and healthy volunteers. ISME J. 6, 320–329 (2012)."). These microbial shifts are not merely correlative but have been shown to influence tumorigenesis through multiple, often interlinked mechanisms. Pathogens such as *F. nucleatum* promote tumor growth via adhesins (FadA, Fap2) that activate β-catenin signaling, modulate E-cadherin-mediated adhesion, and suppress anti-tumor immune responses[29](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR29 "Li, S. et al. Tumorigenic bacteria in colorectal cancer: mechanisms and treatments. Cancer Biol. Med. 19, 147–162 (2021)."),[30](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR30 "Ternes, D. et al. The gut microbial metabolite formate exacerbates colorectal cancer progression. Nat. Metab. 4, 458–475 (2022)."). ETBF secretes *B. fragilis* toxin (BFT), which triggers E-cadherin cleavage, activates NF-κB, and drives pro-inflammatory cytokine release[29](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR29 "Li, S. et al. Tumorigenic bacteria in colorectal cancer: mechanisms and treatments. Cancer Biol. Med. 19, 147–162 (2021)."),[31](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR31 "Lopez, L. R., Bleich, R. M. & Arthur, J. C. Microbiota effects on carcinogenesis: initiation, promotion, and progression. Annu. Rev. Med. 72, 243–261 (2021)."). *Pks⁺ E. coli* produces the genotoxin colibactin, inducing double-strand DNA breaks, chromosomal instability, and mutational signatures found in human CRC[32](#ref-CR32 "Yang, X. et al. Microbial genotoxin-elicited host DNA mutations related to mitochondrial dysfunction, a momentous contributor for colorectal carcinogenesis. mSystems 9, e0088724 (2024)."),[33](#ref-CR33 "Zechner, E. L. & Kienesberger, S. Microbiota-derived small molecule genotoxins: host interactions and ecological impact in the gut ecosystem. Gut Microbes 16, 2430423 (2024)."),[34](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR34 "Tortora, S. C., Bodiwala, V. M., Quinn, A., Martello, L. A. & Vignesh, S. Microbiome and colorectal carcinogenesis: linked mechanisms and racial differences. World J. Gastrointest. Oncol. 14, 375–395 (2022)."). Other microbial metabolites, including secondary bile acids, polyamines, and hydrogen sulfide, can promote proliferation, inhibit apoptosis, and contribute to a mutagenic microenvironment[35](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR35 "Liu, Y., Lau, H. C.-H. & Yu, J. Microbial metabolites in colorectal tumorigenesis and cancer therapy. Gut Microbes 15, 2203968 (2023).").

A particularly relevant mechanistic axis involves mitochondrial dysfunction as a mediator between microbial genotoxicity and CRC progression. Microbial toxins such as colibactin and cytolethal distending toxin (CDT) may not only damage nuclear DNA but also induce mutations in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), compromising oxidative phosphorylation and enhancing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production—conditions that promote genomic instability and malignant transformation[36](#ref-CR36 "Chen, H.-Y. et al. Mitochondrial injury induced by a Salmonella genotoxin triggers the proinflammatory senescence-associated secretory phenotype. Nat. Commun. 15, 2778 (2024)."),[37](#ref-CR37 "Secher, T., Samba-Louaka, A., Oswald, E. & Nougayrède, J.-P. Escherichia coli producing colibactin triggers premature and transmissible senescence in mammalian cells. PLoS ONE 8, e77157 (2013)."),[38](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR38 "Azzi-Martin, L. et al. Cytolethal distending toxin induces the formation of transient messenger-rich ribonucleoprotein nuclear invaginations in surviving cells. PLoS Pathog. 15, e1007921 (2019)."). This mitochondrial-genotoxicity axis represents a novel mechanistic bridge between microbial exposure and the metabolic reprogramming characteristic of tumor cells.

The tumor microenvironment (TME) is both shaped by and responsive to microbiome alterations. Certain bacteria modulate immune infiltration, promoting tumor tolerance by inducing regulatory T cells, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, or by inhibiting cytotoxic lymphocyte activity[31](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR31 "Lopez, L. R., Bleich, R. M. & Arthur, J. C. Microbiota effects on carcinogenesis: initiation, promotion, and progression. Annu. Rev. Med. 72, 243–261 (2021)."),[39](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR39 "Permain, J., Hock, B., Eglinton, T. & Purcell, R. Functional links between the microbiome and the molecular pathways of colorectal carcinogenesis. Cancer Metastasis Rev. 43, 1463–1474 (2024)."). For example, *F. nucleatum* can drive immune evasion via Fap2–TIGIT interactions, suppressing natural killer (NK) cell function, while microbial metabolites such as formate (produced by *F. nucleatum*) activate AhR signaling, enhance cancer stemness, and promote invasive phenotypes[30](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR30 "Ternes, D. et al. The gut microbial metabolite formate exacerbates colorectal cancer progression. Nat. Metab. 4, 458–475 (2022)."),[40](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR40 "Gur, C. et al. Binding of the Fap2 protein of Fusobacterium nucleatum to human inhibitory receptor TIGIT protects tumors from immune cell attack. Immunity 42, 344–355 (2015)."). Additionally, microbial communities influence the balance between tumor-promoting inflammation and anti-tumor immunity, as observed with polyamine-rich environments that fuel epithelial proliferation versus short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) like butyrate, which have anti-inflammatory and anti-neoplastic effects[35](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR35 "Liu, Y., Lau, H. C.-H. & Yu, J. Microbial metabolites in colorectal tumorigenesis and cancer therapy. Gut Microbes 15, 2203968 (2023)."),[41](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR41 "Coutzac, C. et al. Systemic short chain fatty acids limit antitumor effect of CTLA-4 blockade in hosts with cancer. Nat. Commun. 11, 2168 (2020).").

Importantly, microbial metabolites exhibit context-dependent duality. SCFA-producing taxa such as *Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium*, and *Faecalibacterium* reinforce epithelial integrity and immune tolerance, inducing apoptosis in cancer cells[35](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR35 "Liu, Y., Lau, H. C.-H. & Yu, J. Microbial metabolites in colorectal tumorigenesis and cancer therapy. Gut Microbes 15, 2203968 (2023)."),[42](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR42 "Ahmad, A. et al. Gut microbiota and their derivatives in the progression of colorectal cancer: mechanisms of action, genome and epigenome contributions. Heliyon 10, e29495 (2024)."). However, even metabolites traditionally considered beneficial, such as butyrate, can exhibit dual roles depending on context; for instance, overgrowth of specific *Porphyromonas* spp. in CRC patients has been shown to induce cellular senescence and pro-inflammatory responses via excessive butyrate secretion, accelerating tumorigenesis in murine models[21](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR21 "Okumura, S. et al. Gut bacteria identified in colorectal cancer patients promote tumourigenesis via butyrate secretion. Nat. Commun. 12, 5674 (2021)."),[43](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR43 "Belcheva, A. et al. Gut microbial metabolism drives transformation of MSH2-deficient colon epithelial cells. Cell 158, 288–299 (2014)."). This context-dependent effect underscores the complexity of host-microbe metabolic interactions in cancer biology.

Mechanistically, the interplay between microbiota and CRC converges on canonical oncogenic pathways, including Wnt/β-catenin, NF-κB, STAT3, and MAPK signaling cascades[29](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR29 "Li, S. et al. Tumorigenic bacteria in colorectal cancer: mechanisms and treatments. Cancer Biol. Med. 19, 147–162 (2021)."),[31](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR31 "Lopez, L. R., Bleich, R. M. & Arthur, J. C. Microbiota effects on carcinogenesis: initiation, promotion, and progression. Annu. Rev. Med. 72, 243–261 (2021)."). Dysbiotic microbiota can also influence epigenetic landscapes by altering DNA methylation, histone modifications, and non-coding RNA profiles, further modulating gene expression in ways that favor tumor initiation and progression. Moreover, recent experimental studies have provided compelling mechanistic evidence that polymicrobial biofilms act as functional tumor-promoting units within the colonic mucosa. These structured microbial communities induce epithelial IL-6/STAT3 activation, disrupt E-cadherin, and enhance proliferation[17](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR17 "Dejea, C. M. et al. Microbiota organization is a distinct feature of proximal colorectal cancers. Proc Natl. Acad Sci USA 111, 18321–18326 (2014)."), while gnotobiotic models show that biofilms formed by ETBF, *E. coli*, and *F. nucleatum* accelerate tumorigenesis in *Apc**Min/+* mice[16](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR16 "Tomkovich, S. et al. Human colon mucosal biofilms from healthy or colon cancer hosts are carcinogenic. J. Clin. Invest. 129, 1699–1712 (2019)."). Imaging and metagenomic analyses further reveal spatial metabolic zonation, oxygen gradients, and cooperative virulence strategies among biofilm-associated taxa[18](#ref-CR18 "Drewes, J. L. et al. High-resolution bacterial 16S rRNA gene profile meta-analysis and biofilm status reveal common colorectal cancer consortia. npj Biofilms Microbiomes 3, 34 (2017)."),[19](#ref-CR19 "Kvich, L. et al. Biofilms and core pathogens shape the tumor microenvironment and immune phenotype in colorectal cancer. Gut Microbes 16, 2350156 (2024)."),[20](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR20 "Johnson, C. H. et al. Metabolism links bacterial biofilms and colon carcinogenesis. Cell Metab. 21, 891–897 (2015)."), collectively establishing biofilms as dynamic, inflammation-sustaining ecosystems that drive CRC progression.

From an ecological perspective, microbial genotoxins not only damage host DNA but also shape the gut microbial community through interbacterial antagonism, altering competition dynamics and potentially selecting for more virulent or inflammation-adapted strains[33](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR33 "Zechner, E. L. & Kienesberger, S. Microbiota-derived small molecule genotoxins: host interactions and ecological impact in the gut ecosystem. Gut Microbes 16, 2430423 (2024)."). This dynamic ecosystem-level interaction suggests that CRC-associated microbiomes may evolve toward a stable yet pathogenic state that perpetuates tumor-promoting conditions. Furthermore, oral pathogens such as *Fusobacterium*, *Porphyromonas*, and *Prevotella*, often linked to periodontal disease, have been identified within colorectal tumors, supporting the concept of an oral-gut axis in CRC pathogenesis[22](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR22 "Kostic, A. D. et al. Genomic analysis identifies association of Fusobacterium with colorectal carcinoma. Genome Res. 22, 292–298 (2012)."),[34](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR34 "Tortora, S. C., Bodiwala, V. M., Quinn, A., Martello, L. A. & Vignesh, S. Microbiome and colorectal carcinogenesis: linked mechanisms and racial differences. World J. Gastrointest. Oncol. 14, 375–395 (2022)."),[44](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR44 "Nakatsu, G. et al. Gut mucosal microbiome across stages of colorectal carcinogenesis. Nat. Commun. 6, 8727 (2015)."). Such translocation events may be facilitated by systemic inflammation, immune dysregulation, or microbiota-mediated breakdown of mucosal barriers.

Finally, multi-omics approaches integrating metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, metabolomics, and host genomic analyses are refining our understanding of the microbiome-CRC interface. These approaches are revealing disease-specific microbial signatures with potential diagnostic and prognostic utility[30](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR30 "Ternes, D. et al. The gut microbial metabolite formate exacerbates colorectal cancer progression. Nat. Metab. 4, 458–475 (2022)."),[39](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR39 "Permain, J., Hock, B., Eglinton, T. & Purcell, R. Functional links between the microbiome and the molecular pathways of colorectal carcinogenesis. Cancer Metastasis Rev. 43, 1463–1474 (2024)."). Several bacterial taxa and their metabolic products are being explored as non-invasive biomarkers for early CRC detection, complementing current screening modalities such as colonoscopy and fecal occult blood testing[39](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR39 "Permain, J., Hock, B., Eglinton, T. & Purcell, R. Functional links between the microbiome and the molecular pathways of colorectal carcinogenesis. Cancer Metastasis Rev. 43, 1463–1474 (2024)."),[42](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR42 "Ahmad, A. et al. Gut microbiota and their derivatives in the progression of colorectal cancer: mechanisms of action, genome and epigenome contributions. Heliyon 10, e29495 (2024)."). Collectively, the gut microbiome emerges as an active driver of colorectal carcinogenesis, modulating genetic, epigenetic, metabolic, and immunological pathways throughout the adenoma–carcinoma sequence. This review outlines a conceptual roadmap integrating microbial signatures, mechanistic insights, and translational strategies to define the microbiome’s role in CRC pathogenesis.

## Genotoxin-producing bacteria and host mutational signatures

To move from association to causation, this section outlines microbial genotoxins that leave recognizable imprints in human CRC genomes, linking specific taxa to defined DNA lesions and mutational signatures. We first contextualize how colibactin, BFT, CDT, typhoid toxin, and emerging indolimines converge on replication stress, double-strand breaks (DSBs), and repair pathway rewiring, then summarize complementary small-molecule metabolites that broaden this mutagenic spectrum.

### Colibactin

Colibactin, a hybrid nonribosomal peptide–polyketide genotoxin encoded by the *pks* genomic island of certain *Escherichia coli* strains, was first identified by Nougayrède et al. as a bacterial factor capable of inducing DNA DSBs in mammalian cells[45](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR45 "Nougayrède, J.-P. et al. Escherichia coli induces DNA double-strand breaks in eukaryotic cells. Science 313, 848–851 (2006)."). Since then, it has emerged as a potent microbial driver of colorectal carcinogenesis through its capacity to induce defined mutational signatures in host cells[21](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR21 "Okumura, S. et al. Gut bacteria identified in colorectal cancer patients promote tumourigenesis via butyrate secretion. Nat. Commun. 12, 5674 (2021)."),[46](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR46 "Rosendahl Huber, A. et al. Improved detection of colibactin-induced mutations by genotoxic E. coli in organoids and colorectal cancer. Cancer Cell 42, 487–496.e6 (2024)."). The *pks* island encompasses a suite of *clb* genes (*clbA–clbS*) orchestrating a modular biosynthetic pathway that yields a structurally unstable, cyclopropane-containing metabolite capable of alkylating DNA and generating interstrand crosslinks[47](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR47 "Strakova, N., Korena, K. & Karpiskova, R. Klebsiella pneumoniae producing bacterial toxin colibactin as a risk of colorectal cancer development—a systematic review. Toxicon 197, 126–135 (2021)."),[48](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR48 "Zhang, G. & Sun, D. The synthesis of the novel Escherichia coli toxin-colibactin and its mechanisms of tumorigenesis of colorectal cancer. Front. Microbiol. 15, 1501973 (2024)."). These lesions, particularly when unrepaired, precipitate DSBs and promote single-base substitution (SBS)-pks and small insertion/deletion (ID-pks) mutational patterns, now recognized as molecular hallmarks of colibactin exposure in human colorectal tumors[48](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR48 "Zhang, G. & Sun, D. The synthesis of the novel Escherichia coli toxin-colibactin and its mechanisms of tumorigenesis of colorectal cancer. Front. Microbiol. 15, 1501973 (2024)."),[49](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR49 "Berger, H. & Meyer, T. F. Mechanistic dissection unmasks colibactin as a prevalent mutagenic driver of cancer. Cancer Cell 39, 1439–1441 (2021)."). Structural instability of the molecule has hindered direct purification; however, chemical biology approaches and synthetic analogs have elucidated the cyclopropane warhead’s reactivity toward adenine-rich sequences in duplex DNA, providing a mechanistic link between microbial metabolite chemistry and carcinogenic mutagenesis[50](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR50 "Lythgoe, M. P., Mullish, B. H., Frampton, A. E. & Krell, J. Polymorphic microbes: a new emerging hallmark of cancer. Trends Microbiol. 30, 1131–1134 (2022)."),[51](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR51 "Dougherty, M. W. et al. The microbial genotoxin colibactin exacerbates mismatch repair mutations in colorectal tumors. Neoplasia 43, 100918 (2023).").

Epidemiologically, *pks⁺ E. coli* strains are enriched in CRC patients compared with healthy controls, with meta-analyses indicating a statistically significant elevation in CRC risk among colonized individuals[52](#ref-CR52 "Díaz-Gay, M. et al. Geographic and age variations in mutational processes in colorectal cancer. Nature 643, 230–240 (2025)."),[53](#ref-CR53 "Sogari, A. et al. Tolerance to colibactin correlates with homologous recombination proficiency and resistance to irinotecan in colorectal cancer cells. Cell Rep. Med. 5, 101376 (2024)."),[54](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR54 "Gaab, M. E. et al. A meta-analysis on the association of colibactin-producing pks+ Escherichia coli with the development of colorectal cancer. Lab. Med. 54, 75–82 (2023)."). Spatial mapping of tumor-associated microbiota reveals a predilection of colibactin-producing *E. coli* for distal colon and rectal tumors, aligning with dietary and lifestyle factors, such as Western dietary patterns, that foster expansion of these strains[53](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR53 "Sogari, A. et al. Tolerance to colibactin correlates with homologous recombination proficiency and resistance to irinotecan in colorectal cancer cells. Cell Rep. Med. 5, 101376 (2024)."),[55](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR55 "Chagneau, C. V. et al. The pks island: a bacterial Swiss army knife? Colibactin: beyond DNA damage and cancer. Trends Microbiol. 30, 1146–1159 (2022)."),[56](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR56 "Arima, K. et al. Western-style diet, pks island-carrying Escherichia coli, and colorectal cancer: analyses from two large prospective cohort studies. Gastroenterology 163, 862–874 (2022)."). Preclinical murine models corroborate these associations: monoassociation or co-colonization of *pks⁺ E. coli* with ETBF accelerates adenoma–carcinoma progression, particularly in the context of concurrent inflammatory stimuli or APC loss[15](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR15 "Dejea, C. M. et al. Patients with familial adenomatous polyposis harbor colonic biofilms containing tumorigenic bacteria. Science 359, 592–597 (2018)."). In vitro, exposure of human epithelial and fibroblast cells to colibactin-producing bacteria triggers senescence, chromosomal aberrations, and activation of DNA damage response (DDR) pathways, including ATM/ATR signaling, yet fails to elicit robust p53-mediated apoptosis, favoring survival of genomically unstable clones[47](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR47 "Strakova, N., Korena, K. & Karpiskova, R. Klebsiella pneumoniae producing bacterial toxin colibactin as a risk of colorectal cancer development—a systematic review. Toxicon 197, 126–135 (2021)."),[48](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR48 "Zhang, G. & Sun, D. The synthesis of the novel Escherichia coli toxin-colibactin and its mechanisms of tumorigenesis of colorectal cancer. Front. Microbiol. 15, 1501973 (2024).").

At the genome level, Dziubańska-Kusibab et al. first defined a distinct colibactin-associated mutational signature characterized by SBS-pks and ID-pks patterns[57](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR57 "Dziubańska-Kusibab, P. J. et al. Colibactin DNA-damage signature indicates mutational impact in colorectal cancer. Nat. Med. 26, 1063–1069 (2020)."), while Pleguezuelos-Manzano et al. demonstrated causality by exposing human intestinal organoids to *pks⁺ E. coli*, reproducing the same mutational imprint observed in human colorectal cancers[8](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR8 "Pleguezuelos-Manzano, C. et al. Mutational signature in colorectal cancer caused by genotoxic pks+ E. coli. Nature 580, 269–273 (2020)."). Consequently, mutational signature analyses of human CRC specimens have identified recurrent SBSs at AT-rich motifs and crosslink-associated rearrangements attributable to colibactin, thereby positioning this genotoxin as one of the few bacterially derived agents with a defined imprint in human cancer genomes[49](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR49 "Berger, H. & Meyer, T. F. Mechanistic dissection unmasks colibactin as a prevalent mutagenic driver of cancer. Cancer Cell 39, 1439–1441 (2021)."),[51](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR51 "Dougherty, M. W. et al. The microbial genotoxin colibactin exacerbates mismatch repair mutations in colorectal tumors. Neoplasia 43, 100918 (2023)."). These insights extend beyond etiologic attribution, offering potential diagnostic leverage: colibactin-specific mutational signatures could stratify tumors by microbial exposure history, informing surveillance strategies in high-risk populations[21](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR21 "Okumura, S. et al. Gut bacteria identified in colorectal cancer patients promote tumourigenesis via butyrate secretion. Nat. Commun. 12, 5674 (2021)."),[55](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR55 "Chagneau, C. V. et al. The pks island: a bacterial Swiss army knife? Colibactin: beyond DNA damage and cancer. Trends Microbiol. 30, 1146–1159 (2022)."). Moreover, recent findings suggest that colibactin tolerance in tumor cells is not static; chronic exposure selects for clones with restored homologous recombination (HR) proficiency, conferring resistance to DNA-damaging agents such as irinotecan and its active metabolite SN38[53](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR53 "Sogari, A. et al. Tolerance to colibactin correlates with homologous recombination proficiency and resistance to irinotecan in colorectal cancer cells. Cell Rep. Med. 5, 101376 (2024)."). This cross-resistance underscores a translational paradox—while colibactin may initiate tumorigenesis through genotoxic stress, persistent exposure can drive therapeutic refractoriness by enriching DNA repair–competent subpopulations.

Mechanistically, this HR-mediated tolerance likely reflects adaptive rewiring of DNA repair networks under chronic microbial genotoxic pressure, akin to chemoresistance evolution in response to platinum drugs[46](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR46 "Rosendahl Huber, A. et al. Improved detection of colibactin-induced mutations by genotoxic E. coli in organoids and colorectal cancer. Cancer Cell 42, 487–496.e6 (2024)."),[53](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR53 "Sogari, A. et al. Tolerance to colibactin correlates with homologous recombination proficiency and resistance to irinotecan in colorectal cancer cells. Cell Rep. Med. 5, 101376 (2024)."). Such adaptive dynamics expand the oncogenic role of colibactin from a mutagenic initiator to a microbe-derived selective force sculpting tumor evolutionary trajectory. The interplay between colibactin and host DNA repair proficiency also raises the possibility of synthetic lethality–based interventions: inhibiting HR in *pks⁺* tumors could resensitize cells to both microbial and therapeutic DNA-damaging agents[52](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR52 "Díaz-Gay, M. et al. Geographic and age variations in mutational processes in colorectal cancer. Nature 643, 230–240 (2025)."),[53](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR53 "Sogari, A. et al. Tolerance to colibactin correlates with homologous recombination proficiency and resistance to irinotecan in colorectal cancer cells. Cell Rep. Med. 5, 101376 (2024).").

From a host–microbiome interaction standpoint, colibactin’s influence is not confined to local mutagenesis. DNA damage–induced senescence and associated secretory phenotypes may remodel the tumor microenvironment, fostering pro-inflammatory, immunosuppressive niches that synergize with microbial community shifts to accelerate malignant progression[48](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR48 "Zhang, G. & Sun, D. The synthesis of the novel Escherichia coli toxin-colibactin and its mechanisms of tumorigenesis of colorectal cancer. Front. Microbiol. 15, 1501973 (2024)."),[52](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR52 "Díaz-Gay, M. et al. Geographic and age variations in mutational processes in colorectal cancer. Nature 643, 230–240 (2025)."). Additionally, genotoxin-induced epithelial barrier disruption can enhance systemic dissemination of bacterial metabolites and microvesicles, potentially priming distant tissues for metastasis[21](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR21 "Okumura, S. et al. Gut bacteria identified in colorectal cancer patients promote tumourigenesis via butyrate secretion. Nat. Commun. 12, 5674 (2021)."),[50](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR50 "Lythgoe, M. P., Mullish, B. H., Frampton, A. E. & Krell, J. Polymorphic microbes: a new emerging hallmark of cancer. Trends Microbiol. 30, 1131–1134 (2022)."),[58](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR58 "Bautista, J., Fuentes-Yépez, M. P., Adatty-Molina, J. & López-Cortés, A. Microbial signatures in metastatic cancer. Front. Med. 12, (2025)."). These systemic sequelae position colibactin as a multifaceted contributor to both the initiation and propagation of CRC.

Therapeutically, the identification of colibactin biosynthetic genes and regulatory elements presents opportunities for targeted microbiome modulation. Strategies under investigation include bacteriophage-mediated depletion of *pks⁺* strains, competitive exclusion using engineered commensals, and small-molecule inhibitors of key biosynthetic enzymes such as ClbP peptidase[47](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR47 "Strakova, N., Korena, K. & Karpiskova, R. Klebsiella pneumoniae producing bacterial toxin colibactin as a risk of colorectal cancer development—a systematic review. Toxicon 197, 126–135 (2021)."),[55](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR55 "Chagneau, C. V. et al. The pks island: a bacterial Swiss army knife? Colibactin: beyond DNA damage and cancer. Trends Microbiol. 30, 1146–1159 (2022)."). Such interventions could attenuate genotoxic exposure in at-risk individuals or mitigate tumor evolution in established disease. Furthermore, dietary and probiotic interventions aimed at shifting gut microbial composition away from *pks⁺* populations offer preventive potential, particularly in genetically predisposed cohorts[48](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR48 "Zhang, G. & Sun, D. The synthesis of the novel Escherichia coli toxin-colibactin and its mechanisms of tumorigenesis of colorectal cancer. Front. Microbiol. 15, 1501973 (2024)."),[52](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR52 "Díaz-Gay, M. et al. Geographic and age variations in mutational processes in colorectal cancer. Nature 643, 230–240 (2025).").

Collectively, the evidence positions colibactin as a paradigm of microbe–host co-carcinogenesis, distinguished by its chemical specificity, defined genomic imprint, and dual role in both tumor initiation and therapeutic resistance. Its study exemplifies the broader principle that bacterial secondary metabolites can act as direct modulators of cancer genome evolution, bridging molecular microbiology with oncology and opening translational avenues for microbiota-targeted prevention and therapy.

### Bacteroides fragilis toxin (BFT)

BFT, produced by ETBF, is a zinc-dependent metalloprotease that plays a central role in colorectal carcinogenesis through multifaceted effects on the epithelium, immune system, and tumor microenvironment. Mechanistically, BFT cleaves the extracellular domain of E-cadherin, disrupting adherens junction integrity and releasing β-catenin into the cytoplasm, thereby enabling its nuclear translocation and transcriptional activation of genes linked to proliferation, inflammation, and survival[59](#ref-CR59 "Haghi, F., Goli, E., Mirzaei, B. & Zeighami, H. The association between fecal enterotoxigenic B. fragilis with colorectal cancer. BMC Cancer 19, 879 (2019)."),[60](#ref-CR60 "Scott, N., Whittle, E., Jeraldo, P. & Chia, N. A systemic review of the role of enterotoxic Bacteroides fragilis in colorectal cancer. Neoplasia 29, 100797 (2022)."),[61](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR61 "Purcell, R. V., Permain, J. & Keenan, J. I. Enterotoxigenic Bacteroides fragilis activates IL-8 expression through Stat3 in colorectal cancer cells. Gut Pathog. 14, 16 (2022)."). This initial epithelial barrier perturbation not only primes the mucosa for inflammatory infiltration but also fosters conditions conducive to oncogenic transformation. In human and murine models, BFT-mediated E-cadherin degradation has been shown to act as a trigger for pro-inflammatory chemokine production, notably IL-8, through both β-catenin–dependent and Stat3-driven transcriptional programs, with Stat3 activation emerging as a critical mediator in CRC cells[6](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR6 "Wu, S., Lim, K. C., Huang, J., Saidi, R. F. & Sears, C. L. Bacteroides fragilis enterotoxin cleaves the zonula adherens protein, E-cadherin. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA 95, 14979–14984 (1998)."),[9](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR9 "Chung, L. et al. Bacteroides fragilis toxin coordinates a pro-carcinogenic inflammatory cascade via targeting of colonic epithelial cells. Cell Host Microbe 23, 203–214.e5 (2018)."),[61](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR61 "Purcell, R. V., Permain, J. & Keenan, J. I. Enterotoxigenic Bacteroides fragilis activates IL-8 expression through Stat3 in colorectal cancer cells. Gut Pathog. 14, 16 (2022)."),[62](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR62 "Hwang, S., Gwon, S.-Y., Kim, M. S., Lee, S. & Rhee, K.-J. Bacteroides fragilis toxin induces IL-8 secretion in HT29/C1 cells through disruption of E-cadherin junctions. Immune Netw. 13, 213–217 (2013).").

A seminal study by Wu et al. provided the first in vivo evidence that ETBF, via BFT, drives colonic tumorigenesis in *Apc**Min/+* mice through an IL-17–dependent mechanism. In this model, ETBF colonization selectively induces distal colon tumors by activating an IL-17–Stat3–NF-κB inflammatory axis that bridges epithelial and immune compartments[25](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR25 "Wu, S. et al. A human colonic commensal promotes colon tumorigenesis via activation of T helper type 17 T cell responses. Nat. Med. 15, 1016–1022 (2009)."). A defining feature of ETBF-induced tumorigenesis is the IL-17–Stat3–NF-κB signaling relay between colonic epithelial cells (CECs) and mucosal immune populations. Following BFT-induced epithelial injury, IL-17–producing T helper cells amplify NF-κB activity in CECs, leading to the transcriptional upregulation of C-X-C chemokines such as CXCL1, which drive the recruitment of CXCR2+ polymorphonuclear immature myeloid cells to tumor-prone regions of the distal colon[9](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR9 "Chung, L. et al. Bacteroides fragilis toxin coordinates a pro-carcinogenic inflammatory cascade via targeting of colonic epithelial cells. Cell Host Microbe 23, 203–214.e5 (2018)."),[63](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR63 "Thiele Orberg, E. et al. The myeloid immune signature of enterotoxigenic Bacteroides fragilis-induced murine colon tumorigenesis. Mucosal Immunol. 10, 421–433 (2017)."). These infiltrating myeloid cells acquire an immunosuppressive, pro-tumorigenic phenotype, largely monocytic myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MO-MDSCs), under the combined influence of BFT-induced epithelial stress signals and IL-17–driven cytokines[63](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR63 "Thiele Orberg, E. et al. The myeloid immune signature of enterotoxigenic Bacteroides fragilis-induced murine colon tumorigenesis. Mucosal Immunol. 10, 421–433 (2017)."). This myeloid signature not only supports tumor initiation but also sustains a chronic inflammatory microenvironment that accelerates progression.

Beyond immune modulation, BFT orchestrates oncogenic processes through microRNA regulation. ETBF infection downregulates miR-149-3p via METTL14-mediated N[6](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR6 "Wu, S., Lim, K. C., Huang, J., Saidi, R. F. & Sears, C. L. Bacteroides fragilis enterotoxin cleaves the zonula adherens protein, E-cadherin. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA 95, 14979–14984 (1998).")-methyladenosine modification, impairing its maturation and facilitating the derepression of targets such as PHF5A, which in turn modulates alternative splicing of *KAT2A* to activate SOD2 transcription. This axis promotes oxidative stress adaptation and enhances the survival of transformed cells. Importantly, miR-149-3p is also packaged into exosomes, enabling paracrine modulation of T helper 17 (Th17) cell differentiation, thereby reinforcing the inflammatory circuitry initiated by BFT[64](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR64 "Cao, Y. et al. Enterotoxigenic Bacteroidesfragilis promotes intestinal inflammation and malignancy by inhibiting exosome-packaged miR-149-3p. Gastroenterology 161, 1552–1566.e12 (2021)."). The oncogenic relevance of miR-149-3p suppression is further substantiated by its regulation through the lncRNA LRP11-AS1, which acts as a molecular sponge to sequester miR-149-3p, leading to upregulation of CDK4 and cell cycle progression[65](/articles/s41522-025-00883-8#ref-CR65 "Wu, Z., Yu, M., Zeng, Y., Huang, Y. & Zheng, W. LRP11-AS1 mediates enterotoxigenic Bacteroides fragilis-related carcinogenesis in colorectal Cancer via the miR-149-3p/CDK4 pathway. Cancer Gene Ther. 32, 184–197 (2025)."). This reveals a broader paradigm in which BFT-induced noncoding RNA networks contribute to sustained proliferative signaling and immune dysregulation in colorectal carcinogenesis.

This review article, published in npj Biofilms and Microbiomes (Volume 12, Article 21, 2026), examines how the gut microbiome drives colorectal cancer (CRC) through the reprogramming of immune, metabolic, neural, and endocrine axes. CRC is the third most common malignancy and second leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. The article positions the microbiome as a causal and mechanistic contributor to CRC initiation, progression, and therapy response, moving beyond correlation to causation.

Key points:

1. **CRC-associated dysbiosis** is characterized by enrichment of pathobionts (Fusobacterium nucleatum, pks+ Escherichia coli, enterotoxigenic Bacteroides fragilis) and loss of protective SCFA-producing commensals (Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Roseburia).

2. **Genotoxin-producing bacteria and mutational signatures**: Colibactin (from pks+ E. coli) induces SBS-pks and ID-pks mutational patterns found in human CRC genomes. BFT from ETBF cleaves E-cadherin, activates β-catenin/NF-κB/STAT3 signaling, and drives IL-17-dependent tumorigenesis. Other toxins include CDT and indolimines.

3. **Mechanisms**: Microbial toxins cause DNA damage, epithelial barrier disruption, metabolic rewiring, chronic inflammation, immune suppression, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Polymicrobial biofilms act as functional tumor-promoting units.

4. **Context-dependent metabolite duality**: SCFAs like butyrate have anti-inflammatory effects but can also promote tumorigenesis in certain contexts (e.g., excessive butyrate from Porphyromonas spp. induces senescence).

5. **Therapeutic resistance**: Colibactin exposure selects for clones with homologous recombination proficiency, conferring resistance to irinotecan. B. fragilis promotes chemoresistance to 5-fluorouracil and oxaliplatin via Notch1 activation.

6. **Emerging strategies**: Dietary modulation, pre/probiotics, postbiotics, bacteriophage therapy, engineered live biotherapeutics, and fecal microbiota transplantation are highlighted as microbiota-targeted approaches.

The article conceptualizes CRC as a biofilm-structured, microbiome-driven ecosystem disease and aims to reposition the microbiome from a correlative feature to a tractable determinant of CRC pathogenesis and treatment response.

--- SOURCE 4: A roundup of the ISAPP consensus definitions: probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics, postbiotics and fermented foods - International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics (ISAPP) ---
URL: https://isappscience.org/a-roundup-of-the-isapp-consensus-definitions-probiotics-prebiotics-synbiotics-postbiotics-and-fermented-foods

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Dr. Mary Ellen Sanders, PhD, provides a comprehensive overview of the ISAPP (International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics) consensus definitions for five key terms: probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics, postbiotics, and fermented foods. Published on the ISAPP website, the piece emphasizes that ISAPP has worked over the past 8 years to bring clarity to these definitions for scientists and stakeholders.

A critical commonality across probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics, and postbiotics is the requirement that the substance must be shown to confer a health benefit in the target host. Fermented foods are the exception—no health benefit is required, as their utility stems from sensorial, nutritional, and technological benefits.

The article discusses a regulatory challenge: the health benefit requirement in the probiotic definition has been rigorously implemented in the European Union, where the term "probiotic" is largely prohibited because it is seen as a proxy for unapproved health claims. ISAPP maintains that the definitions are meaningless without the health benefit requirement, though the appropriate level of evidence needed to substantiate such benefits remains debatable.

The five consensus definitions are summarized in a table:

- **Probiotics**: Live microorganisms that, when administered in adequate amounts, confer a health benefit on the host (grammatical correction of the 2001 FAO/WHO definition; no mechanism stipulated).
- **Prebiotics**: A substrate that is selectively utilized by host microorganisms conferring a health benefit (distinct from fiber; health benefit and microbiota impact must be demonstrated in the same study).
- **Synbiotics**: A mixture comprising live microorganisms and substrate(s) selectively utilized by host microorganisms that confers a health benefit (two types defined: complementary and synergistic).
- **Postbiotics**: Preparation of inanimate microorganisms and/or their components that confers a health benefit (cells or cellular structures must be retained; filtrates or isolated components are not postbiotics; a killed probiotic is not automatically a postbiotic).
- **Fermented Foods**: Foods made through desired microbial growth and enzymatic conversions of food components (not required to have live microbes characterized to strain level or evidence of health benefit; may have improved taste, digestibility, safety, and nutritional value).

All definitions were published in *Nature Reviews Gastroenterology and Hepatology* (NRGH) and are among the top most viewed articles on the NRGH website.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: ISAPP elaborates criteria for prebiotics - International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics (ISAPP) ---
URL: https://isappscience.org/isapp-elaborates-criteria-for-prebiotics

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics (ISAPP) published an Expert Recommendation on October 2, 2024, in *Nature Reviews Gastroenterology and Hepatology* titled "Classifying compounds as prebiotics—scientific perspectives and recommendations." The paper reinforces the 2017 ISAPP definition of prebiotic: "a substrate that is selectively utilized by host microorganisms conferring a health benefit." It delineates specific criteria for establishing prebiotic status.

Key criteria include: the substance must be a substrate utilized by host microorganisms; must be sufficiently characterized; must be selectively utilized by the host microbiota (demonstrated through reproducible and specific changes in composition or function); must show a demonstrated health benefit via well-controlled studies (typically RCTs) in the target population; must have a hypothesis for how microbiome modulation leads to the health benefit; the health benefit and selective utilization must be demonstrated in the same study (though causal proof is not required); must be safe for intended use; should have confirmatory evidence beyond minimum requirements; and must be administered at a dose shown to elicit both the health benefit and selective utilization.

The paper addresses the challenge of defining selectivity, noting that the complexity of microbiota makes quantification difficult. It emphasizes that prebiotic-induced health benefits should derive from microbiome modulation, and while causality studies are not required for prebiotic status, they are encouraged through methods including database mining, in silico screening, in vitro/in vivo tracking, machine learning, AI, and animal models.

The paper was co-authored by Prof. Bob Hutkins, Prof. Karen Scott, and others. ISAPP also developed a companion prebiotic evidence checklist. The authors note that consumer awareness varies: 18% of Americans have never heard of prebiotics, while 22% are familiar with and actively try to consume them.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Fusobacterium nucleatum promotes colorectal carcinogenesis by modulating E-cadherin/β-catenin signaling via its FadA adhesin ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3770529

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This study published in Cell Host & Microbe (2013) demonstrates that Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn) promotes colorectal carcinogenesis through its FadA adhesin by binding to E-cadherin and activating β-catenin signaling. 

Key findings: Fn adheres to and invades colorectal cancer (CRC) cells via FadA binding to E-cadherin. The binding site is mapped to an 11-amino acid region (ASANWTIQYND) in the EC5 domain of E-cadherin. A synthetic inhibitory peptide derived from this region abolishes FadA-induced CRC cell growth.

FadA binding leads to E-cadherin phosphorylation, β-catenin accumulation in the cytoplasm and translocation to the nucleus, activating β-catenin-regulated transcription (CRT) including LEF/TCF, NF-κB, Myc, and Cyclin D1. Tumor growth and inflammatory responses are differentially regulated: while both require β-catenin, Fn invasion (mediated by clathrin) is required for inflammatory gene activation but not for oncogenic signaling.

In human colon tissue specimens, FadA gene levels were >10-100 times higher in patients with adenomas and adenocarcinomas compared to normal individuals, with a stepwise increase from normal to precancerous to cancerous tissues. In xenograft mouse models, FadAc and wild-type Fn stimulated tumor growth, which was prevented by the inhibitory peptide.

The study identifies FadA as a potential diagnostic marker and therapeutic target for CRC. The authors propose that Fn colonization of normal tissues may predispose hosts to adenoma/adenocarcinoma development, with carcinogenesis accelerating when a mutation occurs.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This review article (published November 29, 2022 in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology) comprehensively examines the role of Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn) in colorectal cancer (CRC) from phenomenon to mechanism. Key findings include:

**Distribution & Timing:** Fn is enriched in adenomas and CRC tissues compared to normal tissue, with abundance increasing with cancer progression. Fn is more prevalent in right-sided CRC (proximal colon > distal colon > rectum) and is associated with molecular features including MSI-H, CIMP-H, BRAF mutation, and CMS1 subtype.

**Colonization & Origin:** Fn cannot stably colonize normal guts with complex microbiota; it requires mucosal disruption or inflammation. Fn originates from the oral cavity and translocates to CRC via two routes: oral cavity-circulatory system-CRC, and oral cavity-alimentary tract-CRC.

**Tropism Mechanisms:** Fn's tropism to CRC is mediated by Fap2 protein binding to Gal-GalNAc (highly expressed in CRC cells) and FadAc adhesin binding to E-cadherin.

**Tumorigenesis:** Fn does not directly induce oncogenic mutations but promotes tumorigenesis only in the presence of pre-existing genetic defects or carcinogens. Fn-induced inflammation and tumorigenesis may be dose-dependent.

**Proliferation & Metastasis:** Fn accelerates CRC proliferation through TLR4/MYD88/NF-κB, Wnt/β-catenin, and PAK1 signaling pathways. Fn promotes metastasis via cytokine secretion (CXCL1, IL-8, CCL20), exosome-mediated signaling, EMT activation, autophagy induction, and enhanced vascular permeability.

**Stemness:** Fn enhances CRC stemness by promoting fatty acid oxidation (in CCSCs) and lipid accumulation (in non-CCSCs), activating Notch signaling via Numb degradation.

**Metabolic Reprogramming:** Fn promotes glycolysis via upregulating ENO1 and ANGPTL4, and regulates lipid metabolism via CYP2J2 and the TLR4/AKT/Keap1/NRF2 pathway.

**Immune Microenvironment:** Fn induces M2 macrophage polarization (via TLR4/IL-6/p-STAT3/c-Myc and NF-κB/S100A9), expands MDSCs, suppresses T cell and NK cell activity via Fap2-TIGIT and CbpF-CEACAM1 interactions, and upregulates PD-L1 expression.

**Treatment Implications:** The review discusses strategies for CRC prevention and treatment targeting Fn, including anti-Fn approaches.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 21: The controversial role of Enterococcus faecalis in colorectal cancer ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in Therapeutic Advances in Gastroenterology (2018) examining the controversial role of Enterococcus faecalis in colorectal cancer (CRC). CRC is the third most frequent cancer worldwide, with only 15% of cases having a genetic background, while 85% are sporadic and linked to environmental factors including diet, lifestyle, and gut microbiota composition.

The gut microbiota plays a crucial role in maintaining intestinal homeostasis, but dysbiosis can contribute to CRC development through chronic inflammation, DNA damage, and immune system modulation. The "bacterial driver-passenger" model proposes that certain bacteria (drivers) cause DNA damage initiating cancer, while tumor microenvironment changes favor opportunistic bacteria (passengers).

E. faecalis is a Gram-positive, facultative anaerobic commensal bacterium that is a member of lactic acid bacteria. It colonizes the human GI tract early in life and is commonly used as a probiotic and in food fermentation. However, its role in CRC is controversial:

**Harmful effects:** E. faecalis can generate ROS and extracellular superoxide that damage colonic epithelial cell DNA, produce metalloprotease that compromises the intestinal epithelial barrier, and activate macrophage MMP-9. Some studies found increased fecal E. faecalis in CRC patients compared to healthy controls.

**Protective effects:** E. faecalis can induce IL-10 expression, attenuate proinflammatory cytokines like IL-8, suppress Th1 and Th17 responses, and some strains (e.g., EC-12, CECT7121) show antitumor properties by suppressing β-catenin signaling, inducing apoptosis in cancer cells, and enhancing immune responses.

The authors suggest that the conflicting roles may be attributed to different strains of E. faecalis, as horizontal gene transfer can lead to mutations that alter virulence. They propose that E. faecalis likely acts as a "passenger" bacterium in CRC rather than a "driver" — it may become pathogenic only when the intestinal environment undergoes alterations (such as those caused by tumorigenesis), allowing uncontrolled growth and potential acquisition of virulence factors. The authors call for more detailed investigation of E. faecalis under different experimental conditions given its widespread use in food manufacturing and as a probiotic.
</summary>

CRC is the third most common malignancy and second leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. The article positions the microbiome as a causal and mechanistic contributor to CRC initiation, progression, and therapy response, moving beyond correlation to causation.

Key points:

1. **CRC-associated dysbiosis** is characterized by enrichment of pathobionts (Fusobacterium nucleatum, pks+ Escherichia coli, enterotoxigenic Bacteroides fragilis) and loss of protective SCFA-producing commensals (Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Roseburia).

--- SOURCE 1: Frontiers | A Novel Postbiotic From Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG With a Beneficial Effect on Intestinal Barrier Function ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/microbiology/articles/10.3389/fmicb.2019.00477/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Frontiers in Microbiology original research article (published March 14, 2019) titled "A Novel Postbiotic From Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG With a Beneficial Effect on Intestinal Barrier Function" by Gao, Li, Wan et al., from Southern Medical University, China.

**Background:** Probiotics like L. rhamnosus GG (LGG) are known to maintain intestinal homeostasis, but the mechanisms are unclear. The authors previously found LGG culture supernatant (LCS) protects neonatal rats from E. coli K1 infection. This study aimed to identify the bioactive constituent.

**Methods:** Using LC-MS/MS analysis, the authors identified a novel secreted protein from LCS, named HM0539 (hypothetical protein HMPREF0539_2242, 37.3 kDa). It was recombinantly expressed, purified, and tested in vitro (Caco-2 cell monolayers) and in vivo (neonatal rat E. coli K1 infection model, DSS-induced colitis mouse model, and LPS/D-galactosamine-induced liver injury model).

**Key Results:**
- HM0539 is a 37.3 kDa protein, 92% similar to a hydrolase from L. rhamnosus, with low sequence identity to the previously known LGG proteins p40 and p75 (13.7% and 18.9% respectively).
- In vitro: HM0539 dose-dependently induced mucin production and MUC2 expression. It protected Caco-2 monolayers from LPS- or TNF-α-induced barrier injury by preserving ZO-1, occludin, and MUC2 expression, and maintaining transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER).
- In neonatal rats: HM0539 accelerated maturation of intestinal defense (enhanced Ki67, MUC2, ZO-1, mucin), reduced intestinal permeability, and reduced E. coli K1 counts in blood and CSF following oral infection.
- In DSS-induced colitis: HM0539 prevented body weight loss, colon shortening, crypt loss, and leukocyte infiltration, and restored ZO-1 and MUC2 levels.
- In LPS/GalN-induced liver injury: HM0539 prevented intestinal barrier dysfunction, bacterial translocation to liver and MLN, reduced serum ALT/AST levels, and decreased proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6).

**Conclusion:** HM0539 is a novel LGG postbiotic (secreted protein) that exerts protective effects on intestinal barrier function and has potential as a therapeutic agent for intestinal barrier dysfunction-related diseases, including colitis and liver injury.
</summary>

This scientific review article from the Journal of Fungi (2020) examines the probiotic yeast Saccharomyces boulardii, focusing on its genetic, physiological, and mechanistic properties that distinguish it from the closely related Saccharomyces cerevisiae and underpin its success as a probiotic.

URL: https://isappscience.org/a-roundup-of-the-isapp-consensus-definitions-probiotics-prebiotics-synbiotics-postbiotics-and-fermented-foods

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Dr. Mary Ellen Sanders, PhD, provides a comprehensive overview of the ISAPP (International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics) consensus definitions for five key terms: probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics, postbiotics, and fermented foods. Published on the ISAPP website, the piece emphasizes that ISAPP has worked over the past 8 years to bring clarity to these definitions for scientists and stakeholders.

A critical commonality across probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics, and postbiotics is the requirement that the substance must be shown to confer a health benefit in the target host. Fermented foods are the exception—no health benefit is required, as their utility stems from sensorial, nutritional, and technological benefits.

The article discusses a regulatory challenge: the health benefit requirement in the probiotic definition has been rigorously implemented in the European Union, where the term "probiotic" is largely prohibited because it is seen as a proxy for unapproved health claims. ISAPP maintains that the definitions are meaningless without the health benefit requirement, though the appropriate level of evidence needed to substantiate such benefits remains debatable.

The five consensus definitions are summarized in a table:

- **Probiotics**: Live microorganisms that, when administered in adequate amounts, confer a health benefit on the host (grammatical correction of the 2001 FAO/WHO definition; no mechanism stipulated).
- **Prebiotics**: A substrate that is selectively utilized by host microorganisms conferring a health benefit (distinct from fiber; health benefit and microbiota impact must be demonstrated in the same study).
- **Synbiotics**: A mixture comprising live microorganisms and substrate(s) selectively utilized by host microorganisms that confers a health benefit (two types defined: complementary and synergistic).
- **Postbiotics**: Preparation of inanimate microorganisms and/or their components that confers a health benefit (cells or cellular structures must be retained; filtrates or isolated components are not postbiotics; a killed probiotic is not automatically a postbiotic).
- **Fermented Foods**: Foods made through desired microbial growth and enzymatic conversions of food components (not required to have live microbes characterized to strain level or evidence of health benefit; may have improved taste, digestibility, safety, and nutritional value).

All definitions were published in *Nature Reviews Gastroenterology and Hepatology* (NRGH) and are among the top most viewed articles on the NRGH website.
</summary>

The International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics (ISAPP) published an Expert Recommendation on October 2, 2024, in *Nature Reviews Gastroenterology and Hepatology* titled "Classifying compounds as prebiotics—scientific perspectives and recommendations." The paper reinforces the 2017 ISAPP definition of prebiotic: "a substrate that is selectively utilized by host microorganisms conferring a health benefit." It delineates specific criteria for establishing prebiotic status.

Key criteria include: the substance must be a substrate utilized by host microorganisms; must be sufficiently characterized; must be selectively utilized by the host microbiota (demonstrated through reproducible and specific changes in composition or function); must show a demonstrated health benefit via well-controlled studies (typically RCTs) in the target population; must have a hypothesis for how microbiome modulation leads to the health benefit; the health benefit and selective utilization must be demonstrated in the same study (though causal proof is not required); must be safe for intended use; should have confirmatory evidence beyond minimum requirements; and must be administered at a dose shown to elicit both the health benefit and selective utilization.

The paper addresses the challenge of defining selectivity, noting that the complexity of microbiota makes quantification difficult. It emphasizes that prebiotic-induced health benefits should derive from microbiome modulation, and while causality studies are not required for prebiotic status, they are encouraged through methods including database mining, in silico screening, in vitro/in vivo tracking, machine learning, AI, and animal models.

The paper was co-authored by Prof. Bob Hutkins, Prof. Karen Scott, and others. ISAPP also developed a companion prebiotic evidence checklist. The authors note that consumer awareness varies: 18% of Americans have never heard of prebiotics, while 22% are familiar with and actively try to consume them.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Fusobacterium nucleatum promotes colorectal carcinogenesis by modulating E-cadherin/β-catenin signaling via its FadA adhesin ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3770529

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This study published in Cell Host & Microbe (2013) demonstrates that Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn) promotes colorectal carcinogenesis through its FadA adhesin by binding to E-cadherin and activating β-catenin signaling. 

Key findings: Fn adheres to and invades colorectal cancer (CRC) cells via FadA binding to E-cadherin. The binding site is mapped to an 11-amino acid region (ASANWTIQYND) in the EC5 domain of E-cadherin. A synthetic inhibitory peptide derived from this region abolishes FadA-induced CRC cell growth.

FadA binding leads to E-cadherin phosphorylation, β-catenin accumulation in the cytoplasm and translocation to the nucleus, activating β-catenin-regulated transcription (CRT) including LEF/TCF, NF-κB, Myc, and Cyclin D1. Tumor growth and inflammatory responses are differentially regulated: while both require β-catenin, Fn invasion (mediated by clathrin) is required for inflammatory gene activation but not for oncogenic signaling.

In human colon tissue specimens, FadA gene levels were >10-100 times higher in patients with adenomas and adenocarcinomas compared to normal individuals, with a stepwise increase from normal to precancerous to cancerous tissues. In xenograft mouse models, FadAc and wild-type Fn stimulated tumor growth, which was prevented by the inhibitory peptide.

The study identifies FadA as a potential diagnostic marker and therapeutic target for CRC. The authors propose that Fn colonization of normal tissues may predispose hosts to adenoma/adenocarcinoma development, with carcinogenesis accelerating when a mutation occurs.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn) has been associated with colorectal cancer (CRC), but causality and underlying mechanisms remain to be established. We demonstrate that Fn adheres to, invades and induces oncogenic and inflammatory responses to stimulate growth of CRC cells through its unique FadA adhesin.", "FadA binds to E-cadherin, activates β-catenin signaling, and differentially regulates the inflammatory and oncogenic responses.", "FadA levels in the colon tissue from patients with adenomas and adenocarcinomas is >10–100 times higher compared to normal individuals.", "A synthetic peptide derived from this region of E-cadherin abolishes FadA-induced CRC cell growth, and oncogenic and inflammatory responses.", "This study unveils a mechanism by which Fn can drive CRC and identifies FadA as a potential diagnostic and therapeutic target for CRC."

--- SOURCE 2: Frontiers | Fusobacterium nucleatum and colorectal cancer: From phenomenon to mechanism ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/cellular-and-infection-microbiology/articles/10.3389/fcimb.2022.1020583/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This review article (published November 29, 2022 in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology) comprehensively examines the role of Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn) in colorectal cancer (CRC) from phenomenon to mechanism. Key findings include:

**Distribution & Timing:** Fn is enriched in adenomas and CRC tissues compared to normal tissue, with abundance increasing with cancer progression. Fn is more prevalent in right-sided CRC (proximal colon > distal colon > rectum) and is associated with molecular features including MSI-H, CIMP-H, BRAF mutation, and CMS1 subtype.

**Colonization & Origin:** Fn cannot stably colonize normal guts with complex microbiota; it requires mucosal disruption or inflammation. Fn originates from the oral cavity and translocates to CRC via two routes: oral cavity-circulatory system-CRC, and oral cavity-alimentary tract-CRC.

**Tropism Mechanisms:** Fn's tropism to CRC is mediated by Fap2 protein binding to Gal-GalNAc (highly expressed in CRC cells) and FadAc adhesin binding to E-cadherin.

**Tumorigenesis:** Fn does not directly induce oncogenic mutations but promotes tumorigenesis only in the presence of pre-existing genetic defects or carcinogens. Fn-induced inflammation and tumorigenesis may be dose-dependent.

**Proliferation & Metastasis:** Fn accelerates CRC proliferation through TLR4/MYD88/NF-κB, Wnt/β-catenin, and PAK1 signaling pathways. Fn promotes metastasis via cytokine secretion (CXCL1, IL-8, CCL20), exosome-mediated signaling, EMT activation, autophagy induction, and enhanced vascular permeability.

**Stemness:** Fn enhances CRC stemness by promoting fatty acid oxidation (in CCSCs) and lipid accumulation (in non-CCSCs), activating Notch signaling via Numb degradation.

**Metabolic Reprogramming:** Fn promotes glycolysis via upregulating ENO1 and ANGPTL4, and regulates lipid metabolism via CYP2J2 and the TLR4/AKT/Keap1/NRF2 pathway.

**Immune Microenvironment:** Fn induces M2 macrophage polarization (via TLR4/IL-6/p-STAT3/c-Myc and NF-κB/S100A9), expands MDSCs, suppresses T cell and NK cell activity via Fap2-TIGIT and CbpF-CEACAM1 interactions, and upregulates PD-L1 expression.

**Treatment Implications:** The review discusses strategies for CRC prevention and treatment targeting Fn, including anti-Fn approaches.

Analysis of 9089 E. coli genomes revealed that pks+ B2 phylogroup strains have significantly increased trinucleotide skewness (bias toward ATA/TAT over AAA/TTT), indicating an evolutionary footprint of self-inflicted damage.

The study concludes that colibactin produces a bacteria-specific mutation pattern different from mammalian cells, and that the resistance protein encoded on the pks island is insufficient to prevent self-inflicted DNA damage. The colibactin-associated mutational bias could potentially serve as a noninvasive method to estimate colibactin exposure in individuals harboring pks+ strains (20-30% of healthy individuals, ~60% of colorectal cancer patients).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 21: The controversial role of Enterococcus faecalis in colorectal cancer ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6044108

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in Therapeutic Advances in Gastroenterology (2018) examining the controversial role of Enterococcus faecalis in colorectal cancer (CRC). CRC is the third most frequent cancer worldwide, with only 15% of cases having a genetic background, while 85% are sporadic and linked to environmental factors including diet, lifestyle, and gut microbiota composition.

The gut microbiota plays a crucial role in maintaining intestinal homeostasis, but dysbiosis can contribute to CRC development through chronic inflammation, DNA damage, and immune system modulation. The "bacterial driver-passenger" model proposes that certain bacteria (drivers) cause DNA damage initiating cancer, while tumor microenvironment changes favor opportunistic bacteria (passengers).

E. faecalis is a Gram-positive, facultative anaerobic commensal bacterium that is a member of lactic acid bacteria. It colonizes the human GI tract early in life and is commonly used as a probiotic and in food fermentation. However, its role in CRC is controversial:

**Harmful effects:** E. faecalis can generate ROS and extracellular superoxide that damage colonic epithelial cell DNA, produce metalloprotease that compromises the intestinal epithelial barrier, and activate macrophage MMP-9. Some studies found increased fecal E. faecalis in CRC patients compared to healthy controls.

**Protective effects:** E. faecalis can induce IL-10 expression, attenuate proinflammatory cytokines like IL-8, suppress Th1 and Th17 responses, and some strains (e.g., EC-12, CECT7121) show antitumor properties by suppressing β-catenin signaling, inducing apoptosis in cancer cells, and enhancing immune responses.

The authors suggest that the conflicting roles may be attributed to different strains of E. faecalis, as horizontal gene transfer can lead to mutations that alter virulence. They propose that E. faecalis likely acts as a "passenger" bacterium in CRC rather than a "driver" — it may become pathogenic only when the intestinal environment undergoes alterations (such as those caused by tumorigenesis), allowing uncontrolled growth and potential acquisition of virulence factors. The authors call for more detailed investigation of E. faecalis under different experimental conditions given its widespread use in food manufacturing and as a probiotic.
</summary>

## Abstract

Growing evidence indicates that the gut microbiota is a central regulator of systemic immunity, acting through epithelial barrier integrity, microbial metabolites, and bidirectional signaling with innate and adaptive immune cells. Within this framework, probiotics have attracted substantial interest as tools for immune modulation; however, their effects are not uniform and should not be generalized across species or formulations. This review synthesizes current evidence on the gut microbiota–immune axis and examines how defined probiotic strains influence immune homeostasis, inflammation, and clinical outcomes. Particular emphasis is placed on strain-specific effects among lactic acid bacteria, bifidobacteria, yeast probiotics, and emerging nontraditional candidates, with attention to mechanisms involving cytokine signaling, regulatory T-cell induction, nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) modulation, toll-like receptor (TLR) pathways, short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), tryptophan metabolites, and bile-acid-dependent signaling. The available literature indicates that the most meaningful immunological effects arise from precisely characterized strains acting in specific host contexts, whereas inconsistent trial design, small sample sizes, variable dosing, and poor strain resolution continue to limit translation. Overall, current data support a shift from generic probiotic use toward mechanism-based, strain-specific, and increasingly personalized strategies for immune modulation.
