## 1. Introduction

Cancer is a complicated group of disorders characterised by aberrant cell proliferation, which can have lethal effects on human health [[1](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B1-biomolecules-15-00879),[2](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B2-biomolecules-15-00879)]. To decrease the worldwide cancer burden, ongoing research and improvements in prevention, initial detection, and treatment are required [[3](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B3-biomolecules-15-00879),[4](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B4-biomolecules-15-00879)]. In most of the countries across the world, cancer is the leading cause of death [[5](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B5-biomolecules-15-00879)]. By the year 2040, it is anticipated that cancer will be the cause of the deaths of around 16.3 million people [[6](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B6-biomolecules-15-00879)]. Significantly, the level of social and economic development in a nation has a major impact on the incidence, prevalence, risk factors, and death rates associated with cancer [[3](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B3-biomolecules-15-00879),[4](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B4-biomolecules-15-00879),[7](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B7-biomolecules-15-00879)]. Nearly 60% of the world’s population lives in Asia, where there are currently half of all cases and 58.3% of cancer-related deaths. Despite making up less than 10% of the world’s population, Europe is responsible for nearly one fifth of cancer cases and fatalities [[4](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B4-biomolecules-15-00879),[8](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B8-biomolecules-15-00879)].

Probiotics are defined as live microorganisms that, when administered in adequate amounts, confer a health benefit on the host [[9](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B9-biomolecules-15-00879),[10](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B10-biomolecules-15-00879),[11](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B11-biomolecules-15-00879),[12](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B12-biomolecules-15-00879)]. Probiotics have drawn a lot of curiosity regarding cancer in recent years, especially because of their potential to regulate the immune system and beneficial effects with anticancer activity [[13](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B13-biomolecules-15-00879)]. The gut microbiome, a complex and diverse microbial community found in the human gut, plays an essential role in general health ([Figure 1](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#fig_body_display_biomolecules-15-00879-f001)) [[14](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B14-biomolecules-15-00879)]. Probiotics have the potential to aid in the maintenance of a balanced and healthy gut microbiome, which is important for many physiological functions and essential for preserving overall health, with an impact on the treatment of cancer [[15](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B15-biomolecules-15-00879),[16](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B16-biomolecules-15-00879),[17](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B17-biomolecules-15-00879)]. Within the scientific field of probiotics, the genus Lactobacillus has been the subject of the most extensive research. Modern taxonomic revisions have divided Lactobacillus into 25 genera, improving our understanding of their functional diversity. The reclassification emphasises the need for precision in probiotic studies, particularly regarding anticancer implications [[18](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B18-biomolecules-15-00879),[19](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B19-biomolecules-15-00879)]. This review examines the unique effects and mechanisms of probiotic strains in relation to various cancer types, along with safety precautions that may make them a viable adjunct therapy agent for cancer treatment and prevention.

![Image 20: Biomolecules 15 00879 g001](https://www.mdpi.com/biomolecules/biomolecules-15-00879/article_deploy/html/images/biomolecules-15-00879-g001-550.jpg)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#fig_body_display_biomolecules-15-00879-f001)

**Figure 1.** Exploring the various health promoting effects of probiotics, such as anticancer, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antiviral, antifungal, antibacterial, cardioprotective, hepatoprotective, health-promoting. 

## 2. Anticancer Mechanisms of Probiotics

Probiotics are receiving consideration due to their potential anticancer properties through multiple types of mechanisms of action. Below are some key ways that probiotics can help prevent and treat cancer [[20](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B20-biomolecules-15-00879),[21](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B21-biomolecules-15-00879),[22](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B22-biomolecules-15-00879),[23](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B23-biomolecules-15-00879)].

### 2.1. Modulation of the Gastrointestinal Microbiota

One of the primary mechanisms by which probiotics can protect against the development of cancer is the modulation of the gastrointestinal microbiome [[15](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B15-biomolecules-15-00879),[24](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B24-biomolecules-15-00879)]. The growth of pathogenic bacteria such as Clostridium difficile, Escherichia coli (E.coli), and Fusobacterium nucleatum can be selectively inhibited by probiotics, as they have been associated with an elevated risk of certain varieties of cancer [[25](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B25-biomolecules-15-00879),[26](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B26-biomolecules-15-00879),[27](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B27-biomolecules-15-00879)]. Bacteriocins, organic acids, and hydrogen peroxide are some of the antimicrobial substances that are produced by probiotics in order to accomplish this goal. These substances have the potential to effectively restrict the growth of hazardous microbes [[28](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B28-biomolecules-15-00879),[29](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B29-biomolecules-15-00879)]. Moreover, probiotics exhibit a significant role in preventing the growth of these pathogenic microbes by maintaining balance, differentiating the gut microbiome, and decreasing the probability of developing cancer. The metabolism of dietary ingredients, for instance, nitrosamines and bile acids, can change carcinogenic compounds [[30](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B30-biomolecules-15-00879)]. Probiotics exhibit a significant role in decreasing carcinogenic substances in the body through regulating the enzymes involved in metabolic conversion [[31](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B31-biomolecules-15-00879),[32](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B32-biomolecules-15-00879)]. Probiotics, which include species of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, have the potential to prevent secondary bile acid production, which has been associated with developing colorectal cancer [[23](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B23-biomolecules-15-00879),[33](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B33-biomolecules-15-00879)].

The natural gut–liver axis balance can be recovered through probiotics application [[34](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B34-biomolecules-15-00879),[35](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B35-biomolecules-15-00879)]. This is achieved through regulating the metabolism of bile acid, decreasing the levels of oxidative stress, and modifying the genes expression in liver cancer. Furthermore, probiotics can enhance the production of tight junction proteins such as occludin as well as claudins, improving the intestinal epithelial barrier. This barrier is crucial for controlling the passage of harmful substances, including carcinogens, from the intestinal lumen into the body [[36](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B36-biomolecules-15-00879),[37](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B37-biomolecules-15-00879)]. They are a potential substance for maintaining the function of intestinal barrier system. Through improving intestinal barrier integrity, probiotics can reduce the host’s interaction with carcinogenic substances and prevent the systemic intake of these substances. Probiotics have the power to change the microbiome of the gut, which may help prevent and treat several types of cancer [[38](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B38-biomolecules-15-00879)]. Various anticancer mechanisms through modulation of the gastrointestinal microbiota can be seen in [Figure 2](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#fig_body_display_biomolecules-15-00879-f002).

![Image 21: Biomolecules 15 00879 g002](https://www.mdpi.com/biomolecules/biomolecules-15-00879/article_deploy/html/images/biomolecules-15-00879-g002-550.jpg)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#fig_body_display_biomolecules-15-00879-f002)

**Figure 2.** Probiotics anticancer mechanisms exhibited through modulation of gastrointestinal microbiota, such as strengthening gut barrier integrity, immune modulation of the gut microbiome, inhibition of carcinogenic pathways, production of anticancer metabolites, and restoration of microbiota balance. 

The composition of the baseline gut microbiota is a significant factor in influencing the efficacy of probiotics. Individual responses to probiotic treatment can be prominently influenced by alterations in the metabolic functions, microbiome diversity, and microbial taxa [[39](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B39-biomolecules-15-00879),[40](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B40-biomolecules-15-00879),[41](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B41-biomolecules-15-00879)]. Better health outcomes are typically linked to greater microbial diversity. Probiotics may be more valuable for patients with a diversified microbiome since it can strengthened with supplementation of the preexisting microbial populations [[42](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B42-biomolecules-15-00879)]. In one study, the baseline microbiome in postmenopausal women with obesity did not predict the therapeutic response to multispecies probiotics despite the fact that probiotics application did change the functional influence of the microbiota on metabolic markers [[41](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B41-biomolecules-15-00879)]. The global microbiome variety and composition in healthy children remained relatively stable despite probiotic administration increasing the abundance of the supplemented strains. This suggests that baseline health status and microbiome stability may restrict the observable benefit of probiotics [[42](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B42-biomolecules-15-00879),[43](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B43-biomolecules-15-00879)]. The composition of the microbiome can be further modulated by age, diet, and health state, which can affect the effectiveness of probiotics. Certain patient populations may benefit from probiotic therapies that are customised depending on these baseline traits [[44](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B44-biomolecules-15-00879)]. While the concept of personalising probiotic treatments by considering patient-specific characteristics such as diets, genetics, and comorbidities is a matter of consideration; nevertheless, the present preclinical and clinical practice is not yet proficient at fully implementing this strategy. The most compelling evidence suggests tailoring treatment to the specific strain of probiotics and the various disease types under treatment. Even though there are studies that acknowledge factors such as obesity, diabetes, and dietary intake (for example, milk and yoghurt) as having an impact on the efficacy of probiotics, these factors have been considered in subgroup studies rather than as part of a personalised regimen [[45](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B45-biomolecules-15-00879),[46](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B46-biomolecules-15-00879),[47](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B47-biomolecules-15-00879)].

### 2.2. Inhibition of the Metabolism of Carcinogenic Substances

Probiotics can establish an intestinal environment that is less favourable to the onset and spread of cancer by focusing on a variety of pathways [[48](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B48-biomolecules-15-00879)]. One of the primary ways that probiotics can help prevent the development of cancer is by blocking the metabolism of carcinogens [[49](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B49-biomolecules-15-00879),[50](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B50-biomolecules-15-00879)]. Some gut bacteria have enzymes that can break down environmental pollutants and food ingredients into compounds that cause cancer, like nitrosamines, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, and heterocyclic amines [[51](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B51-biomolecules-15-00879),[52](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B52-biomolecules-15-00879)]. The activity of these bacterial enzymes can be inhibited by probiotics such as Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium species, which reduce the conversion of these compounds into their carcinogenic forms [[53](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B53-biomolecules-15-00879),[54](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B54-biomolecules-15-00879)]. Lactobacillus acidophilus (L. acidophilus), for instance, has been demonstrated to impede the function of bacterial nitroreductases, which are responsible for transforming nitrosamines into more potent carcinogens [[55](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B55-biomolecules-15-00879),[56](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B56-biomolecules-15-00879),[57](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B57-biomolecules-15-00879)]. Probiotics have the ability to affect the host enzyme activity involved in the metabolism of carcinogens. Lactobacillus rhamnosus (L. rhamnosus) and Bifidobacterium probiotic strains that have been shown to upregulate the expression of phase II detoxification enzymes, which are in charge of conjugating and excreting carcinogens [[54](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B54-biomolecules-15-00879)]. These enzymes comprise glutathione S-transferases and UDP-glucuronosyltransferases. Through boosting the ability of the host to metabolise and remove carcinogens, probiotics have the potential to reduce the risk that carcinogens may either cause or accelerate the growth of cancer [[58](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B58-biomolecules-15-00879)].

Heterocyclic amines and secondary bile acids are two examples of foods that can be transformed into carcinogenic metabolites. These metabolites are produced by particular bacteria that live in the gut. Probiotics have the ability to change the composition of the gut microbiome as well as its metabolism, which in turn reduces the production of compounds that are poisonous to the body [[59](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B59-biomolecules-15-00879),[60](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B60-biomolecules-15-00879)]. Lactobacillus and  Bifidobacterium species have been demonstrated to impede the process of the 7α-dehydroxylation of primary bile acids. This is one of the most important steps in the production of secondary bile acids, which have been associated with an increased probability of developing colorectal cancer [[61](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B61-biomolecules-15-00879),[62](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B62-biomolecules-15-00879)]. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), such as butyrate, acetate, and propionate, exert activities that inhibit the development of cancer. The production of these SCFAs can be increased by the use of probiotics [[63](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B63-biomolecules-15-00879),[64](https://www.mdpi.com/2218-273X/15/6/879#B64-biomolecules-15-00879)]. args.summary: This is a webpage for an open-access review article titled "Probiotics and Cancer: Mechanistic Insights and Organ-Specific Impact," published in the journal *Biomolecules* (Volume 15, Issue 6, 879) on June 16, 2025. The article is authored by Md Faruque Ahmad and colleagues from multiple institutions in Saudi Arabia and India. It presents a comprehensive review of how probiotics modulate the gut microbiome to impact various cancers, including oesophageal, lung, liver, and colorectal cancer. Key mechanisms discussed include modulation of the gastrointestinal microbiota (e.g., inhibiting pathogenic bacteria, enhancing gut barrier integrity, and regulating bile acid metabolism), inhibition of carcinogen metabolism (e.g., reducing bacterial enzyme activity that converts compounds into carcinogens, upregulating phase II detoxification enzymes), and production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) like butyrate that inhibit cancer development. The review also highlights the importance of baseline gut microbiota composition in influencing probiotic efficacy, notes that the genus Lactobacillus has been most extensively researched (with recent taxonomic revisions splitting it into 25 genera), and discusses the potential for probiotics as a complementary approach in cancer management. The article covers protective effects against chemotherapy-induced toxicity and emphasizes that while probiotics show promise, further clinical trials are needed to fully understand the relationships between cancer and probiotics.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384)Abstract

Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most diagnosed cancer and the second leading cause of morbidity worldwide. In Algeria, it ranks second in mortality-related deaths. Poor lifestyle, characterized by a low-fiber diet, insufficient physical activity, tobacco use, and alcohol consumption, is strongly associated with an increased risk of developing this disease. Probiotics have demonstrated anti-inflammatory and antitumor effects in preclinical and clinical studies. The World Health Organization (WHO) and European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) have recognized their safety and effectiveness, classifying them as Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) and Qualified Presumption of Safety (QPS), respectively. Probiotics exhibit immunomodulatory effects and maintain the equilibrium of the gut microbiota. However, the evidence for their clinical efficacy is inadequate, and additional research is requisite to establish them as therapeutic agents rather than simply as dietary supplements. Although probiotics are, in most cases, safe, high-risk patients should exercise caution due to the potential risk of infection. This review examines the current knowledge on probiotic strains, their therapeutic potential for colorectal cancer, limitations, and areas where further research is imperative to improve their efficacy.

**Keywords:**Colorectal cancer, Probiotics, Inflammation, Microbiome, Safety, Efficacy

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384)Introduction

Colorectal cancer ranks as the third most commonly diagnosed cancer globally and stands as the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths. Its prevalence is notably higher among men compared to women [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR1)]. In Algeria, colorectal cancer ranked as the second most prevalent cancer in 2020, following breast cancer [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR2)]. Similarly, colorectal cancer affects men more than women in Algeria, mirroring global trends [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR3)]. Moreover, emerging data underscores that colorectal cancer is the most frequently occurring cancer among Algerian men, with 14.2 new cases per 100,000 men [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR4)].

A diet heavy in animal proteins, especially meat that is red or processed, and poor in fiber is linked to an increased risk of colon cancer [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR5)]. Three main risk factors—adopting a "Western" lifestyle instead of a balanced diet high in fruits and vegetables, heavy tobacco use, and little to no vigorous physical activity—are responsible for the rising incidence of colorectal cancer in emerging nations, especially Algeria [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR4), [5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR5)].

The gut microbiota influences intestinal inflammation through intricate molecular interactions, particularly via Toll-like receptors (TLRs), which are key pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR6)]. TLRs detect microbial components such as lipopolysaccharides and flagellins, triggering signaling pathways that regulate immune responses. In a balanced microbiome, TLR activation supports epithelial barrier function and immune tolerance by enhancing mucosal defense mechanisms [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR6)]. Conversely, microbial dysbiosis leads to aberrant TLR signaling, excessive cytokine production, and immune cell infiltration, perpetuating inflammation and increasing susceptibility to colorectal cancer.

Current treatments for CRC include a combination of chemotherapy, surgery, molecular-targeted therapy, and immunotherapy [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR7)]. The most prevalent treatment is a combination of surgery (colectomy) and chemotherapy with 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR6)]. However, there are now more targeted chemotherapeutic regimens that comprise different agents, such as cetuximab and bevacizumab [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR7)]. This combination has some adverse effects and complications, for instance, postoperative infection [[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR8)] and chemotherapy-induced diarrhea (CID) [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR9)]. Furthermore, low Quality of Life (QoL), depression, and anxiety are associated with lower long-term survival [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR10)].

Probiotics are defined as “Live microorganisms that, when administered in adequate amounts, confer health benefits on the host”. This definition was established by the Joint The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations/World Health Organization (FAO/WHO), Expert Consultation on Evaluation of Health and Nutritional Properties of Probiotics in Food [[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR11)]. They have been studied extensively, especially _Lactobacillus_ and _Bifidobacterium_ [[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR12)], and their safety as dietary supplements has already been defined [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR13)].

Probiotics have exhibited beneficial health effects, such as immunomodulation [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR14)], antioxidant activity [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR15)], antagonism against known pathogenic species through competition for resources and space [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR16)], exclusion by adhesion to the mucosal barrier [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR17)], and production of antimicrobial compounds such as bacteriocins [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR18)]. They have also been shown to exhibit anticarcinogenic activities in vitro [[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR19)] and in vivo [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR20)]. Furthermore, their anti-inflammation activity [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR21)] and maintenance of the mucosal barrier have been demonstrated [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR17)]. These functional qualities are linked directly or indirectly to CRC, making probiotics a suitable adjuvant therapy for colorectal cancer.

Lactic Acid Bacteria (LAB) constitute a group of bacteria that produce lactic acid as the major end product in the fermentation of carbohydrates [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR22)]. It encompasses various genera of probiotic bacteria, including _Lactobacillus_, _Enterococcus_, _Lactococcus_, and _Pediococcus_, among others [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR23)]. _Bifidobacterium_ and _Saccharomyces_ are two additional groups that provide a source of probiotic strains. These three groups have demonstrated promising health effects that can be beneficial in the context of CRC [[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR24)–[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR26)]. Their therapeutic properties have been substantiated in both preclinical and clinical studies [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR27), [28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR28)].

The purpose of this review is to bring together the current knowledge on probiotics regarding their efficacy and safety profile in the context of colorectal cancer. Furthermore, we will explore the potential of these probiotic strains on the psychological well-being of the populations affected by CRC.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384)Colorectal cancer tumorigenesis

The accumulation of sequential mutations in colonic tissues leads to the development of adenomas and carcinomas, known as the adenoma-carcinoma sequence, which accentuates the importance of genetic damage in the process of carcinogenesis [[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR29)]. After the tumor forms, the localized inflammatory micro-environment can promote the accumulation of additional mutations and epigenetic changes via the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive nitrogen intermediates (RNI), as well as pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, which induces more DNA damage and mutation [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR30)].

Environmental factors are more likely to be the cause of CRC than hereditary factors, such as diet,’Western’ lifestyle, specific commensal and pathogens bacteria, and chronic intestinal inflammation [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR30)]. Chronic inflammation is associated with the occurrence and progression of colorectal cancer. Poorly treated Inflammatory bowel disease, and chronic inflammation in the gastrointestinal tract induced by poor lifestyle habits are major risk factors for the development of CRC [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR31), [32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR32)]. Tumor development goes through three phases: initiation, promotion, and then progression.

### Tumor initiation

A tumor-initiating event is required through the accumulation of genetic mutations either by activation of oncogenes or inactivation of tumor-suppressing genes. Mutation can be spontaneous, environmental, or via inflammation [[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR33)]. Inflammation via DNA damage in intestinal epithelial cells, can cause mutation in genes associated with CRC via the production of ROS or reactive nitrogen species (RNS) without any extrinsic factors and thus initiate tumor development [[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR34), [35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR35)].

Sporadic CRC is caused by the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) mutation and inactivation or β-catenin activation which drives the hyperactivation of Wnt, a portmanteau of _Wingless_ and _Int_, signaling pathway which is necessary for the progression from pre-neoplastic cells to aberrant crypt foci and therefore initiation of most CRCs [[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR36), [37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR37)]. Inflammation, via the activation of several cytokine-mediated signaling pathways involved in CRC initiation and promotion notably NF-κB, Akt, TNF, and IL-1 receptor signaling, pushes for β-catenin activation and therefore CRC development [[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR38), [39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR39)].

Environmental factors, such as diet, pollution, and exposure to carcinogens are an equally profound contributor of CRC mutations. For instance, diets high in red or processed meats, low in fiber, and rich in saturated fats increases susceptibility to CRC by promoting oxidative stress and inflammation [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR5)]. More importantly, environmental pollutants, such as air and water contaminants, can yield reactive species that alter the DNA causing mutations that to tumor development. These environmental exposures, when combined with genetic susceptibility, create a complex interplay of factors that drive colorectal carcinogenesis.

Epigenetic alteration of CRC-related genes is mediated through inflammation via the attenuation of tumor suppressor genes [[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR40)]. Chronic inflammation promotes the production of prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) via COX1 and COX2 (Cyclooxygenases) dependent pathways, which induces the expression of DNA methyltransferases DNMT1 and DNMT3B and activates NF-κB signaling [[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR41)]. The cytokines IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF regulate the expression of these enzymes thereby shaping the DNA methylation expression patterns of genes such as NOTCH and p53 [[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR42)]. This cascade promotes tumor initiation, growth, and expansion. Additionally, activation of the receptor EP2 by prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) increases β-catenin nuclear accumulation and transcriptional activity [[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR43)].

#### Toll-like receptors

Toll-like receptors (TLR) are activated in tumorigenesis by commensal and pathogenic bacteria present in the gut or by therapy-induced tumor cell death [[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR44)]. Inflammation can affect epithelial function which allows commensal, pathogenic bacteria, or their products, such as lipopolysaccharide (LPS), which are elements of the surface of gram-negative bacteria, to enter the tumor microenvironment (TME) and induce myeloid cells to invade TME which produce pro-inflammatory cytokines and further promote tumorigenesis [[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR33), [45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR45)]. LPS has been shown to induce an inflammatory response in macrophage cell lines and human colon cancer cells in vitro [[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR46)]. Several studies have shown that LPS leaks through the gut barrier in stress-induced rodents, which stimulates TLRs, notably TLR4, which then results in the generation of inflammatory cytokines down the line [[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR47)]. LPS is a cell wall element of gram-negative bacteria, TLR4 knockout mice have been found to not respond to gram-negative bacteria [[48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR48)]. _Fusobacterium nucleatum_ is a commensal gram-negative bacterium, CRC tissues are enriched with this species and correlate with a worse prognosis [[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR49)]. By promoting the proliferation of CRC cells and colonic tumorigenesis via the activation of TLR4 signaling to NF-κB, _F. nucleatum_ has become the prominent bacterium in CRC fecal and mucosa-associated microbiota [[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR50), [51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR51)]. The role of _Fusobacterium nucleatum_ in colorectal cancer (CRC) stems primarily from its capacity to influence the tumor microenvironment (TME) by promoting immune evasion, inflammation, and the proliferation of cancer cells [[52](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR52)]. One central mechanism is the activation of Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4), which initiates NF-κB signaling pathways [[52](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR52)]. This cascade results in the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, creating an inflammatory environment conducive to tumor development.

Therapy-induced tumor cell death, via radiotherapy and chemotherapy, can also activate TLR via damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) which recruit and activate antigen-presenting cells (APCs) [[53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR53), [54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR54)]. APCs produce tumor-producing cytokines, such as TNF and IL-6, which then activate the IκB kinase (IKK) complex, this complex activates NF-αB via the phosphorylation of IκB that binds to NF-αB [[55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR55), [56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR56)]. Chemotherapy can cause mucositis and intestinal injury by monocytes that generate chemokines like IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α in response to Reactive Oxygen Intermediates (ROI) generated through the activation of NF-κB through TLRs [[57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR57)]. This cascade promotes tumorigenesis and anti-tumor immunity [[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR33)].

#### Apoptosis

Inflammation can induce anti-apoptotic effects via the production of cytokine IL-6 which activates STAT3 and stimulates the expression of anti-apoptotic genes such as Bcl2 and Bcl-xL [[58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR58), [59](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR59)]. Additionally, STAT3 regulates the cell cycle via proliferative genes like cyclin D1 and c-Myc [[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR54)]. NF-αB also has an anti-apoptotic activity mediated via the activation of Bcl2, Bcl-xL, and cFLIP (regulates the extrinsic apoptosis pathway) [[60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR60)]. The pro-tumorigenic activity of COX2 and PEG2 is mediated through the inhibition of apoptosis by up-regulating the expression of Bcl2 via MAPK [[61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR61)].

### Tumor promotion

Tumor promotion refers to the process by which genetically altered pre-cancerous cells, such as those found in aberrant crypt foci, undergo further modifications to benign tumors like adenomas, which gradually evolve into malignant cancers (carcinomas) [[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR33)]. Inflammation via pro-inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors, plays a crucial role in the growth and survival of tumors by promoting angiogenesis and suppressing the immune-mediated tumor elimination response. The tumor micro-environment can also stimulate inflammation via cytokines and growth factors, creating a feedback loop that promotes the further progression of tumors [[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR33)]. These cytokines include but are not limited to TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1, while some others inhibit tumorigenesis such as IL-10 and Transforming Growth Factor beta (TGF-β) [[62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR62)–[65](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR65)].

Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) and microRNA-34 (miR-34) have been implicated in CRC pathogenesis through various mechanisms. Studies have shown that PPARγ is downregulated in CRC tissues [[66](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR66)], and hypermethylation of its gene promoter is associated with CRC development [[67](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR67)]. PPARγ exerts its tumor-suppressive effects through multiple pathways. It inhibits NFκB-mediated gene transcription [[68](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR68)], thereby reducing the expression of target genes that confer growth advantages and chemotherapy resistance. Additionally, PPARγ interferes with the APC/β-catenin [[69](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR69)] and COX-2/ PGE2 signaling pathways [[70](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR70)], both of which play crucial roles in colon carcinogenesis.

MicroRNAs (miRNAs), small non-coding RNAs, regulate gene expression and are critical in cancer development. In (CRC), miR-21 plays an integral function as an oncogene, often overexpressed to promote tumor growth and resistance to treatment by targeting tumor suppressors like _PTEN_ and _PDCD4_ [[71](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR71)]. On the other hand, miR-34, a tumor suppressor activated by p53, inhibits the Wnt/β-catenin pathway by downregulating β-catenin [[71](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR71)]. Loss of miR-34, due to genetic or epigenetic changes, can bypass p53’s tumor-suppressing effects, driving tumor progression. These contrasting roles highlight the complex miRNA involvement in CRC.

In parallel, miR-34 serves as a key downstream target of p53, a well-known tumor suppressor. Upon activation, p53 directly binds to the promoter regions of the miR-34a and miR-34b/c genes, inducing their transcription. In addition to its role as a key downstream target of p53, miR-34a is a short non-coding regulatory RNA that functions as a tumor suppressor by inhibiting the post-transcriptional expression of multiple proto-oncogenes. This regulation impedes cell proliferation pathways that are essential for tumor growth [[72](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR72)]. MiR-34 also functions as an effector of p53, mediating its tumor-suppressing activities. Notably, in the context of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway, miR-34 suppresses the expression of β-catenin. The loss of miR-34, either through chromosomal deletion or epigenetic silencing, can lead to Wnt signaling activation independent of p53 mutations. This allows cancer cells to circumvent p53's tumor-suppressing functions while activating pathways that drive cancer progression [[73](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR73)].

Interestingly, both PPARγ and miR-34 converge on the regulation of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway, a key driver of colorectal carcinogenesis. While miR-34 directly suppresses β-catenin expression, PPARγ interferes with the APC/β-catenin signaling axis. This dual inhibition suggests a potentially synergistic tumor-suppressive effect in CRC.

### Tumor progression and metastasis

In later stages of cancer, inflammation can still be a major factor in tumor progression from adenoma to carcinoma and then metastasis. Inactivation of p53 via mutation in the TP53 gene in advanced stages of colorectal cancer hinders epithelial integrity and leads to the microbial activation of NF-αB and STAT3 [[74](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR74)]. NF-αB and STAT3 facilitate the migration and invasion of pre-metastatic cells [[75](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR75)]. Downstream pro-inflammatory cytokines, particularly IL-6 and IL-11, are associated with the promotion of metastasis via the regulation of Trefoil factor family 3 (Tff3) [[76](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR76)]. Chemokines stimulate migration toward the blood vessels, whereas TNF increases vascular permeability and facilitates the proliferation of metastatic colon cancer cells [[77](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR77), [78](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR78)]. Additionally, COX2 is required for the transition from adenoma to carcinoma via the action PGE2 [[79](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR79)].

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384)Probiotics and the gut microbiome

The gut microbiota is a diverse and complex ecosystem of a myriad of microorganisms ranging from bacteria, fungi, archaea, and even viruses. This ecosystem consists of bacteria (which make up the majority), fungi, archaea, and viruses. The four most frequently found bacterial phyla in the gut are Actinomycetes 2%, Bacillota (formerly known as Firmicutes) 53.9%, Bacteroidetes 35.4%, and Proteobacteria 4.5%. Other less prevalent phyla include Actinobacteria and Verrucomicrobia [[80](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR80), [81](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR81)]. For fungi, the most common genera are _Candida_, _Saccharomyces_, and _Aspergillus_. For the virome, bacteriophages are the most identified, but some studies have also highlighted the presence of giant viruses [[82](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR82)]. Finally, for the archaeome, the most common species are _Methanobrevibacter smithii_ and _Methanosphaera stadtmanae_ [[83](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR83)].

During adulthood, the composition, diversity, and abundance of the gut microbiome tend to stabilize [[84](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR84)]. The composition of the adult microbiota is predominantly shaped during infancy, with delivery mode (vaginal or cesarean), feeding practices (breastfeeding or formula), and antibiotic usage in the duration of pregnancy and the early years of infancy, emerging as pivotal determinants [[84](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR84)]. Antibiotic usage during pregnancy and infancy has been associated with the development of childhood obesity [[85](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR85), [86](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR86)].

Nevertheless, this equilibrium can be disrupted by several factors, including diet, antibiotic use, and other environmental factors, resulting in dysbiosis, which can lead to inflammation and damage to the intestinal barrier [[87](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR87)].

In the context of CRC, diet plays a major factor in the dysbiosis of the gut microbiota, 'Westernized' diet, rich in red and processed meat and poor in dietary fibers, is the one of major contributors to the onset of colorectal cancer. This type of diet reduces the diversity of gut microbiota, as evident when we compare the microbiome of 'Westerners' or industrialized populations and hunter-gatherers and agrarian’ communities. The latter shows a greater diversity [[88](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR88)].

A comparative study on the Hadza tribe in Tanzania, known for their hunter-gatherer lifestyle, revealed that industrialized populations, represented by Americans, tend to have an intestinal microbiota dominated by Bacteroidaceae and Verrucomicrobia, the latter is a phylum of mucin-degrading bacteria that includes _Akkermansia muciniphila_. In contrast, the gut microbiota of traditional populations is enriched with _Prevotellaceae_ [[89](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR89)]. Moreover, they found that the traditional population exhibited a functional capacity to utilize plant carbohydrates, while Americans demonstrated a higher mucin-utilization capacity, associated with a lower intake of dietary fibers [[89](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR89)]. Another comparative study on rural children of Burkina Faso demonstrated a higher abundance of _Prevotella_ (genus of the family of _Prevotellaceae_) and _Xylanibacter_, known for their ability to degrade cellulose and xylan, compared to European children [[88](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR88)].

Dietary fibers are essential for maintaining a healthy and diverse gut microbiota, as the indigenous gut population into short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), notably butyrate, propionate, and acetate, ferments them. These SCFAs serve as an energy source for colonocytes [[90](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR90)].

In this context, patients with CRC exhibit a lower abundance of SCFA-producing bacteria compared to healthy individuals, resulting in a distinct composition of the gut microbiota [[91](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR91)]. Fecal samples from patients with CRC and advanced colorectal adenomas demonstrate a significant depletion of butyrate-producing bacteria [[92](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR92)]. Most of these butyrate-producing bacteria belong to the Bacillota phylum [[91](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR91)].

The onset and progression of colorectal cancer (CRC) are intricately linked to the elevated presence of pathogenic or pro-inflammatory species, particularly from the Proteobacteria and Fusobacteria phyla, along with a corresponding reduction in beneficial species from the Bacillota phylum [[93](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR93)].

Analysis of CRC tumorigenesis at the microbiome level reveals the abundance of several phyla, notably Bacteroidetes, Bacillota, and Fusobacteria, and a reduction in Proteobacteria. At the genus level, the analysis shows an increase in _Fusobacterium_, _Peptostreptococcus_, _Streptococcus_, and _Ruminococcus_, along with a decline in _Lactobacillus_ and _Granulicatella_ [[94](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR94), [95](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR95)].

Furthermore, there is a reduction in the abundance of intestinal probiotic species such as _Bifidobacterium_, _Lactobacillus_, and _Bacteroides_, accompanied by an increase in the numbers of pathogenic bacteria like _E. coli_, _Bacteroides fragilis_, and _Fusobacterium_. These pathogenic bacteria play a significant role in CRC tumorigenesis by releasing toxic chemicals that damage the intestinal epithelium and induce chronic inflammation [[96](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR96)]. Animal studies have also demonstrated that axenic mice are more susceptible to developing inflammatory-induced CRC than regular mice [[97](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR97)].

This demonstrates the crucial role played by the gut microbiota in creating a conducive environment that promotes the growth of colonic preneoplastic lesions and, consequently, CRC carcinogenesis [[98](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR98)].

Probiotics either can be natural inhabitants of the gastro-intestinal (GI) tract or isolated from various environmental sources (Table[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#Tab1)), and they represent diverse phyla. For instance, the _Lactobacillus_ genus, part of the Lactic acid bacteria group, falls under the Bacillota phylum [[99](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR99), [100](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR100)]. Another extensively studied and well-documented group of probiotic strains is _Bifidobacterium_, which belongs to the Actinomycetota phylum [[100](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR100)]. Lastly, _Saccharomyces_ also known as ‘baking yeast’, is among the most common and ancient microorganisms used. They were used in a wide range of applications, from baking to the production of fermented beverages [[101](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR101)]. This group of eukaryotic organisms belongs to the Ascomycota phylum of the Fungus kingdom [[102](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR102)].Table 1Common Sources of some probiotic strainsCategoriesSourcesProbioticReferencesMilk and derivativesKefir _Lactobacillus plantarum_; _Lactobacillus delbrueckii;_ _Streptococcus salivarius; Lactobacillus acidophilus; Lactobacillus casei; Lactococcus lactis_[[131](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR131)]Milk[[161](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR161)]Yogurt[[162](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR162)][[163](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR163)]Fruits & VegetablesVegetables _Pediococcus acidilactici; Lactobacillus farciminis;_ _Lactobacillus plantarum; Lactobacillus satsumensis; Leuconostoc mesenteroides; Saccharomyces cerevisiae; Lactobacillus paracasei_[[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR18), [164](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR164)]Prickly pears, Blackberries, Figs[[165](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR165)]OtherHuman feces _Lactobacillus salivarius; Lactobacillus plantarum_[[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR16)]

Probiotics modulate gut microbiota dysbiosis through various mechanisms (Figs. [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#Fig1), [2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#Fig2) and [3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#Fig3)). They compete with pathogenic bacteria for nutrients and growth factors. Moreover, they produce antimicrobial compounds like bacteriocins and lactic acid, which inhibit or eliminate pathogenic bacteria from the intestinal lumen [[103](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR103)]. The continuous probiotic consumption over 16 days in CRC patients undergoing colectomy successfully restored the diversity of their intestinal microbiota to a level similar to that of healthy individuals [[104](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR104)]. Furthermore, in mice with DSS-induced colitis, the abundance of _Lactobacillus_ was reduced; however, supplementation with fatty acids from fermented milk helped mitigate the dysbiosis caused by Dextran sodium sulfate (DSS) and restore the microbiota, enriching it with _Lactobacillus_ once more [[105](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR105)].Fig.1Influence of probiotics on signaling pathways in colorectal cancerFig.2Probiotic modulation of NF-kB signaling in colorectal cancer. _TNF-α_ Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha, _TNFR_ Tumor Necrosis Factor Receptor, _IKK_ IκB Kinase, _IκB_ inhibitor of κB, _NF-κB_ Nuclear Factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells, _p50/p65_ Subunits of NF-κB, _COX-2_ Cyclooxygenase-2, _Bcl-2_ B cell lymphoma 2; _Bcl-xL_ B cell lymphoma extra largeFig.3Probiotics as modulators of cellular signaling. _PAMPs_ Pathogen-associated molecular patterns, _TLR_ Toll-like receptor, _MAPK_ Mitogen-activated protein kinase, _PI3K_ Phosphoinositide 3-kinase, _mTORC_ mTOR complex, _GSK-3β_ Glycogen synthase kinase 3 beta, _APC_ Adenomatous polyposis coli, _PPARγ_ Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma, _CREB_ cAMP response element-binding protein, _CRC_ Colorectal cancer, _TFF3_ Trefoil factor family 3, _Cyclin E2_ Cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 2, _CDK4_ Cyclin-dependent kinases 4 and 6; c-Myc, _N-Myc_ Oncogenes that promote cell proliferation, _miR-34a_ MicroRNA that acts as a tumor suppressor

In contrast, a systematic review evaluating the efficacy of probiotics in correcting dysbiosis of the 'normal' microbiota resulting from disease or disruptive events underscores that while some probiotic strains show promise in correcting dysbiosis, the effects of most strains are overstated. Further research is essential to gain a more comprehensive understanding of individual strains' abilities to restore the microbiota to a healthy state [[106](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR106)].

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384)Probiotics and CRC

### Pro-apoptosis effect of probiotics

Probiotics have demonstrated in both in vitro human colon cancer cells and in mice models that they exhibit antiproliferative capacities through apoptosis. Increased expression of p53, by DNA damage or external stress like inflammation, mediates the upregulation of p21, as they work in tandem, which leads to the arrest of the cell cycle in the G1 phase. This cascade balances BAX/Bcl-2 towards apoptosis [[107](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR107)]. Upregulation of p53 and TGF expression, via the use of exopolysaccharide (EPS) extracted from _L. acidophilus_, in colon cancer cell line inhibited the viability up to 80.65% [[108](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR108)].

Studies conducted on several strains of _Lactobacillus_, using their cell-free supernatant (CFS) or EPS, have revealed that they induce apoptosis through the upregulation of the pro-apoptosis gene BAX, cleaved caspase 3 and downregulation of Bcl-2 in cultures of colon cancer cell lines [[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR19), [109](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR109)]. In an Azoxymethane (AOM)/DSS mice model, attenuated _L. plantarum_ increased the expression levels of BAX and reduced that of Bcl-2. Additionally, it had a suppressive effect against neoplastic development [[107](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR107)].

Previous research has shown that DDIT3 is involved in apoptosis via the dysregulation of BAX/Bcl-2 balance in the Endoplasmic Reticulum stress response pathway [[110](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR110), [111](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR111)]. JNK activation is associated with apoptosis, both intrinsic and extrinsic pathways [[112](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR112), [113](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR113)]. Konishi et al. [[114](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR114)] demonstrated that a colon cancer cell line treated with ferrichrome extracted from _L. casei_ showed an up-regulation in DDIT3 and an activation of JNK, where the inhibition of the latter reduced ferrichrome-mediated apoptosis. These findings suggest that apoptosis may be mediated via JNK-DDIT3 in the Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER) stress response pathway.

Apoptosis can also be induced via the Akt/NF-α pathway as previously discussed. Several studies have demonstrated that inhibition of such pathways leads to activation of pro-apoptotic elements. Down-regulation of phosphorylated-IκBα, which regulates the activity of NF-αB, as well as decreased expression levels of phosphorylated-Akt1, Bcl-xl, pro-caspase3 and pro-caspase 9 coupled with upregulation of BAX, cleaved caspase 3 and cleaved caspase 9 (which are the active form of caspase and are implicated in apoptosis). This cascade leads to decreased viability of human colon cancer cells treated with either CFS of _L. fermentum_ or heat-killed S. cerevisiae [[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR19), [115](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR115)]. In addition, _Clostridium butyricum_ attenuates apoptosis and inflammation caused by _Staphylococcus aureus_ [[116](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR116)].

### Antiproliferative and anti-inflammatory effects of probiotics

Probiotics have an anti-inflammatory capacity via different pathways. The inhibition of the TLR4 pathway is one such way. LPS activates the TLR4 signaling cascade and results in the overexpression of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, TNF-α, IL-1β, and COX2. EPS from probiotic strain _L. plantarum_ L14 inhibits the expression of these cytokines via the interaction with TLR4 [[117](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR117)]. TLR4 can bind to LPS just as it can to gram-positive elements such as EPS and Lipoteichoic acid (LTA) [[117](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR117), [118](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR118)]. However, LPS can only bind to TLR4 as demonstrated in a previous study on TLR4-deficient mice treated with high concentrations of LPS and did not develop an immune response, which can mean that the TLR4 pathway is the only signaling pathway that regulates the immunological response to LPS [[119](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR119)].

Additionally, EPS can upregulate IκBα which inhibits NF-αB and thus attenuates the inflammatory response through the NF-αB signaling pathway [[108](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947384#CR108)]. This is a scientific review article titled "Probiotics in colorectal cancer prevention and therapy: mechanisms, benefits, and challenges," published in Discover Oncology on March 26, 2025 (PMCID: PMC11947384). The authors are Djilali Seghir Morsli and colleagues from institutions in Algeria, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Kazakhstan.

**Key Points:**

- Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most diagnosed cancer and second leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide. In Algeria, it ranks second in mortality.
- Poor lifestyle factors (low-fiber diet, insufficient physical activity, tobacco use, alcohol) are strongly associated with increased CRC risk.
- Current CRC treatments include surgery, chemotherapy (e.g., 5-fluorouracil), molecular-targeted therapy, and immunotherapy, with adverse effects including postoperative infection, chemotherapy-induced diarrhea, and reduced quality of life.

**Probiotics and CRC Mechanisms:**

- Probiotics (defined by FAO/WHO as "Live microorganisms that, when administered in adequate amounts, confer health benefits on the host") include Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, and Saccharomyces.
- They exhibit immunomodulation, antioxidant activity, pathogen antagonism, production of antimicrobial compounds (bacteriocins), and anticarcinogenic activities.
- Probiotics modulate gut dysbiosis, which is characterized in CRC patients by reduced SCFA-producing bacteria, lower Lactobacillus/Bifidobacterium, and increased pathogenic species (Fusobacterium, E. coli, Bacteroides fragilis).
- Key mechanisms: inhibition of TLR4/NF-κB signaling, upregulation of pro-apoptotic genes (BAX, caspase 3), downregulation of anti-apoptotic Bcl-2, modulation of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway, and promotion of apoptosis via JNK-DDIT3 ER stress response.

**Safety and Regulatory Status:**

- WHO and EFSA have recognized probiotics as Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) and Qualified Presumption of Safety (QPS), respectively.
- However, high-risk patients should exercise caution due to potential infection risk.

**Conclusions:**

- Evidence for clinical efficacy is inadequate; further research is needed to establish probiotics as therapeutic agents rather than just dietary supplements.
- The review examines current knowledge on probiotic strains, therapeutic potential for CRC, limitations, and areas requiring further research.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452)Abstract

Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a leading cause of human mortality worldwide. As conventional anticancer therapy not always being effective, there is growing interest in innovative “drug-free” cancer treatments or interventions that improve the efficacy of established therapy. CRC is associated with microbiome alterations, a process known as dysbiosis that involves depletion and/or enrichment of particular gut bacterial species and their metabolic functions. Supplementing patient treatment with traditional probiotics (with or without prebiotics), next-generation probiotics (NGP), or postbiotics represents a potentially effective and accessible complementary anticancer strategy by restoring gut microbiota composition and/or by signaling to the host. In this capacity, restoration of the gut microbiota in cancer patients can stabilize and enhance intestinal barrier function, as well as promote anticarcinogenic, anti-inflammatory, antimutagenic or other biologically important biochemical pathways that show high specificity towards tumor cells. Potential benefits of traditional probiotics, NGP, and postbiotics include modulating gut microbiota composition and function, as well as the host inflammatory response. Their application in CRC prevention is highlighted in this review, where we consider supportive _in vitro_, animal, and clinical studies. Based on emerging research, NGP and postbiotics hold promise in establishing innovative treatments for CRC by conferring physiological functions _via_ the production of dominant natural products and metabolites that provide new host-microbiota signals to combat CRC. Although favorable results have been reported, further investigations focusing on strain and dose specificity are required to ensure the efficacy and safety of traditional probiotics, NGP, and postbiotics in CRC prevention and treatment.

**Keywords:**Colorectal cancer, Traditional probiotics, Next-generation probiotics, Postbiotics, Gut microbiota

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452)INTRODUCTION

Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most commonly diagnosed cancer in males and the second in females worldwide; thus a significant change in lifestyle is required to facilitate effective CRC prevention[[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B1)]. CRC is a heterogeneous disease of the intestinal epithelium, comprising the colon, rectum, and anus. It is characterized by a dysregulated immune response, accumulation of stem cell mutations, intestinal barrier disruption, and dysbiosis, which is often regarded as an unfavorable alteration in gut microbiota composition and function. Up to 90% of CRC risk is thought to be lifestyle-dependent, primarily due to dietary or environmental factors including feeding patterns that modulate consumption of fiber, red and processed meat or alcohol consumption, and low omega-3 fatty acids and vitamin D intake. Obesity, lack of physical activity, and smoking are also significant risk factors that promote CRC-associated microbiota changes[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B2)]. CRC is linked with microbiome alterations, which include depletion and/or enrichment in particular bacterial species that are present in CRC patients (extensively reviewed by Torres-Maravilla _et al_[[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B3)], Ternes _et al_[[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B4)], Janney _et al_[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B2)], Fong _et al_[[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B5)], and Wirbel _et al_[[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B6)]).

The human microbiota is a complex ecosystem of bacteria, viruses, eukaryotes, and archea, which can regulate a variety of host physiological functions including digestion, immune response, metabolism, disease pathogenesis, elimination of toxins, and biosynthesis of key compounds such as essential vitamins and cofactors. Microbiota can even modulate gut-brain axis function to alter, for example, anxiety and mood. Symbiotic bacteria that colonize the human gut can be classified into several phyla comprising Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes, followed by Proteobacteria, Fusobacteria, Actinobacteria, Verrucomicrobia, and Spirochaetes. Microbiome composition varies between healthy individuals, as well as in CRC patients[[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B7)]. CRC-associated bacteria that have been identified to date include enrichment of _Fusobacterium nucleatum_, _Enterococcus faecalis_, _Streptococcus gallolyticus_, entero-toxigenic _Bacteroides fragilis_, _Escherichia coli_, _Peptostreptococcus_ spp., and _Ruminococcus_ spp. By contrast, _Lactobacillus_ spp., _Bifidobacterium_ spp., _Faecalibacterium_ spp., _Roseburia_ spp., _Clostridium_ spp., _Granulicatella_ spp., _Streptococcus thermophilus_, and other species of _Lachnospiraceae_ family are depleted in CRC (Table [1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#T1))[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B2)-[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B5)]. These altered microbiota signatures can potentially be used to provide future diagnostics, and their presence/absence may contribute to the pathogenesis or prevention/treatment of CRC. However, the pathophysiological role of dysbiosis in CRC still remains unclear, since microbiota changes may reflect changes in host health status and some bacteria may even confer protection as a compensatory response to disease progression. This complexity is clearly evident by the report of specific bacteria associated with tumor initiation phase (driver bacteria) whereas other bacteria are associated with tumor development during progressive stages of CRC (passenger bacteria). Driver bacteria reportedly contribute to the formation of a tumor microenvironment that is comprised of normal epithelial cells and cancer cells. In this milieu, secreted microbial metabolites trigger damage to normal host cells, thus reprograming their metabolism to change the intestinal microenvironment and microbiome profile towards a more “CRC supportive” composition[[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B8)-[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B10)]. Potential driver bacteria include _Bacteroides fragilis_, _Escherichia coli_, _Enterococcus Faecalis_, _Bacillus_, _Bradyrhizobium_, _Methylobacterium_, _Streptomyces_, _Shigella_, _Citrobacter_, _Salmonella_, _Intrasporangiaceae_, and _Sinobacteraceae_. On the other hand, passenger bacteria occupy an existing tumor microenvironment where they are thought to either promote or inhibit CRC progression. Reported passenger bacteria include species _Fusobacterium_, _Parvimonas_, _Peptostreptococcus_, _Campylobacter_, _Streptococcus_, _Schwartzia_, _Burkholderiales_, _Caulobacteraceae_, _Delftia_, _Oxalobacteraceae_, _Faecalibacterium_, and _Sutterella_[[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B8)-[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B11)]. The host gut microbiota and immune system play important roles in CRC prevention and development. Therefore, probiotics, next-generation probiotics (NGP), or postbiotics could be used as weapons to prevent CRC, to support the treatment and to improve the clinical outcomes in CRC patients.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452)TRADITIONAL PROBIOTICS

Probiotics are defined as “live, non-pathogenic microorganisms that, when administered in adequate amounts, may confer a health benefit on the host”[[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B12)]. Probiotics have a centuries-long history of safe use as prevention and adjuvant therapy in combating human diseases. They are also promising candidates in modulating human gut microbiota composition and function in CRC patients. Traditional widely used probiotics mainly belong to _Bifidobacterium_ spp., _Lactobacillus_ spp. and other lactic-acid-producing bacteria, including species belonging to _Streptococcus, Enterococcus_, and _Lactococcus_, complemented by yeasts of the genus _Saccharomyces_. The beneficial effects of probiotics, functioning in a species and/or strain-specific manner, include sustaining a healthy microbiome, reversing dysbiosis, preventing pathogenic infections and mucosal adhesion of pathogens, stabilizing and enhancing intestinal barrier function. Probiotic bacteria may achieve these beneficial functions in part by producing anti-carcinogenic, anti-inflammatory, anti-mutagenic and other biologically important compounds such as short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), vitamin K, or B-group vitamins[[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B5),[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B7),[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B13),[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B14)].

Current research builds on a foundation of work demonstrating that gut microbiota modulation through administration of probiotics and/or prebiotics plays an important role in CRC prevention and therapy. In a randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial, 60 patients underwent surgical CRC resection, of whom 29 received the probiotic powder (_Bifidobacterium animalis_ subsp. _lactis_ HY8002 [1 × 10 8 CFU], _Lactobacillus casei_ HY2782 [5 × 10 7 CFU], and _Lactobacillus plantarum_ HY7712 [5 × 10 7 CFU]) and 31 placebo, for 4 wk, starting at 1 wk preoperatively. The treatment group receiving probiotic powder showed an increase in abundance of _Bifidobacterium_, _Akkermansia_, _Parabacteroides_, _Veillonella_, _Lactobacillus_, _Erysipelatoclostridium_ and a reduction in bacteria associated with CRC, such as _Prevotella_, _Alloprevotella_, _Fusobacterium_, and _Porphyromonas_. Lower serum zonulin, improved postoperative bowel function, and postoperative recovery were evident in the probiotic group compared with placebo[[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B15)]. In another randomized clinical trial, a group of 31 CRC patients received probiotic supplement _Bifidobacterium longum_ BB536 (5 × 10 10 CFU/2 g/daily) preoperatively for 7–14 d and postoperatively for 2 wk. Attenuated postoperative inflammatory responses (high-sensitivity C-Reactive protein), reduced risk of postoperative infectious complications, and accelerated health recovery after colorectal resection were evident in the treatment group. Hospital stay was significantly shortened and correlated significantly with increased Actinobacteria and decreased Firmicutes after probiotic intervention[[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B16)]. Aisu _et al_[[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B17)] administered BIO THREE® 2 mg _Enterococcus faecalis_ T110, 10 mg _Clostridium butyricum_ TO-A, and 10 mg _Bacillus mesentericus_ TO-A to 75 CRC patients 15 d prior to the surgery. Incidence of postoperative complications and superficial incisional infections were lower, and these health effects were as shown to associate with an increased mean proportion of beneficial _Bifidobacterium_, postoperatively, even though this organism was not administered as part of the probiotic regime. The change in microbial diversity and improved integrity of the mucosal barrier were also observed by Liu _et al_[[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B18)] after _Lactobacillus plantarum_ CGMCC 1258, _Lactobacillus acidophilus_ LA-11, _Bifidobacterium longum_ BL-88 (2.6 × 10 14 CFU/2 g/daily) administration 6 d preoperatively and 10 d postoperatively to CRC patients. The numbers of beneficial bacteria, including _Bifidobacteria_ and _Lactobacilli_, increased in the probiotic group after surgery, whereas they decreased in the placebo group. By contrast, Enterobacteriales and _Pseudomonas_, were decreased in the probiotic group whereas they increased in the placebo group. Based on a number of clinical trials, the preoperative oral intake of probiotics combined with the postoperative treatment in patients who need gastrointestinal surgery is potentially recommended. Larger rigorously controlled clinical trials are required to endorse these preliminary positive outcome studies since avoidance of probiotic use has also been recommended in patients with immunodeficiency and dysbiosis. ## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452)NGP

One potential approach to achieve CRC prevention and treatment is through NGP administration. As described above, the most frequently used probiotics belong to _Bifidobacterium_ spp. and _Lactobacillus_ spp. However, recent studies using metagenomic approaches have revealed the importance of further identification and characterization of commensal species, mainly anaerobic ones, residing in the gastrointestinal tract that play an important role in regulating the immune system and maintaining overall gut health. Growing evidence suggests that dysbiosis may contribute to CRC progression as well as several other diseases[[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B19)-[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B22)]. Although there is no official definition of NGP, it is generally defined as live microorganisms identified on the basis of comparative microbiota analyses between healthy and sick individuals/animals that, when administered with strain-specificity and in dose dependent manner, confer health benefits on the host[[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B23),[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B24)]. Compared with healthy individuals, patients with CRC possess a different compositional structure and physiological activity of the gut microbiota with SCFAs-producing bacteria being depleted. This suggests that SCFAs-producing bacteria might potentially exhibit anti-inflammatory and anticarcinogenic properties, as well as being NGP candidates in CRC prevention and therapy. SCFAs, primarily acetate, propionate, and butyrate, are key physiological metabolites of the microbial fermentation of dietary fiber in the colon. Butyrate is the major energy source for colonocyte homeostasis, promoting growth stimulation and production of protective cytokines that maintain gut barrier integrity and function[[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B14),[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B25)-[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B27)]. Furthermore, increasing levels of SCFAs in the gut helps to create a favorable microenvironment for beneficial bacteria by inhibiting the growth and adhesion of pathogens, and by enhancing vitamin bioavailability, mineral absorption and promoting mucosal integrity. Most butyrate-producing bacteria in the human colon belong to the Firmicutes phylum, clostridial clusters IV and XIVa, the most dominant species being _Faecalibacterium prausnitzii_ and _Eubacterium rectale,_ followed by _Eubacterium_ spp. as well as _Anaerostipes_ spp. and _Roseburia_ spp. In addition to butyrate-producing bacteria, other NGP candidates with important regulatory effects on gut homeostasis include _Akkermansia muciniphila_, non-toxigenic _Bacteroides fragilis_, _Propionibacterium freudenreichii,_ and some strains of _Bacillus_ spp. and _Clostridium_ spp., which belong to Generally Recognized As Safe microorganisms[[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B7),[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B28),[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B29)].

Chronic oral administration of _Butyricicoccus pullicaecorum_ BCRC 81109 (butyrate producing bacteria) to BALB/cByJNarl male mice decreased colon tumor progression over 9 wk. This protection against CRC clinical outcomes was linked to activation of the SCFAs transporter solute carrier family 5 member 8 and/or G-protein-coupled receptor (GPR) 43[[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B30)]. Chen _et al_[[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B25)] also observed in an _in vivo_ animal study that application of butyrate producing bacteria _Clostridium butyricum_ ATCC 19398 (2 × 10 9 CFU/0.2 mL 3 times a week for 12 wk) inhibited intestinal tumor development by an increasing apoptosis of CRC cells, by modulating the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway. There was also a reduction in pathogenic bacteria and bile acid-biotransforming bacteria, whereas an increase in beneficial _Lactobacillus_ spp. and SCFAs-producing _Rumincoccaceae_ and _Eubacterium_ spp. was evident. Thus, reduction in colonic secondary bile acids increased cecal SCFAs levels and activated G-protein coupled receptors, GPR43 and GPR109A, which were mechanistically implicated. Growth of CRC cell lines (HCT-116 and SW1116) was significantly inhibited by strains _Bacillus subtilis_ ATCC 23857 and _Clostridium butyricum_ ATCC 19398, and by their main metabolites bacitracin and butyrate. mRNA levels of important receptors and transcriptional factors related to inflammation for example, TLR4, MYD88, nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB), interleukin 22 (IL-22), and survivin were decreased and expression of p21 WAF1 was increased after treatment of SW1116 cells with _Bacillus subtilis_ and _Clostridium butyricum_ NGP[[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B31)]. Purified components produced by NGP cells were also studied and inhibition of human cancer cell proliferation by controlling the cell cycle was detected. Polysaccharide A purified from _Bacteroides fragilis_ NCTC9343 (non-toxigenic) induced the production of the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-8[[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B32)] and aspartic protease Amuc_1434 (recombinant enzyme) from _Akkermansia muciniphila_ upregulated the expression of tumor protein 53, increased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels and promoted apoptosis of LS174T cells[[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B33)]. Pahle _et al_[[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B34)] employed _Clostridium perfringens_ enterotoxin (CPE) in CPE gene therapy to selectively target claudin-3 and claudin-4 expressing colon carcinomas _in vitro_ and _in vivo_ by using a translation optimized CPE expressing vector. Elevated toxicity of the optimized CPE expressing vector was evident in claudin-positive cells 48 h after the transfection, with toxicity rates of 76%–92% and rapid cytotoxic effects such as membrane disruption and necrosis. Further _in vivo_ studies focused on the efficiency of NGP application in CRC are listed in Table [3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#T3) and postbiotics derived from NGP are considered below.

Reduced gene expression of TLR4–MYD88–NF-κB, IL-22 and increase of P21 waf1 and Tlr3 mRNA levels in intestinal mucosa Chen _et al_[[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9346452#B31)]
