## 1. Introduction

Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is widely recognized as a major global health challenge, with its prevalence rising sharply over recent decades as a result of population aging, urbanization, sedentary lifestyles, and dietary transitions toward energy-dense, nutrient-poor foods [[1](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B1-diabetology-07-00059),[2](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B2-diabetology-07-00059),[3](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B3-diabetology-07-00059)]. Epidemiological data consistently indicate that T2DM accounts for more than 90% of all diabetes cases worldwide, underscoring its dominant contribution to the global diabetes burden [[1](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B1-diabetology-07-00059),[4](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B4-diabetology-07-00059),[5](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B5-diabetology-07-00059)]. T2DM is a leading contributor to cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and premature mortality, substantially amplifying its clinical and public health impact [[2](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B2-diabetology-07-00059),[4](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B4-diabetology-07-00059),[5](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B5-diabetology-07-00059)]. In parallel, the socioeconomic burden of diabetes is considerable, with global health expenditures approaching one trillion US dollars annually and projected to increase further, highlighting the urgent need for effective prevention and management strategies [[1](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B1-diabetology-07-00059),[6](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B6-diabetology-07-00059)]. The growing burden of T2DM is largely driven by modifiable risk factors, particularly elevated body mass index, physical inactivity, and unhealthy dietary patterns characterized by low fiber intake, with high BMI accounting for more than half of global T2DM-related disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) [[7](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B7-diabetology-07-00059),[8](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B8-diabetology-07-00059)]. This burden is further compounded by high rates of undiagnosed disease and persistent disparities in access to care, especially in low- and middle-income countries [[9](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B9-diabetology-07-00059)].

At the mechanistic level, type 2 diabetes mellitus is a complex metabolic disorder driven by insulin resistance in skeletal muscle, liver, and adipose tissue, together with progressive pancreatic β-cell dysfunction. Impaired peripheral glucose uptake, increased hepatic gluconeogenesis, and altered lipid metabolism initially lead to compensatory hyperinsulinemia, which ultimately fails as β-cell mass and function decline, resulting in persistent hyperglycemia [[2](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B2-diabetology-07-00059),[10](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B10-diabetology-07-00059),[11](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B11-diabetology-07-00059),[12](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B12-diabetology-07-00059)]. A hallmark of this process is chronic low-grade inflammation, supported by macrophage activation and pro-inflammatory cytokine signaling, which further disrupts insulin action and metabolic homeostasis [[13](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B13-diabetology-07-00059),[14](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B14-diabetology-07-00059)]. In parallel, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and lipotoxicity amplify cellular damage and metabolic inflexibility, while sustained activation of inflammatory pathways, including nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) and the NLR Family Pyrin Domain containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome, creates a self-perpetuating cycle of metabolic stress that drives disease progression and contributes to both microvascular and macrovascular complications in type 2 diabetes [[15](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B15-diabetology-07-00059),[16](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B16-diabetology-07-00059),[17](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B17-diabetology-07-00059),[18](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B18-diabetology-07-00059),[19](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B19-diabetology-07-00059)].

Growing evidence identifies the gut microbiota as a central regulator of metabolic homeostasis and an important contributor to the pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes mellitus [[20](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B20-diabetology-07-00059),[21](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B21-diabetology-07-00059),[22](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B22-diabetology-07-00059),[23](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B23-diabetology-07-00059)]. Dysbiosis in T2DM is consistently associated with increased intestinal permeability and lipopolysaccharide-driven metabolic endotoxemia, which promotes chronic low-grade inflammation and insulin resistance [[24](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B24-diabetology-07-00059),[25](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B25-diabetology-07-00059),[26](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B26-diabetology-07-00059)]. In parallel, a reduced abundance of short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria and impaired microbial bile acid metabolism further disrupt gut barrier function and key metabolic signaling pathways involved in glucose and lipid homeostasis [[27](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B27-diabetology-07-00059),[28](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B28-diabetology-07-00059),[29](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B29-diabetology-07-00059)]. Importantly, the gut microbiota represents a dynamic and modifiable ecosystem, and emerging microbiota-targeted interventions have demonstrated potential to improve glycemic control and inflammatory profiles, although heterogeneity across studies highlights the need for further well-designed clinical trials [[30](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B30-diabetology-07-00059),[31](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B31-diabetology-07-00059),[32](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B32-diabetology-07-00059)].

In this context, dietary fibers and prebiotics have attracted increasing interest as key nutritional modulators of the gut microbiota and metabolic homeostasis in type 2 diabetes mellitus [[33](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B33-diabetology-07-00059),[34](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B34-diabetology-07-00059),[35](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B35-diabetology-07-00059)]. Many dietary fibers and prebiotic compounds escape digestion in the upper gastrointestinal tract and reach the colon, where they interact directly with intestinal microbes, exerting prebiotic effects, reshaping microbial communities, and enhancing the production of beneficial metabolites such as short-chain fatty acids [[33](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B33-diabetology-07-00059),[34](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B34-diabetology-07-00059),[35](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B35-diabetology-07-00059),[36](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B36-diabetology-07-00059)]. By selectively stimulating SCFA-producing bacteria, dietary fibers and prebiotics support gut barrier integrity, reduce metabolic endotoxemia and inflammation, and improve insulin sensitivity [[33](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B33-diabetology-07-00059),[34](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B34-diabetology-07-00059),[35](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B35-diabetology-07-00059),[36](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B36-diabetology-07-00059)]. These microbiota-dependent mechanisms position dietary fibers and prebiotics as central dietary components in strategies aimed at restoring metabolic homeostasis in T2DM.

The convergence of microbiota research and nutritional science has opened new avenues for personalized and mechanism-driven approaches to T2DM management. Targeting the gut microbiota through dietary fibers and prebiotics represents a promising adjunct strategy for addressing upstream pathogenic mechanisms in T2DM. This narrative review is based on a focused evaluation of experimental and clinical studies retrieved primarily from PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus. The literature search focused on publications from the past decade that addressed dietary fibers, prebiotics, gut microbiota, and type 2 diabetes mellitus, with a particular emphasis on mechanistic, translational, and clinical evidence. Reference lists of relevant articles were also screened to identify additional pertinent studies. This review aims to synthesize current evidence on the effects of dietary fibers and prebiotics on gut microbiota composition and function in T2DM, elucidate underlying molecular and microbial mechanisms, and discuss their therapeutic potential and clinical implications.

## 2. Gut Microbiota in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus

The human gut microbiota plays a fundamental role in maintaining metabolic homeostasis through its involvement in energy harvest, glucose and lipid metabolism, immune regulation, and preservation of intestinal barrier integrity [[37](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B37-diabetology-07-00059),[38](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B38-diabetology-07-00059)]. Commensal microorganisms and their metabolites, particularly short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), modulate host metabolic pathways, support gut barrier function, and contribute to the regulation of immune responses, thereby limiting metabolic endotoxemia [[38](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B38-diabetology-07-00059),[39](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B39-diabetology-07-00059)]. Accumulating evidence from both human and experimental studies has identified the gut microbiota as a critical contributor to the pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), with affected individuals consistently exhibiting alterations in microbial composition and function, commonly referred to as dysbiosis [[20](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B20-diabetology-07-00059),[29](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B29-diabetology-07-00059),[40](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B40-diabetology-07-00059),[41](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B41-diabetology-07-00059)]. This dysbiotic state, characterized by reduced microbial diversity, depletion of SCFA-producing bacteria, and enrichment of pro-inflammatory taxa, is closely associated with increased intestinal permeability, impaired microbial metabolic activity, and systemic inflammation, which collectively promote insulin resistance through disrupted host-microbe signaling and translocation of bacterial components such as lipopolysaccharides [[21](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B21-diabetology-07-00059),[23](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B23-diabetology-07-00059),[24](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B24-diabetology-07-00059),[25](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B25-diabetology-07-00059),[28](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B28-diabetology-07-00059)].

One of the hallmark features of type 2 diabetes mellitus-associated dysbiosis is impaired gut barrier integrity, leading to increased intestinal permeability and enhanced translocation of bacterial components, particularly lipopolysaccharides (LPS), into the systemic circulation [[21](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B21-diabetology-07-00059),[24](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B24-diabetology-07-00059),[42](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B42-diabetology-07-00059),[43](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B43-diabetology-07-00059),[44](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B44-diabetology-07-00059)]. This process results in metabolic endotoxemia, which activates innate immune signaling pathways, most notably through toll-like receptor 4 and nuclear factor-κB, thereby promoting chronic low-grade inflammation [[45](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B45-diabetology-07-00059),[46](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B46-diabetology-07-00059),[47](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B47-diabetology-07-00059)]. The resulting inflammatory milieu interferes with insulin receptor signaling in key metabolic tissues, including the liver, skeletal muscle, and adipose tissue, contributing to the development and progression of insulin resistance [[24](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B24-diabetology-07-00059),[41](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B41-diabetology-07-00059),[43](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B43-diabetology-07-00059),[46](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B46-diabetology-07-00059),[47](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B47-diabetology-07-00059)]. Clinical and mechanistic studies further demonstrate that individuals with T2DM exhibit reduced expression of intestinal tight junction proteins, increased markers of gut permeability, and elevated circulating LPS or LPS-binding protein levels, which correlate with poor glycemic control and systemic inflammation [[42](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B42-diabetology-07-00059),[44](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B44-diabetology-07-00059),[48](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B48-diabetology-07-00059)]. In this context, although the term “elevated lipopolysaccharide (LPS)” is widely used to describe metabolic endotoxemia, no universally accepted clinical reference range exists, owing to methodological variability across studies. In clinical investigations, metabolic endotoxemia is therefore typically defined relative to control populations, often characterized by approximately two- to three-fold higher circulating LPS or LPS-binding protein concentrations in individuals with metabolic disease [[49](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B49-diabetology-07-00059),[50](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B50-diabetology-07-00059)]. Collectively, these findings highlight impaired gut barrier function as a central link between microbiota dysbiosis, immune activation, and metabolic dysfunction in T2DM, supporting the therapeutic rationale for strategies aimed at restoring intestinal integrity and modulating the gut microbiota [[21](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B21-diabetology-07-00059),[42](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B42-diabetology-07-00059),[43](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B43-diabetology-07-00059),[51](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B51-diabetology-07-00059)].

In parallel, type 2 diabetes mellitus is associated with profound qualitative and quantitative alterations in microbial metabolic capacity, most consistently reflected by a reduced abundance of SCFA-producing bacteria, including Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Roseburia species [[29](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B29-diabetology-07-00059),[40](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B40-diabetology-07-00059),[52](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B52-diabetology-07-00059),[53](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B53-diabetology-07-00059),[54](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B54-diabetology-07-00059)]. The depletion of these taxa results in diminished production of SCFAs, particularly butyrate, which play a central role in maintaining intestinal epithelial integrity, regulating immune responses, and supporting metabolic homeostasis [[55](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B55-diabetology-07-00059),[56](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B56-diabetology-07-00059),[57](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B57-diabetology-07-00059)]. Reduced SCFA availability compromises tight junction function and amplifies inflammatory signaling, facilitating metabolic endotoxemia [[55](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B55-diabetology-07-00059),[56](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B56-diabetology-07-00059),[57](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B57-diabetology-07-00059)]. In addition, SCFAs directly modulate glucose and lipid metabolism through G protein-coupled receptor signaling and epigenetic mechanisms such as histone deacetylase inhibition; their deficiency further disrupts insulin signaling and exacerbates insulin resistance in T2DM [[55](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B55-diabetology-07-00059),[56](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B56-diabetology-07-00059),[57](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B57-diabetology-07-00059)]. Given that dietary fibers and prebiotics are the primary substrates for colonic SCFA production, these microbial alterations are highly sensitive to dietary modulation. It should be noted that SCFA-mediated inhibition of histone deacetylases and activation of G-protein-coupled receptors are largely derived from experimental models, and isoform- and tissue-specific effects in humans remain incompletely characterized.

Disruption of bile acid metabolism represents another key mechanism linking the gut microbiota to metabolic dysregulation in T2DM. Intestinal microbes regulate bile acid deconjugation and transformation through specific bacterial enzymes, thereby shaping the composition of the bile acid pool and the balance between primary and secondary bile acids [[58](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B58-diabetology-07-00059),[59](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B59-diabetology-07-00059),[60](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B60-diabetology-07-00059)]. These microbiota-driven changes directly influence the activation of host bile acid receptors, particularly the farnesoid X receptor (FXR) and Takeda G protein-coupled receptor 5 (TGR5), which play central roles in the regulation of glucose metabolism, lipid homeostasis, energy expenditure, and inflammatory signaling [[59](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B59-diabetology-07-00059),[61](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B61-diabetology-07-00059),[62](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B62-diabetology-07-00059),[63](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B63-diabetology-07-00059),[64](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B64-diabetology-07-00059)]. In the context of T2DM-associated dysbiosis, altered microbial bile acid metabolism leads to impaired FXR and TGR5 signaling, contributing to increased insulin resistance, disrupted glucose and lipid metabolism, and heightened cardiometabolic risk [[60](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B60-diabetology-07-00059),[62](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B62-diabetology-07-00059),[65](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B65-diabetology-07-00059),[66](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B66-diabetology-07-00059)]. Both human and experimental studies further support the relevance of this pathway, demonstrating that modulation of the gut microbiota or bile acid signaling can influence metabolic outcomes in T2DM [[26](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B26-diabetology-07-00059),[58](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B58-diabetology-07-00059),[65](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B65-diabetology-07-00059),[67](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B67-diabetology-07-00059)].

Emerging evidence indicates that specific dietary fibers and prebiotics can differentially influence bile acid composition by modulating the abundance and activity of bile acid-transforming gut bacteria [[68](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B68-diabetology-07-00059),[69](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B69-diabetology-07-00059),[70](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B70-diabetology-07-00059),[71](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B71-diabetology-07-00059)]. Fermentable fibers, including inulin, fructooligosaccharides, resistant starch, and arabinoxylan, have been shown to increase microbial bile salt hydrolase activity and promote the conversion of primary to secondary bile acids, thereby influencing FXR and TGR5 signaling pathways involved in glucose and lipid metabolism [[68](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B68-diabetology-07-00059),[69](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B69-diabetology-07-00059),[72](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B72-diabetology-07-00059)]. However, individual differences in baseline bile acid pools, gut microbiota composition, and host metabolic status substantially shape the metabolic response to fiber and prebiotic interventions [[73](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B73-diabetology-07-00059),[74](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B74-diabetology-07-00059),[75](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B75-diabetology-07-00059)]. These inter-individual variations may partly explain the heterogeneous effects of dietary fibers on insulin sensitivity and underscore the need for personalized approaches [[72](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B72-diabetology-07-00059),[73](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B73-diabetology-07-00059),[76](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B76-diabetology-07-00059)].

Importantly, the gut microbiota represents a dynamic and modifiable ecosystem, making it an attractive therapeutic target in T2DM. Interventions aimed at restoring microbial composition and function, including dietary fiber supplementation and prebiotic intake have demonstrated potential to improve glycemic control, reduce systemic inflammation, and enhance insulin sensitivity in both preclinical models and clinical studies [[31](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B31-diabetology-07-00059),[77](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B77-diabetology-07-00059),[78](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B78-diabetology-07-00059),[79](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B79-diabetology-07-00059)]. Meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials indicate that microbiota-targeted strategies are associated with modest reductions in fasting plasma glucose, HbA1c, fasting insulin, and HOMA-IR, accompanied by decreased pro-inflammatory cytokine levels and enrichment of beneficial taxa such as Actinobacteria and Lactobacillus [[31](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B31-diabetology-07-00059),[77](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B77-diabetology-07-00059),[78](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B78-diabetology-07-00059),[79](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B79-diabetology-07-00059)]. High-fiber diets and prebiotics, in particular, increase microbial diversity, promote the abundance of health-associated genera including Faecalibacterium and Akkermansia, and enhance short-chain fatty acid production, correlating with improved metabolic outcomes [[80](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B80-diabetology-07-00059),[81](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B81-diabetology-07-00059)]. Probiotics and synbiotics have shown modest but consistent improvements in glycemic indices and inflammatory markers, with multi-strain formulations generally outperforming single-strain products [[31](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B31-diabetology-07-00059),[78](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B78-diabetology-07-00059),[79](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B79-diabetology-07-00059)]. While fecal microbiota transplantation is emerging as a promising adjunctive approach, supported by early evidence of beneficial microbial engraftment and improved metabolic parameters [[20](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B20-diabetology-07-00059),[26](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B26-diabetology-07-00059)], dietary fibers and prebiotics remain the most accessible, safe, and scalable microbiota-targeted strategies for long-term management of T2DM.

Nevertheless, the current evidence base is limited by substantial heterogeneity in study design, intervention type and duration, microbial assessment methodologies, and patient characteristics, as well as relatively short follow-up periods [[30](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B30-diabetology-07-00059),[31](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B31-diabetology-07-00059),[80](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B80-diabetology-07-00059),[82](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B82-diabetology-07-00059)]. These limitations restrict generalizability and preclude definitive recommendations for microbiota modulation as standard therapy in T2DM. Consequently, large-scale, long-term randomized trials incorporating standardized interventions, clinically meaningful endpoints, and comprehensive metagenomic analyses are required to clarify the therapeutic relevance and translational potential of microbiota-targeted strategies in type 2 diabetes [[30](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B30-diabetology-07-00059),[82](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B82-diabetology-07-00059)]. The complex interactions between gut microbiota dysbiosis, intestinal barrier dysfunction, microbial metabolites, and host metabolic pathways are summarized in [Figure 1](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#fig_body_display_diabetology-07-00059-f001).

![Image 15: Diabetology 07 00059 g001](https://www.mdpi.com/diabetology/diabetology-07-00059/article_deploy/html/images/diabetology-07-00059-g001-550.jpg)[](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#fig_body_display_diabetology-07-00059-f001)

**Figure 1.** Gut microbiota-mediated mechanisms contributing to type 2 diabetes mellitus. 

## 3. Fibers, Prebiotics, and Microbiota Modulation: Mechanisms and Clinical Evidence

Dietary natural products, including fibers and prebiotics, polyphenols and bioactive food components, probiotics, synbiotics, and postbiotics, play a significant role in modulating the gut microbiota and influencing metabolic outcomes in type 2 diabetes [[83](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B83-diabetology-07-00059),[84](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B84-diabetology-07-00059),[85](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B85-diabetology-07-00059),[86](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B86-diabetology-07-00059)].

### 3.1. Fibers and Prebiotics: Definition, Sources, and Relevant Nutraceuticals

Dietary fibers are non-digestible carbohydrate polymers naturally present in plant-based foods, such as vegetables, whole grains, fruits, and legumes, that resist enzymatic degradation and absorption in the small intestine. As a result, they reach the colon largely intact, where they serve as primary substrates for microbial fermentation [[87](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B87-diabetology-07-00059),[88](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B88-diabetology-07-00059),[89](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B89-diabetology-07-00059)].

Prebiotics represent a functionally distinct subset of dietary fibers that selectively stimulate the growth and/or activity of beneficial gut microorganisms, particularly short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-producing bacteria, thereby conferring metabolic health benefits to the host [[90](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4540/7/3/59#B90-diabetology-07-00059)]. This is a scientific review article published in Diabetology (2026, Volume 7, Issue 3, Article 59) titled "Dietary Fibers and Prebiotics for Gut Microbiota Modulation in Type 2 Diabetes: Mechanisms and Therapeutic Potential" by Ioan Cristian Crăciun, Dan Claudiu Măgureanu, Ioana Corina Bocsan, Anca Elena Crăciun, Anca Dana Buzoianu, and Maria Adriana Neag from "Iuliu Hațieganu" University of Medicine and Pharmacy, Cluj-Napoca, Romania.

**Background:** Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a prevalent metabolic disorder where gut microbiota dysbiosis contributes to insulin resistance, metabolic inflammation, and impaired glucose homeostasis. Dietary fibers and prebiotics selectively modulate gut microbiota composition and function and may offer metabolic benefits.

**Methods:** The review examined experimental and clinical studies assessing effects of dietary fibers and prebiotics on microbial diversity, short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, intestinal barrier function, bile acid signaling, and glycemic control in T2DM.

**Key Findings:**
- T2DM is associated with reduced abundance of SCFA-producing bacteria (e.g., Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Roseburia), increased intestinal permeability, metabolic endotoxemia, and altered bile acid metabolism.
- T2DM-associated dysbiosis is characterized by reduced microbial diversity, depletion of SCFA-producing bacteria, and enrichment of pro-inflammatory taxa.
- Impaired gut barrier integrity leads to increased lipopolysaccharide (LPS) translocation, activating toll-like receptor 4 and NF-κB pathways, promoting chronic low-grade inflammation that disrupts insulin receptor signaling.
- Dietary fibers and prebiotics enhance SCFA production, support gut barrier integrity, and modulate inflammatory and metabolic pathways.
- Reduced SCFA availability compromises tight junction function and amplifies inflammatory signaling.
- Disruption of bile acid metabolism through altered FXR and TGR5 signaling further contributes to metabolic dysregulation.
- Clinical evidence shows modest improvements in glycemic and inflammatory parameters (reductions in fasting plasma glucose, HbA1c, fasting insulin, HOMA-IR), though outcomes vary according to fiber type, dose, and baseline microbiota composition.
- Meta-analyses indicate microbiota-targeted strategies are associated with decreased pro-inflammatory cytokine levels and enrichment of beneficial taxa such as Actinobacteria and Lactobacillus.
- High-fiber diets increase microbial diversity and promote health-associated genera including Faecalibacterium and Akkermansia.

**Conclusions:** Dietary fibers and prebiotics are promising, low-risk strategies for gut microbiota modulation in T2DM. However, further standardized, long-term randomized studies integrating microbiome profiling and clinically meaningful endpoints are required to support precision nutrition approaches. The current evidence base is limited by heterogeneity in study design, intervention type and duration, microbial assessment methodologies, and short follow-up periods.

## Abstract

Oligosaccharide prebiotics, such as inulin, fructooligosaccharides (FOS), and galactooligosaccharides (GOS), have demonstrated significant effects on gut microbiota and host health across in vitro, animal, and clinical studies. These studies consistently report an increase in beneficial bacteria, particularly Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, leading to higher production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) such as acetate, propionate, and butyrate. These metabolic changes are linked to improved integrity of the epithelial barrier, reduced inflammatory signaling, modulation of immune responses, and enhanced metabolic balance. Biotechnological production methods, including enzymatic synthesis, microbial fermentation, and controlled depolymerization of plant polysaccharides, allow for precise control over the degree of polymerization and the types of glycosidic linkages. This control directly affects the fermentability, microbial selectivity, and functional effectiveness of the prebiotics. When incorporated into functional food systems, oligosaccharide prebiotics can enhance physicochemical properties such as texture, sweetness, and stability, all while maintaining their biological performance. Advanced delivery technologies, such as nano- and microencapsulation, improve thermal stability, resistance to gastrointestinal degradation, and targeted colon-specific release. Additionally, synbiotic formulations can further enhance the effectiveness of these prebiotics by promoting microbial colonization and sustained availability of SCFAs. Therapeutic benefits have been observed across various models of gastrointestinal health, metabolism, immune responses, and the gut-brain axis. These benefits involve mechanisms such as GPCR activation, histone deacetylase inhibition, and cytokine regulation. However, several challenges remain, including dose-dependent gastrointestinal intolerance, variability in individual microbiomes, degradation during processing, regulatory hurdles, and high costs of downstream processing. Overall, these findings highlight oligosaccharide prebiotics as versatile and scalable biotechnological ingredients, emphasizing the need for standardized production methods, precise dosing, and long-term clinical validation.

## Introduction

Functional foods are crucial in modern healthcare, offering benefits beyond essential nutrition. Enriched with bioactive compounds, they help prevent chronic diseases and promote overall well-being (Topolska et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR179 "Topolska K, Florkiewicz A, Filipiak-Florkiewicz A (2021) Functional Food—Consumer Motivations and Expectations. Int J Environ Res Public Health 18:5327. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph18105327
                  
                ")). Recent changes in food consciousness have led us to invest in functional foods, including prebiotics, probiotics, and synbiotics (Al-Habsi et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR5 "Al-Habsi N, Al-Khalili M, Haque SA et al (2024) Health Benefits of Prebiotics, Probiotics, Synbiotics, and Postbiotics. Nutrients 16:3955. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/nu16223955
                  
                ")). The research area extends to postbiotics, gut microbiome, and further genomic studies such as nutrigenomics and nutrigenetics (Lagoumintzis and Patrinos [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR97 "Lagoumintzis G, Patrinos GP (2023) Triangulating nutrigenomics, metabolomics and microbiomics toward personalized nutrition and healthy living. Hum Genomics 17:109. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1186/s40246-023-00561-w
                  
                ")). Probiotics are food supplements generally containing living bacteria, such as yoghurt, whereas prebiotics are typically foods having inert fibres, such as fruits, vegetables, and grains (Marco et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR129 "Marco ML, Sanders ME, Gänzle M et al (2021) The International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics (ISAPP) consensus statement on fermented foods. Nat Rev Gastroenterol Hepatol 18:196–208. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1038/s41575-020-00390-5
                  
                ")). Prebiotics, a key component of functional foods, are nondigestible ingredients that selectively stimulate beneficial gut microorganisms, such as bifidobacteria and lactic acid bacteria (Victoria Obayomi et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR183 "Victoria Obayomi O, Folakemi Olaniran A, Olugbemiga Owa S (2024) Unveiling the role of functional foods with emphasis on prebiotics and probiotics in human health: A review. J Funct Foods 119:106337. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jff.2024.106337
                  
                ")). They are naturally present in plant sources like chicory, onion, garlic, bananas, tomato, corn starch/cobs, apple peels, citrus fruits, sugar beet pulp, yeast cell walls, bamboo, birchwood, oats, barley, soybeans, crustacean shells, asparagus, mushrooms, chitin, konjac root, agave plant, artichoke, cereal brans, brown algae, larch tree, psyllium husk etc. (Chowdhury et al. [2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR36 "Chowdhury S, Das S, Bhattacharjee D et al (2015) Prebiotics—clinical relevance. Indian J Nat Prod Resour 6:91–97")). They can also be produced using microorganisms and their enzymes through fermentation processes (Lockyer and Stanner [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR120 "Lockyer S, Stanner S (2019) Prebiotics – an added benefit of some fibre types. Nutr Bull 44:74–91. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1111/nbu.12366
                  
                ")). Prebiotics are classified as natural or synthetic, but are generally grouped based on their resistance to digestion, fermentation by the gut microbiota, and health benefits. The general class of prebiotics includes oligosaccharides, polyols, and dietary fibers (Davani-Davari et al. [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR40 "Davani-Davari D, Negahdaripour M, Karimzadeh I et al (2019) Prebiotics: Definition, Types, Sources, Mechanisms, and Clinical Applications. Foods 8:92. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/foods8030092
                  
                ")). Prebiotics are characterised by three key attributes: (a) their ability to withstand acidity, enzymatic hydrolysis by the host, and gastro-intestinal absorption; (b) their capacity to undergo fermentation by the gut microbiota; and (c) their selective promotion of the growth and/or metabolic activity of beneficial intestinal bacteria that contribute to host health and well-being (Gibson et al. [2004](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR61 "Gibson GR, Probert HM, Loo J, Van et al (2004) Dietary modulation of the human colonic microbiota: updating the concept of prebiotics. Nutr Res Rev 17:259–275. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1079/NRR200479
                  
                ")). Among these, oligosaccharide prebiotics have gained attention for their ability to modulate gut microbiota, enhance immune function, and support metabolic health (Zeng et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR208 "Zeng M, van Pijkeren J, Pan X (2023) Gluco-oligosaccharides as potential prebiotics: Synthesis, purification, structural characterization, and evaluation of prebiotic effect. Compr Rev Food Sci Food Saf 22:2611–2651. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1111/1541-4337.13156
                  
                ")). Oligosaccharides, prebiotics found naturally or synthesised, such as fructooligosaccharides (FOS), galactooligosaccharides (GOS), xylooligosaccharides (XOS), and others, serve as key prebiotic ingredients in functional foods (Table[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#Tab1)). Homogenised samples of oligosaccharides and glycoconjugates can also be obtained chemically, enzymatically, or by other biological methods for systematic studies (Lv et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR127 "Lv Z, Liu H, Hao H et al (2023) Chemical synthesis of oligosaccharides and their application in new drug research. Eur J Med Chem 249:115164. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/J.EJMECH.2023.115164
                  
                ")). With the growing applications in functional foods and therapeutics, oligosaccharide-based prebiotics are promising to shape the future of preventive healthcare and nutrition. This review explores the innovations and challenges in utilising oligosaccharide prebiotics in functional foods and therapeutics, highlighting their potential in disease prevention and healthcare advancements.

## Comparative analysis of oligosaccharide prebiotics with other functional ingredients

### Differences between prebiotics, probiotics, and postbiotics

Probiotics are live microorganisms that act through various means, including competing for colonization sites and nutrients, inhibiting growth by producing SCFAs and bacteriocins, modulating the immune response, and improving gut barrier integrity. Examples of probiotics include yogurt, kefir, sauerkraut, kimchi, and miso. Prebiotics are non-living, specialised plant fibers that are selectively utilised by host microbes to alter the microbiome’s composition and activity, promoting reproduction and metabolism of intestinal probiotics. Examples of prebiotics can be bananas, onions, garlic, asparagus, and chicory root. Postbiotics are inactivated bacteria and bacterial components, including cell structures, secretory molecules, and metabolites, which play a vital role in restoring intestinal flora and improving blood glucose levels, exerting a wide range of actions. Examples of postbiotics include SCFAs such as butyrate, amino acids, vitamins B and K, and antimicrobial peptides (Collado et al. [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR37 "Collado MC, Vinderola G, Salminen S (2019) Postbiotics: facts and open questions. A position paper on the need for a consensus definition. Benef Microbes 10:711–720. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3920/BM2019.0015

### Synergistic effects of prebiotics with other bioactive

Synergistic combinations of prebiotics with probiotics, postbiotics, and other bioactive compounds enhance modulation of the gut microbiota beyond the effects of individual components. ## Structural Diversity and Sources of Oligosaccharide Prebiotics

> Oligosaccharides exhibit significant structural diversity, directly influencing their biological functions and prebiotic efficacy. Several factors, including molecular size, composition, and degree of polymerisation, influence the prebiotic capacity of oligosaccharides. These structural characteristics can significantly affect their interactions with the gut microbiota, thereby impacting their prebiotic efficacy. One key aspect is the degree of polymerisation (DP), with oligosaccharides typically having a DP of less than 10, which affects their fermentability and selective utilisation by the gut microbiota (Ooi et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR146 "Ooi MCY, Zhang X, Beaudry CM et al (2022) Chromatographic preparation of food-grade prebiotic oligosaccharides with defined degree of polymerization. Food Chem. 
>                   https://doi.org/10.1016/j.foodchem.2021.131542
>                   
>                 ")). Their monosaccharide composition varies, including common sugars such as glucose, galactose, and fructose, as well as less common sugars such as rhamnose and arabinose. The specific monosaccharides and their linkages determine the oligosaccharide’s functionality (Liu et al. [2021a](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR113 "Liu H, Wei X, Zu S et al (2021a) Separation and identification of neutral oligosaccharides with prebiotic activities from apple pectin. Food Hydrocoll. 
>                   https://doi.org/10.1016/j.foodhyd.2021.107062
>                   
>                 ")). Additionally, linkage types, particularly the configuration of glycosidic bonds (e.g., β1→4, β1→3), play a crucial role in determining resistance to enzymatic digestion and subsequent microbial metabolism (Zeng et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR208 "Zeng M, van Pijkeren J, Pan X (2023) Gluco-oligosaccharides as potential prebiotics: Synthesis, purification, structural characterization, and evaluation of prebiotic effect. Compr Rev Food Sci Food Saf 22:2611–2651. 
>                   https://doi.org/10.1111/1541-4337.13156
>                   
>                 ")). The conformation of oligosaccharides, influenced by factors such as hydroxyl group orientation and ring puckering, shapes their global conformational dynamics (Yang et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR199 "Yang S, Wu C, Yan Q et al (2023) Nondigestible Functional Oligosaccharides: Enzymatic Production and Food Applications for Intestinal Health. Annu Rev Food Sci Technol 14:297–322. 
>                   https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-food-052720-114503
>                   
>                 ")). The molecular size of oligosaccharides, particularly those smaller than 3 kDa, often correlates with a higher prebiotic index due to enhanced fermentation by specific probiotic strains, further highlighting the importance of their structural attributes in modulating gut health (Yoo et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR202 "Yoo S, Jung S-C, Kwak K, Kim J-S (2024) The Role of Prebiotics in Modulating Gut Microbiota: Implications for Human Health. Int J Mol Sci 25:4834. 
>                   https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms25094834
>                   
>                 ")).

Natural oligosaccharides are highly regarded for their nutritional benefits and complex biological activities, contributing to gut health and overall well-being. In contrast, synthetic oligosaccharides provide precise structural control and enhanced versatility, making them valuable for advanced technological and research applications. A clear understanding of the differences in their production, structure, and functionality is essential for selecting the most suitable type based on specific requirements (Chen et al. [2024b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR31 "Chen Y, Sui X, Wang Y et al (2024b) Preparation, structural characterization, biological activity, and nutritional applications of oligosaccharides. Food Chem X 22:101289. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fochx.2024.101289
                  
                ")). Table[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#Tab4) compiles various oligosaccharide prebiotics, their sources, and their reported therapeutic benefits, as reported in the literature.

## Mechanisms of action of oligosaccharide prebiotics

Oligosaccharides selectively promote the growth of beneficial gut bacteria, including Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium (Sulek et al. [2014](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR170 "Sulek K, Vigsnaes LK, Schmidt LR et al (2014) A combined metabolomic and phylogenetic study reveals putatively prebiotic effects of high molecular weight arabino-oligosaccharides when assessed by invitro fermentation in bacterial communities derived from humans. Anaerobe 28:68–77. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.anaerobe.2014.05.007
                  
                ")). The fermentation of oligosaccharides by gut bacteria produces SCFAs, such as acetate, propionate, and butyrate, which are crucial for gut health. These SCFAs lower gut pH, maintaining a healthy gut environment and preventing the growth of harmful bacteria (Kazlauskaite et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR87 "Kazlauskaite R, Cheaib B, Humble J et al (2022) Deploying an in vitro Gut model to assay the impact of the mannan-oligosaccharide prebiotic bio-Mos on the atlantic salmon (salmo salar) gut microbiome. Microbiol Spectr 10(3), 10:e01953–21. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1128/spectrum.01953-21
                  
                ")). SCFAs help maintain gut homeostasis by maintaining luminal pH, enhancing mucus secretion, and giving energy to colonocytes (Fusco et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR58 "Fusco W, Lorenzo MB, Cintoni M et al (2023) Short-Chain Fatty-Acid-Producing Bacteria: Key Components of the Human Gut Microbiota. Nutrients 15:2211. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/nu15092211
                  
                ")). Recent studies show their function in gene expression, cell proliferation, cell differentiation, apoptosis, and inflammation (Chen et al. [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR28 "Chen N, Wu J, Wang J et al (2021) Short chain fatty acids inhibit endotoxin-induced uveitis and inflammatory responses of retinal astrocytes. Exp Eye Res. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.exer.2021.108520
                  
                ")). Non-digestible oligosaccharides are certain kinds of oligosaccharides that are resistant to hydrolysis and absorption in the upper gastrointestinal tract. However, gut bacteria can ferment these oligosaccharides in the large intestine, producing SCFAs (Duan et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR48 "Duan H, Wang L, Huangfu M, Li H (2023) The impact of microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids on macrophage activities in disease: Mechanisms and therapeutic potentials. Biomed Pharmacother 165:115276. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biopha.2023.115276
                  
                ")).

Specific oligosaccharides, such as FOS, have shown promising results in alleviating colitis symptoms by modulating the gut microbiota and enhancing the production of anti-inflammatory metabolites through activation of the aromatic hydrocarbon receptor(Yang et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR198 "Yang C, Du Y, Li Q et al (2024) Fructo-oligosaccharides Alleviated Ulcerative Colitis via Gut Microbiota-Dependent Tryptophan Metabolism in Association with Aromatic Hydrocarbon Receptor Activation in Mice. J Agric Food Chem 72:27912–27922. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jafc.4c07248
                  
                ")). FOS has been shown to modulate tryptophan metabolism, leading to the production of beneficial metabolites, such as IAA and IPA, which activate the AhR/IL-22 axis and enhance gut health (Yang et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR198 "Yang C, Du Y, Li Q et al (2024) Fructo-oligosaccharides Alleviated Ulcerative Colitis via Gut Microbiota-Dependent Tryptophan Metabolism in Association with Aromatic Hydrocarbon Receptor Activation in Mice. J Agric Food Chem 72:27912–27922. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jafc.4c07248
                  
                ")). In the colon, XOS enhances strain-specific preferences for fermentation by bifidobacteria and other commensals, producing short-chain fatty acids that moderate immune responses and reinforce intestinal barrier integrity, thereby fostering host health (Schropp et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR161 "Schropp N, Stanislas V, Michels KB, Thriene K (2023) How Do Prebiotics Affect Human Intestinal Bacteria?—Assessment of Bacterial Growth with Inulin and XOS In Vitro. Int J Mol Sci. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms241612796
                  
                ")). FOS has been shown to promote cell proliferation, increase SCFA production, and enhance the inhibition of biofilm formation by pathogenic bacteria, suggesting its potential as a prebiotic to strengthen probiotic effects on the skin (Shao et al. [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR162 "Shao L, Li T, Yang S et al (2025) The prebiotic effects of fructooligosaccharides enhance the growth characteristics of Staphylococcus epidermidis and enhance the inhibition of Staphylococcus aureus biofilm formation. Int J Cosmet Sci 47:155–167. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1111/ics.13020
                  
                ")). XOS and β-glucans modulate gut microbiota and SCFA levels in diabetic rats. While XOS improved blood glucose without altering _Lactobacillus_ or _Roseburia_, β-glucan increased both bacterial populations and SCFA (Zahara et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR205 "Zahara I, Mahati E, Sulchan M et al (2024) Effect of xylo-oligosaccharides and β-glucan on gut microbiota and short chain fatty acid in diabetic rats. J Adv Biotechnol Experimental Ther 7:167. 
                  https://doi.org/10.5455/jabet.2024.d15
                  
                ")). Figure[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#Fig2) illustrates the mechanism of action of oligosaccharide prebiotics.

## Short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production and impact on gut health

Oligosaccharides reach the colon and are fermented by the gut microbiota to produce SCFAs, including acetate, propionate, and butyrate (Duan et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR48 "Duan H, Wang L, Huangfu M, Li H (2023) The impact of microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids on macrophage activities in disease: Mechanisms and therapeutic potentials. Biomed Pharmacother 165:115276. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biopha.2023.115276
                  
                ")). These SCFAs are key metabolic byproducts of dietary fiber fermentation and play crucial roles in gut health, energy metabolism, and immune regulation. The production of SCFAs depends on specific bacterial species, with Bifidobacteria primarily generating acetate, while other saccharolytic bacteria contribute to propionate and butyrate synthesis (Fusco et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR58 "Fusco W, Lorenzo MB, Cintoni M et al (2023) Short-Chain Fatty-Acid-Producing Bacteria: Key Components of the Human Gut Microbiota. Nutrients 15:2211. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/nu15092211
                  
                ")). SCFAs significantly contribute to colonic health by exerting anti-inflammatory effects, enhancing gut barrier integrity, providing energy for colonocytes, and modulating gut pH, thereby influencing microbial composition. Their mechanisms of action include activating G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) such as GPR41 and GPR43, which regulate immune responses and metabolic homeostasis, and inhibiting histone deacetylases (HDACs), leading to changes in gene expression that support gut health (Wang et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR187 "Wang L, Zhang G, Li Q et al (2024) Carrageenan oligosaccharide alleviates intestinal damage via gut microflora through activating IMD/relish pathway in female Drosophila melanogaster. FASEB J. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1096/fj.202301218R
                  
                ") b). Beyond the gut, SCFAs impact systemic health through gut-organ axes, influencing the liver, brain, and cardiovascular system while contributing to glucose regulation, energy metabolism, and immune modulation. Increasing colonic propionate production with SCFAs has been suggested as an approach to reduce liver fat in NAFLD patients (Chambers et al. [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR220 "Edward S, Chambers Claire S, Annette B, Rugyendo Douglas J, Tom M, Catriona P, Tedford Jimmy D, Louise B, Thomas Arne N, Akbar Natalie E, Rohini R, Mark S, Pinelopi RT, Gary M (2019) Frost The effects of dietary supplementation with inulin and inulin‐propionate ester on hepatic steatosis in adults with non‐alcoholic fatty liver disease Diabetes Obesity and Metabolism 21(2) 372–376. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1111/dom.13500
                  
                ")). SCFAs impact neuroimmune signalling by modulating the production of neurotropic factors and reducing neuroinflammation. For instance, a high-fiber diet increases SCFA levels, which correlates with decreased hippocampal inflammation and increased brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) levels (Church et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR218 "Church JS, Bannish JAM, Adrian LA, Rojas Martinez K, Henshaw A, Schwartzer JJ (2023) Serum short chain fatty acids mediate hippocampal BDNF and correlate with decreasing neuroinflammation following high pectin fiber diet in mice. Front Neurosci 17:1134080. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3389/fnins.2023.1134080
                  
                ")). Their therapeutic potential extends to conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), where they have shown promise in treating ulcerative colitis. A study on DSS-treated C57BL/6J mice demonstrated that gavage with SCFA-producing bacterial strains, _Bifidobacterium bifidum H3-R2_,_Propionibacterium freudenreichii B1_, and _Clostridium butyricum C1-6_ led to significant improvements in colonic health, reduced inflammatory markers, and altered gut microbiome composition (Yang et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR221 "Yang S, Shang J, Liu L, Tang Z, Meng X (2022) Strains producing different short-chain fatty acids alleviate DSS-induced ulcerative colitis by regulating intestinal microecology. Food Funct 13(23):12156–12169. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1039/d2fo01577c
                  
                ")). Understanding this connection between prebiotic fermentation and SCFA production is essential for leveraging oligosaccharides in functional foods and therapeutics aimed at promoting overall health.

## Influence on gut-brain axis, immune modulation, and anti-inflammatory properties

Oligosaccharides exhibit anti-inflammatory properties by improving gut barrier integrity and reducing pro-inflammatory cytokines. For example, carrageenan oligosaccharides (COS) prevent intestinal inflammation and maintain gut morphology (Wang et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR187 "Wang L, Zhang G, Li Q et al (2024) Carrageenan oligosaccharide alleviates intestinal damage via gut microflora through activating IMD/relish pathway in female Drosophila melanogaster. FASEB J. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1096/fj.202301218R
                  
                ")). HMOs also reduce inflammation in conditions like asthma by modulating gut microbiota and SCFA production (Han et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR69 "Han X, Wang Z, Cao H et al (2024) Dietary human milk oligosaccharides reduce allergic airway inflammation by modulating SCFAs level and ILC2 activity. Immunology 173:562–574. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1111/imm.13845
                  
                ")). DFO has been shown to boost immune responses and modulate gut microbiota, reducing inflammation (Pansai et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR148 "Pansai N, Chakree K, Takahashi Yupanqui C et al (2020) Gut microbiota modulation and immune boosting properties of prebiotic dragon fruit oligosaccharides. Int J Food Sci Technol 55:55–64. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1111/ijfs.14230
                  
                ")).

Oligosaccharides such as FOS and GOS can modulate the immune system by influencing gut microbiota, which, in turn, affects gut-associated lymphoid tissue and immune responses (Vijayasarathy et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR184 "Vijayasarathy M, Prabhu YA, Pavithra S et al (2022) Immune response of fructo and galacto-oligosaccharides. In: Ed(s) Kesharwani RK, Rao TJM, Keservani RK . Prebiotics and Probiotics in Disease Regulation and Management. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1002/9781394167227.ch2
                  
                ")). Specific HMOs, such as 2′-fucosyllactose (2′-FL) and 6′-sialyllactose (6′-SL), have been shown to reduce allergic airway inflammation and modulate immune responses via gut microbiota-derived SCFAs (Han et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR69 "Han X, Wang Z, Cao H et al (2024) Dietary human milk oligosaccharides reduce allergic airway inflammation by modulating SCFAs level and ILC2 activity. Immunology 173:562–574. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1111/imm.13845
                  
                "); Kim et al. [2024b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR91 "Kim J-Y, Lee S, Kim G et al (2024b) Ameliorating effect of 2′-fucosyllactose and 6′-sialyllactose on lipopolysaccharide-induced intestinal inflammation. J Dairy Sci 107:4147–4160. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3168/jds.2024-24325
                  
                ")). POS can enhance immune responses by increasing immunoglobulin levels and reducing pro-inflammatory cytokines, thus protecting against viral infections (Sori et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR168 "Sori N, Kunnummal SP, Peddha MS, Khan M (2022) Prophylactic effect of pectic oligosaccharides against poly I: C- induced virus-like infection in BALB/c mice. J Food Biochem. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1111/jfbc.14459
                  
                ")).

## Oligosaccharide prebiotics in functional foods

Oligosaccharides, composed of two to ten monosaccharide residues, are extensively used in the food industry due to their nutritional value, organoleptic qualities, and functional properties that benefit human health. The most used oligosaccharides include GOS, FOS, XOS, MOS, IOS, and AOS (Narisetty et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR139 "Narisetty V, Parhi P, Mohan B et al (2022) Valorization of renewable resources to functional oligosaccharides: Recent trends and future prospective. Bioresour Technol. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biortech.2021.126590
                  
                ")). MOS is used mainly in animal feed and functional foods to modulate the gut microbiome (Faustino et al. [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR53 "Faustino M, Durão J, Pereira CF et al (2024) Up-scalable approaches for yeast mannan oligosaccharides (MOS) production: characterization and immunomodulatory properties. Food Bioprod Process 144:32–42. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fbp.2023.12.005
                  
                ")), while IOS (Kumar et al. [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR95 "Kumar S, Tissopi T, Mutturi S (2023) The successful synthesis of industrial isomaltooligosaccharides lies in the use of transglycosylating α-glucosidases: a review. Carbohydr Polym Technol Appl. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.carpta.2023.100325
                  
                ")) and AOS (Liu et al. [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR114 "Liu J, Yang S, Li X et al (2019) Alginate Oligosaccharides: Production, Biological Activities, and Potential Applications. Compr Rev Food Sci Food Saf 18:1859–1881. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1111/1541-4337.12494
                  
                ")) are valued for their bioactive properties, including antioxidant and prebiotic effects. Additionally, FOS serves as a low-calorie sweetener, enhancing the taste of various food products (Narisetty et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR139 "Narisetty V, Parhi P, Mohan B et al (2022) Valorization of renewable resources to functional oligosaccharides: Recent trends and future prospective. Bioresour Technol. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biortech.2021.126590
                  
                ")).

Oligosaccharides can be synthesized through multiple methods, including chemical synthesis, enzymatic reactions, and depolymerization of polysaccharides (Chen et al. [2024b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR31 "Chen Y, Sui X, Wang Y et al (2024b) Preparation, structural characterization, biological activity, and nutritional applications of oligosaccharides. Food Chem X 22:101289. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fochx.2024.101289
                  
                ")). Chemical synthesis, involving complex protection and deprotection steps, is less favored for large-scale production due to its complexity (Talens-Perales et al. [2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR172 "Talens-Perales D, Polaina J, Marín-Navarro J (2015) Enzyme engineering for oligosaccharide biosynthesis. In: Shukla P. Ed(s) Frontier Discoveries and Innovations in Interdisciplinary Microbiology. Springer, New Delhi. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/978-81-322-2610-9_2
                  
                ")). Enzymatic synthesis, using enzymes such as glycosyltransferases, transglycosidases, glycosidases, and glucansucrases, is preferred for its specificity and efficiency. Glycosyltransferases catalyze the transfer of sugar moieties to form glycosidic bonds, while transglycosidases and glycosidases are commonly used due to their high specificity (Plou et al. [2007](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR154 "Plou FJ, Segura AGD, Ballesteros A (2007) Application of glycosidases and transglycosidases in the synthesis of oligosaccharides. In: Polaina J, MacCabe AP. (eds) Industrial Enzymes. Springer, Dordrecht. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/1-4020-5377-0_9
                  
                ")). Depolymerization methods, such as enzymatic and acid hydrolysis, are widely used to break down polysaccharides into oligosaccharides. Enzymatic hydrolysis, using enzymes like alginate lyases, is favored for its reproducibility and lower cost, while acid hydrolysis is less specific (Zhu et al. [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR216 "Zhu B, Ni F, Sun Y et al (2019) Elucidation of degrading pattern and substrate recognition of a novel bifunctional alginate lyase from Flammeovirga sp. NJ-04 and its use for preparation alginate oligosaccharides. Biotechnol Biofuels 12. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1186/s13068-019-1352-8
                  
                ")). Physical methods, including mechanical extraction, are also employed to obtain oligosaccharides from natural sources (de Moura et al. [2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR41 "de Moura FA, Macagnan FT, da Silva LP (2015) Oligosaccharide production by hydrolysis of polysaccharides: a review. Int J Food Sci Technol 50:275–281. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1111/ijfs.12681
                  
                ")).

In the food industry, oligosaccharides serve a variety of purposes. They are widely used as prebiotics, supporting the growth of beneficial gut bacteria, enhancing gut health, and promoting overall well-being. As low-calorie sweeteners, oligosaccharides such as FOS are used to reduce calorie content while maintaining sweetness. They are also incorporated into functional foods for their health benefits, including immune modulation, cholesterol reduction, and anti-inflammatory properties (Narisetty et al. [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR139 "Narisetty V, Parhi P, Mohan B et al (2022) Valorization of renewable resources to functional oligosaccharides: Recent trends and future prospective. Bioresour Technol. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biortech.2021.126590
                  
                ")). Furthermore, oligosaccharides act as stabilizers and bulking agents, improving the texture and stability of food products (Giese et al. [2011](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR62 "Giese EC, Hirosi T, De Lourdes Corradi M et al (2011) Production, properties and applications of oligosaccharides. Semina:Ciencias Agrarias 32:683–700. 
                  https://doi.org/10.5433/1679-0359.2011v32n2p683
                  
                ")).

Despite their numerous benefits, large-scale production of oligosaccharides presents challenges. Hydrolysis of polysaccharides is considered the most effective approach due to its reproducibility and cost-effectiveness. However, downstream processing (DSP) remains a significant obstacle, as efficient methods are needed to isolate oligosaccharides from the reaction mixture. Overcoming these challenges would enable the broader application of oligosaccharides in the food industry (de Moura et al. [2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR41 "de Moura FA, Macagnan FT, da Silva LP (2015) Oligosaccharide production by hydrolysis of polysaccharides: a review. Int J Food Sci Technol 50:275–281. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1111/ijfs.12681
                  
                "); Kruschitz and Nidetzky [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR94 "Kruschitz A, Nidetzky B (2020) Downstream processing technologies in the biocatalytic production of oligosaccharides. Biotechnol Adv. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biotechadv.2020.107568
                  
                ")).

The unique physicochemical and physiological properties of oligosaccharides make them valuable in the food, pharmaceutical, and cosmetic industries. One of the primary roles of oligosaccharides in food formulation is texture enhancement. Interactions with starch can significantly influence the pasting and retrogradation behaviors of starch-containing foods. For instance, FOS and other oligosaccharides modify the viscosity and gelatinization properties of starch, thereby improving texture (Woodbury and Mauer [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR192 "Woodbury TJ, Mauer LJ (2023) Oligosaccharide, sucrose, and allulose effects on the pasting and retrogradation behaviors of wheat starch. Food Res Int. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.foodres.2023.113002
                  
                ")). Additionally, oligosaccharides can act as emulsifiers and stabilizers, like polysaccharides, enhancing the consistency and texture of various food products (Nobre et al. [2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13205-026-04776-1#ref-CR142 "Nobre C, Cerqueira MÂ, Rodrigues LR et al (2015) Production and Extraction of Polysaccharides and Oligosaccharides. and Their Use as New Food Additives. In Pandey et al., Ed(s). Industrial Biorefineries and White Biotechnology, Elsevier. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-444-63453-5.00021-5
                  
                ")).

Oligosaccharides also contribute to the stability of food formulations by extending product shelf life by limiting starch retrogradation, thereby helping

args.key_excerpts: "Oligosaccharide prebiotics, such as inulin, fructooligosaccharides (FOS), and galactooligosaccharides (GOS), have demonstrated significant effects on gut microbiota and host health across in vitro, animal, and clinical studies."
args.summary:
This is a review article titled "Oligosaccharide prebiotics in functional foods and therapeutics: innovations and challenges" published in 3 Biotech (Volume 16, article number 254, 2026) by K.S. Sandra, Megh Pravin Vithalkar, Vishnusai Beere, H.B. Bharath, B. Satyanarayana, Mohamed Rafiq, Yogendra Nayak, and others. The article examines oligosaccharide prebiotics such as inulin, fructooligosaccharides (FOS), and galactooligosaccharides (GOS) and their effects on gut microbiota and host health.

Key points from the review:

- These prebiotics consistently increase beneficial bacteria (Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus) and short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) like acetate, propionate, and butyrate, which are linked to improved epithelial barrier integrity, reduced inflammation, immune modulation, and enhanced metabolic balance.
- Biotechnological production methods include enzymatic synthesis, microbial fermentation, and controlled depolymerization of plant polysaccharides, allowing precise control over degree of polymerization and glycosidic linkages.
- In functional foods, oligosaccharide prebiotics enhance texture, sweetness, and stability while maintaining biological performance.
- Advanced delivery technologies like nano- and microencapsulation improve thermal stability, resistance to gastrointestinal degradation, and targeted colon-specific release.
- Synbiotic formulations can further enhance effectiveness by promoting microbial colonization and sustained SCFA availability.
- Therapeutic benefits have been observed in gastrointestinal health, metabolism, immune responses, and the gut-brain axis through mechanisms including GPCR activation, histone deacetylase inhibition, and cytokine regulation.
- Challenges include dose-dependent gastrointestinal intolerance, variability in individual microbiomes, degradation during processing, regulatory hurdles, and high costs of downstream processing.
- The article compares prebiotics with probiotics and postbiotics, discusses synergistic effects, structural diversity, mechanisms of action, SCFA production, and applications in functional foods.
- Oligosaccharides serve as low-calorie sweeteners, stabilizers, bulking agents, and texture enhancers in food products.
- The review emphasizes the need for standardized production methods, precise dosing, and long-term clinical validation.
