## Abstract

### Purpose of Review

The incidence of allergies is increasing and has been associated with several environmental factors including westernized diets. Changes in environment and nutrition can result in dysbiosis of the skin, gut, and lung microbiota altering the production of microbial metabolites, which may in turn generate epigenetic modifications. The present review addresses studies on pectin-mediated effects on allergies, including the immune modulating mechanisms by bacterial metabolites.

### Recent Findings

Recently, microbiota have gained attention as target for allergy intervention, especially with prebiotics, that are able to stimulate the growth and activity of certain microorganisms. Dietary fibers, which cannot be digested in the gastrointestinal tract, can alter the gut microbiota and lead to increased local and systemic concentrations of gut microbiota _-_ derived short chain fatty acids (SCFAs). These can promote the generation of peripheral regulatory T cells (T reg) by epigenetic modulation and suppress the inflammatory function of dendritic cells (DCs) by transcriptional modulation.

The dietary fiber pectin (a plant-derived polysaccharide commonly used as gelling agent and dietary supplement) can alter the ratio of _Firmicutes_ to _Bacteroidetes_ in gut and lung microbiota, increasing the concentrations of SCFAs in feces and sera, and reducing the development of airway inflammation by suppressing DC function.

### Summary

Pectin has shown immunomodulatory effects on allergies, although the underlying mechanisms still need to be elucidated. It has been suggested that the different types of pectin may exert direct and/or indirect immunomodulatory effects through different mechanisms. However, little is known about the relation of certain pectin structures to allergies.

## Introduction

The manifestation of allergies frequently is associated with a dysbiosis of the gut microbiome, which can be affected by environmental factors, cesarean section, antiseptic agents, lack of breastfeeding, certain drugs, and a low-fiber/high-fat diet [[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR1), [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR2)]. In contrast, homeostasis of gut microbiota can be achieved by the intake of prebiotics [[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR3), [4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR4)]. The International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics (ISAPP) defined prebiotics as “a substrate that is selectively fermented by a host microorganism that allows specific changes, both in the composition and/or activity in the gastrointestinal microflora that confers benefits upon host well-being and health” [[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR5),[6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR6),[7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR7)]. To be classified as prebiotics, the compounds must meet the following criteria: (I) non-digestible and resistant to breakdown by stomach acid and enzymes in the human gastrointestinal tract, (II) selectively fermented by intestinal microorganisms of the host, and (III) selectively targeting and stimulating the growth and activity of beneficial bacteria in the gut [[8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR8), [9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR9)].

Prebiotics beneficially influence the health of the host by either (I) indirectly increasing the secretion of bacteria-derived metabolites into the intestinal tract, in turn influencing many molecular and cellular processes, or by (II) directly affecting the immune response of certain cells, e.g., epithelial and immune cells [[10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR10)]. Therefore, prebiotics are considered as an immune active agent conferring a health benefit [[11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR11), [12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR12)].

Dietary fibers are polymers with three or more monomeric units (MU) which are mainly derived from edible parts of plants, certain types of animals (e.g., crustacean), or analogous carbohydrates that are neither digested nor absorbed in the human intestine [[13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR13)]. Therefore, they pass through the upper part of the gastrointestinal tract into the large intestine where they are fermented by advantageous bacteria stimulating their growth and activity, which confer them prebiotic activity [[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR12), [14](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR14), [15](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR15)]. Dietary fibers consist of carbohydrates as non-digestible oligosaccharides (e.g., short-chain and long-chain fructooligosaccharides (sc/lc FOS) and galactooligosaccharides (GOS), inulin) [[16](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR16)]; non-starch polysaccharides such as pectin, chitins, beta-glucan; and other plant components such as cellulose [[17](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR17),[18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR18),[19](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR19)], resistant starch [[20](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR20)], or resistant dextrin [[21](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR21)]. They also consist of non-carbohydrates, like lignin, that can also act as a dietary fiber (Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#Fig1)).

[Full size image](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z/figures/1)

Dietary fibers (overview). Dietary fibers are polymers mainly derived from edible parts of plants, certain types of animals or analogous carbohydrates that are neither digested nor absorbed in the human intestine. They can be divided into carbohydrates and non-carbohydrates (e.g., lignin). Carbohydrate fibers can be further subdivided in non-digestible oligosaccharides or polysaccharides such as non-starch-, resistant starch-, or dextran polysaccharides

Dietary fibers confer health benefits comprising decreased risks of coronary heart disease, colon cancer, and type 2 diabetes. Clinically, fiber deficiency increases the risk of colon, liver, and breast cancer, and increases mortality and death from both cancerous and non-cancerous diseases [[22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR22)].

Supplementation of prebiotics as food ingredients has been proposed to prevent several inflammatory diseases [[23](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR23),[24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR24),[25](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR25),[26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR26),[27](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR27)] as well as allergies [[10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR10), [28](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR28), [29](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR29), [30](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR30), [31](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR31),[32](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR32)]. Cohort studies have indicated that one of the factors preceding the development of food allergies is gut dysbiosis [[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR2), [33](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR33), [34](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR34)]. Therefore, gut microbiota have gained attention as a target of intervention against allergies, especially with prebiotics.

So far, most studies exploring the effect of dietary fiber on the allergic immune response used non-digestible oligosaccharides [[10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR10), [35](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR35), [36](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR36)]. Human milk–derived non-digestible oligosaccharides comprise short-chain galacto- (scGOS), long-chain fructo- (lsFOS), and acidic pectin–derived oligosaccharides (pAOS), which are together referred to as galacto-, fructo-, and acidic oligosaccharides (GFAs). Dietary fibers undergo microbial fermentation by commensal gut bacteria producing short-chain fatty acids (SCFA) with immune modulating properties [[37](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR37), [38](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR38)]. Long-term deficiency of dietary fiber intake increases the susceptibility to airway allergic disease (AAD), whereas proper fiber supplementation effectively promotes balanced Th1/Th2 immunity, significantly attenuates allergic inflammatory responses, and optimizes the structure of intestinal microbiota, which suggests its potential for novel preventive and therapeutic intervention strategies [[39](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR39)]. Taking this into consideration, this review gives an in-depth overview of the reported effects of dietary fiber pectin on the immunomodulation of allergic diseases.

## Pectin: Characteristics and Immune Modulating Effects

### Pectin Structure

Pectin is a dietary fiber accumulating in the primary cell walls and intercellular tissues of terrestrial plants, where it plays an important role as hydrating agent and cementing material [[40](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR40), [41](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR41)]. Pectin is a heterogeneous and complex acidic hetero-polysaccharide with a molecular mass of typically 50,000–150,000 g/mol, depending on extraction method and source material [[42](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR42)]. It contains a linear backbone of at least 65% galacturonic acid (GalA), which can either be free or methyl-esterified at the carboxyl groups present at C-6 (Fig.[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#Fig2)) [[43](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR43), [44](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR44)]. The pectin macromolecule contains fragments of linear and branched regions of polysaccharides such as homogalacturonan, rhamnogalacturonan, xylogalacturonan, and apiogalacturonan [[45](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR45), [46](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR46)]. In native, non-processed pectin, approximately 80% of carboxyl groups of GalA are esterified with methanol and present as methyl esters. Thus, the ratio of esterified GalA groups to total GalA groups is termed the degree of esterification (DE). Pectins are classified as high methoxy pectin (HMP) with DE > 50% or low methoxy pectin (LMP) with DE < 50% (Fig.[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#Fig2)) [[44](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR44)]. The majority of natural pectins is HMP (~ 80% DE), whereas LMP is more common in processed foods [[47](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR47), [48](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR48)]. The degree of esterification determines the properties of pectin in food technology as HMP can form a gel under acidic conditions (pH ~ 3) in the presence of high sugar concentrations, while LMP form gels by interaction with divalent cations, particularly Ca 2+ [[47](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR47), [48](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR48)]. Both HMP and LMP appear to possess immunomodulatory effects in mice. LMP likely is more efficiently fermented by the microbiota in the ileum, whereas HMP is mainly fermented in the proximal colon [[49](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR49)]. Moreover, it is suggested that structural features determine the effect of pectin on the immune system. Evidence has been provided that the backbones of pectin macromolecules have immunosuppressive activity [[50](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR50)].

Depolymerization of purified pectin or the raw materials by partial enzymatic hydrolysis leads to production of Pectin-derived oligosaccharides (POS) which were indicated as new prebiotic candidates [[51](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR51)]. The main suggested properties of POS stimulation are (I) growth of beneficial bacteria in the colon, (II) apoptosis of colon cancer cells, and (III) protection again various pathogens [[51](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR51)]. The different POS can include galacturonic acid (GalA), rhamnose (Rha), arabinose (Ara), and galactose (Gal) [[52](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR52)]. GFAs, consisting of pAOS, have shown to lower immune responses in cow-milk-allergic (CMA) mice, to enhance regulatory T cell (T reg) frequencies, and to induce mucosal IL-10 and TGF-β transcription while suppressing the allergic effector response [[53](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR53)]. Both animal studies and human clinical trials showed that dietary intervention with these dietary oligosaccharides early in life could lead to the prevention of atopic dermatitis, food allergy, and allergic asthma [[10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR10), [37](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR37), [54](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR54), [55](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR55)]. In line with this, supplementation with two mixtures of scGOS/lcFOS or scGOS/lcFOS/pAOS decreased the OVA-induced airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness in mice [[56](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR56)]. Moreover, OVA-specific IgE titers were decreased by more than 25%, although this effect was not significant [[56](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR56)]. The effects of the oligosaccharide mixture containing pAOS appeared to be more pronounced than the effects of the scGOS/lcFOS mixture without pAOS [[56](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR56)].

### Pectin-Mediated Health-Promoting Effects

Pectin and dietary fibers in general are considered to provide diverse health benefits including slow gastric emptying [[57](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR57)], improvement of physical bowel function [[58](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR58)], reduced glucose and cholesterol absorption [[59](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR59)], and increase of fecal mass [[60](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR60), [61](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR61)]. Pectin is recognized as a prebiotic that is not degraded by either human saliva or gastric acid and is resistant to pepsin, trypsin, and rennet [[62](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR62), [63](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR63)]. Several studies demonstrated that pectins from different sources such as apple [[64](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR64)] or citrus [[65](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR65)] can serve as valuable carbon sources for gut bacteria [[66](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR66)•]. The ability to degrade pectins seems to be a common trait among Gram-negative _Bacteroides_ species in the human colon [[67](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR67)], whereas only few Gram-positive bacterial species like _Firmicutes_ seem to ferment either pectin or its breakdown products [[68](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR68)]. Pectin is fermented by beneficial microbiota mainly in the large intestine (colon), generating the SCFAs acetate, propionate, and butyrate, all of which have beneficial health effects [[69](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR69), [70](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR70)]. Evidence suggests that SCFAs can affect the epigenome through metabolic regulatory receptors, potentially reducing obesity, diabetes, atherosclerosis, mucosal inflammation, carcinogenesis, and allergy [[22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR22), [71](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR71), [72](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR72), [73](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR73),[74](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR74)].

The average daily intake of pectin from fruit and vegetables has been estimated to be around 5 g, considering a fruit and vegetable consumption of 500 g per day [[75](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR75)]. Several studies reported that high-fiber diets improve diabetic control via decrease of both glucose and cholesterol absorption as well as lowered serum triglyceride levels [[76](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR76), [77](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR77)]. It was found that several dietary fibers lead to delayed absorption of glucose and fatty acids from the upper small intestine, decreasing available substrates for triglyceride synthesis [[78](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR78)]. In humans, pectin consumption (15 g/day over a period of 4 weeks) has been shown to slightly reduce blood LDL cholesterol levels by 3–7% [[79](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR79), [80](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR80)]. This effect likely depends on the source of pectin, since apple and citrus pectin were found to be more effective than orange pulp fiber pectin [[79](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR79)]. However, the mechanism appears to be related to an increase of viscosity in the intestinal tract, leading to a reduced absorption of cholesterol from either bile or food [[75](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR75), [81](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR81)]_._ Studies propose that the SCFA propionate leads to activation of the adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK), which is one of the regulators for glucose metabolism in the liver [[65](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR65), [82](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR82),[83](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR83),[84](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR84)]. Activated AMPK inhibits acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) leading to a decrease of lipogenesis [[65](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR65)]. Other studies in Apo E–deficient mice comparing high-cholesterol diet (HCD) with or without pectin supplementation showed improved lipid profiles and reduced atherosclerotic plaques in the HCD/pectin group [[81](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR81)]. The study suggested that microbiota-dependent butyrate production inhibits intestinal cholesterol absorption, leading to decreased levels of atherosclerosis [[85](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR85)].

Furthermore, pectin has favorable effects on maintaining the intestinal barrier, which consists of a thick mucus layer protecting the intestinal epithelial tissue. Recent studies found that intervention with pectin in mice led to increased amount of colonic gel-forming mucin 2 (MUC2), the expression of which is related to both the thickness of mucus layer and gut health [[86](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR86)].

Supplementation with LMP reduced type 1 diabetes (T1D) incidence in non-obese diabetic (NOD) mice by positively impacting cecal microbiota, enhancing the production of immune modulating bacterial SCFAs, as well as improving intestinal integrity in the cecum [[87](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR87)]. The maintenance of gut homeostasis by LMP further results in modulated gut-pancreatic autoimmune responses and in protection against T1D development [[87](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR87)]. Other studies revealed that pectin supplementation improved insulin and glucose profiles and reverse calorie restriction (CR)–induced insulin resistance in the rat CR model [[88](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR88)]. By suppressing pro-inflammatory cytokine production, LMP was shown to have anti-inflammatory effects [[89](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR89)]. A fiber-rich diet was also shown to improve glycemic control in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus [[90](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR90)].

It is suggested that pectin binds metals in the digestive tract, preventing their absorption [[91](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR91)]. Consequently, orally administered pectin is known to (I) remove heavy metals, (II) decrease lead absorption, and (III) reduce strontium bone and blood levels [[92](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR92), [93](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR93)].

Furthermore, pectin shows beneficial anti-cancer effects. Studies revealed that pH-modified citrus pectins (MCP), rich in galactoside residues, significantly diminish the number of lung metastases in C57BL/6 mice [[94](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR94), [95](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR95)]. This suggests that the galactoside residues impair cell–cell interactions by competing with the endogenous ligands of galactoside-binding proteins such as galectin-3 [[94](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR94), [95](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR95)]. Further studies found that modified apple pectin induces apoptosis in colorectal cancer cells by a dose-dependent increase of caspase 3, -8, and -9 expression [[96](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR96)].

A further health claim associated with pectin affects Alzheimer’s disease. A recent study suggests an impact of pectin polysaccharide on Aβ 42, an important molecule for pathology of Alzheimer’s disease, by inhibition of its aggregation [[97](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR97)].

Moreover, it has been suggested that pectin has beneficial effects on the manifestations of IgE-mediated food and respiratory allergy [[98](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR98)••].

### Effect of Pectin on the Immune Response and Allergic Sensitization

Pectin displays diverse immunomodulatory properties, comprising both direct effects on immune cells and indirect effects mediated by bacterial metabolites upon fermentation of pectin in the gut (Fig.[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#Fig3)) [[99](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR99), [100](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR100)•].

Immune modulation by pectin. Immune modulation by dietary fibers can either be indirectly mediated by their fermentation into short chain fatty acids (SCFAs) or directly caused by the pectin, e.g., via the blockage of the pro-inflammatory TLR2/1 pathway. Several positive health effects are associated with consumption of pectin such as maintaining the intestinal barrier, immune modulation like the activation of immune cells (T, B, NK cells), and the inhibition of inflammatory responses

Dietary fibers can directly interact with intestinal cells and mucosal immune cells [[101](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR101)], affecting immune cell responses by interaction with pattern recognition receptors (PRRs). Thereby distinct binding capacities of different pectins may cause the reported differences in immunomodulatory efficiency [[102](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR102), [103](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR103)]. The best characterized PRRs in the intestine are Toll-like receptors (TLRs), which were shown to also recognize dietary fibers [[104](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR104), [105](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR105)]. It was elucidated in human DCs and the mouse macrophage cell line RAW264.7 in vitro that pectin binds the ectodomain of Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) by electrostatic interactions and specifically inhibits the pro-inflammatory TLR2-TLR1 pathway while the tolerogenic TLR2-TLR6 pathway remains unaffected (Fig.[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#Fig3)) [[105](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR105)]. This effect was predominantly achieved with pectin having a low DE [[105](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR105)].

The immunomodulatory effects of pectin mainly depend on the content of galacturonic acid residues and the DE. Pectin with DE up to 80–90% inhibited iNOS and COX2 expression in murine peritoneal macrophages and inhibited MAPK phosphorylation, IKK kinase activity, and NF-κB activation more efficiently than pectin with lower DE (Fig.[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#Fig3)) [[106](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR106)]. In this context, highly esterified pectin was able to bind LPS, modifying its binding to TLR4 [[50](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR50), [106](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR106)]. Additionally, MCP with a decreased molecular weight and DE was shown to activate cytotoxic T cells, B cells, as well as NK cells in a dose-dependent manner [[107](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR107)]. Comparing the immunomodulatory effects of native and modified pectin on the example of citrus pectin showed, both types of pectin led to upregulated levels of IFN-γ in the spleen [[108](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR108)]. MCP, but also native citrus pectin, led to increased levels of TNF-a-, IFN-γ-, and IL-17 secretion, likely regulated by IL-4 [[108](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR108)]. Unbranched galacturonan regions were shown to increase the anti-inflammatory properties of pectin [[109](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR109)].

The role of pectin in the manifestation of type 1 allergies is controversially discussed. Different pectins are described to either promote or prevent allergies [[98](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR98)••, [110](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR110),[111](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR111),[112](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR112),[113](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR113),[114](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR114)]. The matrix effect of pectin-rich fruits has been suggested to reduce the digestibility of food allergens and thereby to facilitate the process of allergic sensitization in atopic individuals [[115](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR115)]. In line with this, the addition of apple pectin to purified kiwi allergen was able to protect the allergen from pepsin digestion in vitro [[115](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR115)]. An independent study showed that pectin reduces the accessibility of cleavage sites and/or epitope sequences of β-lactoglobulin through a non-specific interaction [[116](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR116)]. Other studies also reported anaphylaxis induced by pectin (Table [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#Tab1)) [[110](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR110), [111](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR111), [113](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR113)]. Pectin-mediated allergy was reported after drinking a pectin-containing smoothie [[110](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR110)]. In line with this, a positive skin prick test to both pectin and cashew was reported, and cross-reactivity between pectin and cashew was considered [[110](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR110), [114](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR114)]. Reports from the 1990s found that continued airborne exposure to pectin in the workplace was associated with the development of occupational asthma [[117](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR117),[118](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR118),[119](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR119)]. Jaakkola et al. reported 3 patients that developed occupational asthma after frequent inhalation of pectin [[119](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR119)]. Two patients showed immediate reduction in lung functions after an inhalation challenge with pectin and positive SPT, while the third showed a late response (10 h after the challenge) and dermographism after the SPT. Of the 3 patients only one had a positive RAST to pectin [[119](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR119)].

In vivo, oral administration of citrus pectin prevented the induction of immune tolerance induced by feeding of a high dose of OVA [[120](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR120)]. Citrus pectin feeding inhibited the development of the oral tolerance in the OVA-treated mice. Mice fed with pectin showed similar titers of antigen-specific serum IgG and similar levels of delayed-type hypersensitivity responses as those animals not tolerant. Here, citrus pectin increased the levels of serum OVA-specific IgG1 and IgE [[120](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR120)].

In contrast, other studies reported a beneficial effect of pectin on allergic sensitization by alteration of the intestinal microbiota [[39](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR39)]. Increased numbers of beneficial bacteria like _Bifidobacterium_ and the higher production rate of bacteria-derived SCFAs were suggested to lower the risk of food allergies [[121](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR121)]. Pectin containing more than 80% galacturonic acid residues was found both to decrease macrophage activity and inhibit delayed-type hypersensitivity reactions [[50](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR50)]. Moreover, alkali-soluble pectin suppressed IgE production in a human myeloma cell line in vitro [[112](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR112)]. Other results also indicate that administration of Asian pear pectin-sol (a pH and enzymatically modified pectin in colloidal dispersion) in sensitized mice suppressed allergic asthmatic reactions [[122](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR122)]. However, little is known whether pectin from different plant sources and different degrees of esterification exert distinct immune modulating properties.

### Modulation of Gastrointestinal Microbiota by Pectin

Pectin and POS are fermented in the colon by different bacterial genera such as _Bifidobacteria_, _Lactobacilli_, _Enterococcus_, _Eubacterium rectale_, _Faecalibacterium prausnitzii_, _Clostridium_, _Anaerostipes_, and _Roseburia_ spp _._ in order to promote their growth [[68](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR68), [69](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR69), [123](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR123), [124](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR124)]. The degradation of pectin is facilitated by different bacteria-derived enzymes such as pectinases, methylesterases, acetylsterases, and lyases [[125](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR125),[126](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR126),[127](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR127)], generating different POS that will vary depending on microbiota composition and pectin structure [[69](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR69), [100](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR100)•, [128](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR128),[129](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR129),[130](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR130),[131](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR131),[132](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR132)].

As mentioned before, the biological properties of both pectin and POS depend on different features such as molecular weight (MW) and type and structure of constituents (e.g., galacturonic acid or rhamnose) and DE [[51](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR51), [128](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR128)]. It is reported that pectin from orange, lemon, and sugar beet with high degree of methylation increase the colonization by _Bifidobacterium_, _Bacteroides_, and _Eubacterium_ species, while the POS derived from the same sources promoted the presence of _Bifidobacterium species, Bacteroides_, and _Lactobacillus_ when compared to the primary pectin [[133](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR133)••]. Pectins with high DE are degraded slower than the ones with lower DE and are reported to remain in the intestine for up to 24 h [[134](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR134),[135](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR135),[136](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR136)], while pectins with lower DE were easily metabolized [[135](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR135),[136](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR136),[137](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR137),[138](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR138)]. In vitro fermentation studies of pectin and POS using human fecal samples have shown an increase in the number of _Bifidobacteria_, _Eubacterium rectale_, _Clostridium coccoides,_ and _Bacteroides prevotella_, with an elevated production of acetate, propionate and butyrate (summarized in Table [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#Tab2)) [[40](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR40), [129](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR129)]. The shift observed in the microbiota correlates with clinical effects of POS: POS-supplemented infant formulae was shown to both increase the number of _Bifidobacteria_ and _Lactobacilli_ and minimize the alteration of fecal microbiota after cessation of breast-feeding [[139](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR139)].

**Table 2 Pectin effects reported using in vitro fermentation systems**

[Full size table](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z/tables/2)

It is well accepted that an increase in bacteria-derived SCFAs promotes a protective effect in the intestine [[74](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR74), [140](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR140),[141](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR141),[142](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR142)]. In line with this, the composition of the gut microbiota can influence the development of the immune system and homeostatic processes at which the dysbiosis of microbial composition can increase the susceptibility for immune-mediated diseases, like asthma or allergy (reviewed in [[143](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR143)•]).

Compared to LMP, the fermentation of HMP increased the abundance of _Prevotella_ and _Ruminococcus_ species and was paralleled by higher levels of the SCFA propionate [[100](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR100)•, [144](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR144)]. Particularly, levels of _Ruminococcus_-derived propionate are enhanced when stimulated with rhamnose and fucose, both of which are structural subunits of pectin. This indicates that a higher production of propionate could relate with a high pectin content of rhamnose and fucose, as well as its slower fermentation process [[145](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR145),[146](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR146),[147](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR147)]. The SCFA acetate is reported to be produced by many different genera, but mainly by _Bifidobacteria_ and _Lactobacilli_ (Table [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#Tab2)) [[148](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR148), [149](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR149)]. Propionate is mainly produced by _Bacteroidetes_ and _Firmicutes_ (via the succinate pathway) [[146](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR146), [150](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR150)], while butyrate is produced by _Eubacterium rectale_, _Roseburia intestinalis_, _Faecalibacterium prausnitzii_, and some _Clostridia specie_ s (both from pyruvate via butyryl CoA:acetate CoA transferase and directly from acetate (Fig.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#Fig4)) [[151](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR151), [152](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11882-021-01020-z#ref-CR152)].

For example, acetate can be produced by many different genera; propionate is mainly produced by _Bacteroidetes_ and _Firmicutes_, while butyrate is mainly produced by _Clostridia_ species. This is a scientific article titled "The Dietary Fiber Pectin: Health Benefits and Potential for the Treatment of Allergies by Modulation of Gut Microbiota," published on 10 September 2021 in Current Allergy and Asthma Reports (Volume 21, Article 43). It is an open-access review article by Blanco-Pérez et al., with 29k Accesses and 204 Citations.

**Purpose:** The review addresses studies on pectin-mediated effects on allergies, including immune-modulating mechanisms by bacterial metabolites. The incidence of allergies is increasing and has been associated with environmental factors including westernized diets leading to gut dysbiosis.

**Key Findings on Pectin:**
- Pectin is a dietary fiber (plant-derived polysaccharide) commonly used as gelling agent and dietary supplement, with a molecular mass of 50,000–150,000 g/mol.
- It contains at least 65% galacturonic acid (GalA) and is classified as high methoxy (HMP, DE > 50%) or low methoxy pectin (LMP, DE < 50%).
- Pectin is fermented by gut microbiota (particularly Gram-negative Bacteroides species) into short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs): acetate, propionate, and butyrate.

**Health Benefits:**
- Reduces blood LDL cholesterol by 3–7% (at 15 g/day over 4 weeks)
- Delays glucose absorption, improves glycemic control
- Maintains intestinal barrier by increasing mucin 2 (MUC2) expression
- Anti-cancer effects (pH-modified citrus pectin reduces lung metastases; apple pectin induces apoptosis in colorectal cancer cells)
- Removes heavy metals, reduces lead absorption
- Beneficial effects on Alzheimer's disease via inhibition of Aβ42 aggregation

**Immunomodulatory Effects:**
- Pectin can directly bind TLR2 ectodomain, inhibiting pro-inflammatory TLR2-TLR1 pathway while preserving tolerogenic TLR2-TLR6 pathway
- SCFAs promote peripheral regulatory T cells (Treg) by epigenetic modulation and suppress dendritic cell (DC) inflammatory function
- Pectin alters the ratio of Firmicutes to Bacteroidetes in gut and lung microbiota
- Effects on allergies are controversial: some studies show pectin can protect allergens from digestion (facilitating sensitization), while others show beneficial effects by altering microbiota and increasing SCFAs

**Conclusion:** Pectin has shown immunomodulatory effects on allergies, though underlying mechanisms still need to be elucidated. Different types of pectin may exert direct and/or indirect immunomodulatory effects through different mechanisms, but little is known about the relation of certain pectin structures to allergies.

# Pectin in diet: Interactions with the human microbiome, role in gut homeostasis, and nutrient-drug interactions

## Highlights

*   •Pectins are dietary components in fruits and vegetables of several health benefits. 
*   •Pectin metabolism is mediated _via_[gut microbiota](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/intestine-flora) to [SCFAs](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/short-chain-fatty-acid) for absorption and cellular benefits. 
*   •Culture-dependent and independent approaches identified key pectinolytic organisms in gut bacteria. 
*   •A review of [microbial community](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/microbial-community) shifts associated with pectin [ingestion](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/ingestion) in the human GIT is presented. 
*   •Pectin modulates gut inflammatory and immune status in a structure-dependent manner. 

## Abstract

Pectins are a part of daily diet as well as food additives that are indigestible polysaccharides by human enzymes, however, they can be easily degraded by gut bacteria with the production of short chain fatty acids (SCFAs). Knowledge of pectin gut homeostasis and further how pectin affect gut bacterial communities is insufficient and limited. This review focuses on providing the whole story of how pectin functions as prebiotics in the gut. Understanding the interplay between functional and immunological responses inside animal or human gut as influenced by pectin in diets is provided. The interaction between pectin and [gut microbiota](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/gut-microbiota) is presented from both sides, in terms of how pectin affects gut microbiome and or the fermentation products produced in response by gut bacteria. This knowledge can be used to define preferred dietary pectins, targeting beneficial bacteria, and favoring balanced microbiota communities in the gut to maximize pectins’ health benefits.

## Introduction

Pectins are naturally occurring anionic heteropolysaccharide polymers that are rich in polygalacturonic acid. Pectins are especially abundant in fruits _e.g._ apples, plums, pears and citrus from which it is extracted and used as a gelling agent (Renard, Crépeau, & Thibault, 1995). In addition to vascular plants, pectin is also abundant in the cell wall of Streptophyta and green algae (Chlorophyta), members of which have a global distribution in aquatic freshwater and marine habitats (Domozych, 2001).

Structurally, pectin is one of the most complex naturally occurring plant polysaccharides (Mohnen, 2008). Homogalacturonan (HG) is the most abundant form of pectin, representing up to 60–65 % of pectin (Mohnen, 2008). HG is a polymer of α-1,4-linked d-galacturonic acid units. The galacturonic acid backbone in HG could be methyl esterified at _O_-6 and at _O_-2, or _O_-3 positions. Rhamnogalacturonan I is the second most abundant type of pectin, constituting 20–35 % of pectin (Mohnen, 2008). The backbone in Rhamnogalacturonan I (RG-1) are alternating alpha linked d-galacturonic acid and l-rhamnose. Side chains of arabinan, galactan, or arabinogalactan occur in approximately half the l-rhamnose subunits in RG-I; these units are substituted at the _C-4_ position with side-chains. Finally, the most complex type of pectin is Rhamnogalacturonan II (RG-II), which constitutes approximately10 % of pectin. Its structure is largely conserved across plant species and consists of an oligo-HG decorated with side branches of 13 different types of sugars in 21 different linkages (Ndeh et al., 2017). HG backbone is often heavily substituted giving rise to additional pectin motifs such as xylogalacturonan, apiogalacturonan-1, galactogalacturonan or arabinogalacturonan.

Pectin is a non-digestible carbohydrate, and its degradation in the human GIT is mediated by a fraction of the microbial community residing in the human intestine (Fig. 1). The prevailing anaerobic conditions in the human GIT tract promotes incomplete fermentative degradation processes, leading to the production of fermentation end products _e.g._ short chain fatty acids (SCFA). As such, the pectin molecule as well as its partial and complete degradation products interact with human GIT cells and mediate a wide range of physiological and immunological functions. Indeed, pectin is increasingly recognized to play an important role in gut inflammation, immunomodulation, and drug/nutrient interactions and have been promoted as a diet supplement for improving cholesterol levels, lowing blood pressure, and promoting overall gut health.

As an indigestible substrate, pectin represents an excellent model to assess human-microbiome interactions and how the human cells and the human microbiome act synergistically as a single holobiome unit for the host’s benefit. Prior microbiome-oriented studies have assessed mechanisms of pectin degradation in the GIT and the impact of pectin ingestion on the microbial community. Similarly, physiology/human/pharmacology-oriented studies have examined how pectin modulates human heath at the cellular levels. However comprehensive efforts to link microbial metabolism of pectin in the human GIT, with pectin (and its products) impact on the physioloigical/pharmacological levels have been sparse.

Here, we aim to provide a holistic overview of pectin’s fate and impact on the human GIT. We follow the fate of pectin post ingestion and evaluate the microbial communities mediating its degradation in the human GIT. Subsequently, we examine how pectin and its products, generated by microbial degradation, impact gut inflammation, immunology, nutrient and drug absorption. The review hence aims to bridge a gap between microbiome research and human physiology and highlight the interconnectivity between dietary intake, microbiome community structure and activity, and human health effects.

Pectin turnover represents a crucial process in global carbon cycling not only in the human GIT tract, but also in a wide range of terrestrial, plant-rich habitats _e.g._ forests (Yeager et al., 2017), as well as marine and aquatic environments where green algae survives and blooms (Hallegraeff, 1993; Hoshaw & McCourt, 1988). ## Summary and conclusions

Pectin degradation in the human GIT is entirely mediated by microorganisms. The initial debranching and depolymerization of the complex pectin structure is carried out by a relatively small fraction of the overall community in the GIT. This is a scientific review article published in Carbohydrate Polymers (Volume 255, 1 March 2021) that examines the role of pectin in diet, its interactions with the human gut microbiome, and its effects on gut homeostasis, inflammation, immunity, and nutrient-drug interactions.

**Key Points:**

- **Pectin Structure & Sources:** Pectins are anionic heteropolysaccharides abundant in fruits (apples, plums, pears, citrus) and vegetables. The main structural types are Homogalacturonan (HG, 60-65%), Rhamnogalacturonan I (RG-I, 20-35%), and Rhamnogalacturonan II (RG-II, ~10%).

- **Gut Microbiome Degradation:** Pectin is indigestible by human enzymes but is degraded by gut bacteria. Pectinolytic organisms include genera Bacteroides (Phylum Bacteroidetes), Clostridium, Eubacterium, Faecalibacterium, and Monoglobus (Phylum Firmicutes). The authors note that pectin degradation was first observed in the human colon as early as 1941.

- **Fermentation Products:** Pectin degradation produces short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) via anaerobic fermentation, which are then absorbed and provide cellular benefits.

- **Gut Inflammation & Immunity:** Pectin exhibits anti-inflammatory activity that is significantly influenced by the presence of neutral sugar side chains and degree of methyl esterification (DM). It protects against intestinal inflammation through both gut microbiota-dependent and -independent pathways. Pectin interacts with gut-associated lymphoreticular tissue and initiates immunomodulating effects through pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), mainly TLRs.

- **Nutrient-Drug Interactions:** Due to structural features and gelling properties, pectin can influence the absorption of nutrients and drugs. Low-methylated pectin (DE<50) decreases peptic digestibility of proteins more strongly than high-methylated pectin.

- **Research Gap:** The authors emphasize that prior studies have separately assessed pectin degradation mechanisms and physiological effects, but comprehensive efforts to link microbial metabolism of pectin with its impact on physiological/pharmacological levels have been sparse.

The article has 138 references and has been cited by 183 other publications. Funding was provided by the United States National Science Foundation (grant number 2016423).

# What is the evidence that probiotics are protective against colorectal cancer?

# From the Guidelines

**The current evidence suggests that probiotics may have a protective effect against colorectal cancer, although the evidence is not yet conclusive, and more research is needed to fully understand their potential benefits**. The most recent study, published in 2023, found that manipulation of the gut microbiome has the potential to influence colorectal cancer (CRC) risk, with a level of agreement of 62% among experts [1](#ref-1). This study also found that stool-based microbial markers have the potential to predict immunotherapy and chemotherapy responses in patients with CRC, with a level of agreement of 92% among experts [1](#ref-1).

### Key Findings

* A systematic review of clinical trials showed that probiotic/synbiotic administration improved enteric microbiota by reducing the abundance of potentially harmful bacteria, such as *Fusobacterium, Enterococcus, Porphyromonas, Pseudomonas* [1](#ref-1).
* Emerging evidence suggests that microbiota modulation can be associated with reduction in CRC-related bacteria and potentially CRC risk [1](#ref-1).
* A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial involving patients who had colonic polypectomy found that oral treatment with a synbiotic formula led to significant changes in gut microbiota, reduced colorectal proliferation, and improved epithelial barrier function [1](#ref-1).

### Recommendations

* **Physicians should offer advice on modification of lifestyle habits that could modulate gut microbiota, including low animal protein intake, low fat intake, and high fiber consumption, as well as administration of probiotics** [1](#ref-1).
* Regular consumption of probiotics through fermented foods (yogurt, kefir, sauerkraut) or supplements containing multiple strains at doses of at least 1-10 billion CFU daily may be beneficial [1](#ref-1).
* Probiotics should be considered as part of a comprehensive approach to colorectal cancer prevention that includes regular screening, a high-fiber diet, limited red meat consumption, regular exercise, and avoiding smoking and excessive alcohol [1](#ref-1).

### Limitations

* The level of evidence of the current recommendations is limited, with a classification of II-2 or III, and more definitive recommendations on the use of probiotics in clinical practice will need more support from data in future large-scale studies [1](#ref-1).
* There exists significant interindividual variation in gut microbiome, influenced by factors such as age, sex, dietary habits, smoking, body mass index, and antibiotic use, which should be taken into account when interpreting the results of studies on probiotics and CRC risk [1](#ref-1).

# From the Research

### Evidence of Probiotics in Colorectal Cancer Prevention

* The composition of gut microbiota is associated with the development of colorectal cancer (CRC) and other gut dysbiosis, and modulation of gut microbiota by probiotics and prebiotics could positively influence the cross-talk between the immune system and microbiota, preventing inflammation and CRC [2](#ref-2).
* Probiotics supplementation in patients with CRC improved their quality of life, enhanced gut microbiota diversity, reduced postoperative infection complications, and inhibited pro-inflammatory cytokine production [3](#ref-3).
* Probiotic supplementation protects CRC patients from treatment-associated adverse effects, and the beneficial impact of probiotic supplementation depends on several factors such as strain, dosage, duration of the intervention, host physiology, and other food supplements [4](#ref-4).
* Probiotics have properties that make them useful in the management and prevention of colorectal cancer, and can provide a new avenue to reduce the occurrence of this malignancy and enhance patients' quality of life [5](#ref-5).

### Mechanisms of Probiotics in Colorectal Cancer Prevention

* Probiotics have antitumor activity with various mechanisms such as nonspecific physiological and immunological mechanisms, alteration of the intestinal microflora, inactivation of cancerogenic compounds, competition with putrefactive and pathogenic microbiota, and improvement of the host's immune response [6](#ref-6).
* Probiotics can reduce the problems associated with chemotherapy and surgery when used synergistically, and can also increase the efficacy of chemotherapeutic medications [5](#ref-5).
* Targeted drug delivery and TRAIL collaboration techniques are other effective and promising methods that involve probiotics [5](#ref-5).

### Degree of Protection

* The degree of protection offered by probiotics against colorectal cancer is still being researched, and larger clinical trials of selected or a cocktail of probiotics are needed to confirm the efficacy, dosage, and interactions with chemotherapeutic agents [3](#ref-3).
* The beneficial effects of probiotics in patients with CRC have been observed regardless of the stage of cancer, and there is an opportunity for probiotics to be used in mainstream health care as a therapy in the fight against CRC, especially in early stages [3](#ref-3).

args.summary:
This webpage synthesizes evidence on whether probiotics are protective against colorectal cancer (CRC), last updated June 15, 2025. It draws from both clinical guidelines and research studies.

**From the Guidelines:** Current evidence suggests probiotics may have a protective effect against CRC, but the evidence is not yet conclusive. A 2023 study found gut microbiome manipulation can influence CRC risk (62% expert agreement), and stool-based microbial markers may predict immunotherapy/chemotherapy responses (92% agreement). Key findings include: probiotic/synbiotic administration reduces harmful bacteria (Fusobacterium, Enterococcus, Porphyromonas, Pseudomonas); microbiota modulation may reduce CRC-related bacteria; and a randomized trial found synbiotic treatment improved gut microbiota, reduced colorectal proliferation, and improved epithelial barrier function after polypectomy. Recommendations include lifestyle advice (low animal protein/fat, high fiber, probiotics), regular consumption of probiotics via fermented foods or supplements (1-10 billion CFU daily), and use as part of a comprehensive prevention approach including screening, diet, exercise, and avoidance of smoking/excess alcohol. Limitations: evidence level is II-2 or III; significant interindividual variation in gut microbiome exists.

**From the Research:** Probiotics can improve quality of life, enhance gut microbiota diversity, reduce postoperative infections, and inhibit pro-inflammatory cytokines in CRC patients. Protection depends on strain, dosage, duration, host physiology, and other factors. Mechanisms include antitumor activity via immunological mechanisms, altering intestinal microflora, inactivating carcinogens, competing with pathogenic microbiota, and improving immune response. Probiotics may also reduce chemotherapy/surgery complications and increase chemotherapeutic efficacy. The degree of protection is still being researched; larger clinical trials are needed. Beneficial effects have been observed across all cancer stages, with potential for use in mainstream healthcare, especially in early stages.

### **Abstract**

**Objectives:** Colorectal cancer (CRC) is highly prevalent worldwide and is a leading cause of cancer-related death. Probiotics, prebiotics, and synbiotics have recently attracted attention as preventive measures against colorectal neoplasms. We aimed to analyze the findings of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on the effects of probiotics, prebiotics, and synbiotics in patients at a high risk of CRC, outlining the challenges and future prospects of using probiotics to prevent colorectal tumors and providing evidence for clinical physicians in particular.

**Methods:** PubMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library databases were searched for relevant studies published up to January 7, 2022. RCTs conducted on populations with a high risk of CRC who received probiotics, prebiotics or synbiotics in comparison with placebo, candidate agent or no treatment were included. The primary outcome was the incidence or recurrence of any colorectal neoplasms. Additional outcomes included their effects on the diversity of gut microbiota and relevant inflammatory biomarkers. Safety outcomes were also analyzed. Two authors independently screened and selected studies based on pre-specified eligible criteria, performed data extraction and risk-of-bias assessment independently.

**Results:** Nine RCTs were included in the systematic review and meta-analysis. Probiotic supplementation significantly reduced adenoma incidence, but no significant benefit was observed in CRC incidence. Additionally, probiotics modulated gut microbiota and inflammatory biomarkers.

**Conclusion:** Probiotics may have beneficial effects in the prevention of CRC. More RCTs with larger sample sizes are warranted to further confirm these findings.
