## 5. BIFIDOBACTERIUM SPECIES

### 5.1 Genus Overview

The genus Bifidobacterium belongs to the Actinobacteria phylum and contains over 50 species. Bifidobacteria are members of the intestinal microbiota of mammals and other animals, and some strains are able to exert health-promoting effects. They use a unique fructose 6-phosphate pathway (bifid shunt) for monosaccharide degradation. The Xfp enzyme activity is a key taxonomic test. Seven phylogenetic groups exist, partially correlating with ecological niches (e.g., B. asteroides group in insects, B. pullorum in birds). Common human-associated species include B. adolescentis, B. breve, B. longum, B. bifidum, B. catenulatum, and B. pseudocatenulatum [9].

Bifidobacteria are among the first microbial colonizers of the intestines of newborns, and play key roles in the development of their physiology, including maturation of the immune system and use of dietary components. Bifidobacteria showed dominance during the early colonization of intestinal microbiota in infants. Breast-fed infants harbor more complex Bifidobacterium microbiota than formula-fed infants. Human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs) drive bifidobacterial development. B. bifidum, B. longum subsp. infantis, and B. breve are the most abundant species in breast-fed neonates. Bifidobacteria numbers and diversity decrease with age. In adults, bifidobacteria constitute about 4% of total fecal microbiota [6, 9].

Some Bifidobacterium strains are considered probiotic microorganisms because of their beneficial effects, and they have been included as bioactive ingredients in functional foods, mainly dairy products, as well as in food supplements and pharma products. Well-documented scientific evidence of their activities is currently available for bifidobacteria-containing preparations in some intestinal and extraintestinal pathologies [9].

### 5.2 Bifidobacterium longum

Bifidobacterium longum is a commensal gastrointestinal tract (GIT) inhabitant that is recognized as a significant member of the human gut microbiota and is the most abundant species in the infant gut (representing 56.2% of species in Bifidobacteriales, the most abundant class at 80.6%). It includes four subspecies: B. longum ssp. infantis, B. longum ssp. longum, B. longum ssp. suis, and B. longum ssp. suillum. Levels decline with age, falling to 2-14% in adults and further in the elderly [10].

**Mechanisms of Action:** The species produces beneficial bioactive molecules including short-chain fatty acids (acetate, lactate), exopolysaccharides, and serine protease inhibitors (serpins). These contribute to intestinal defenses, pathogen protection, immune modulation, and anti-inflammatory effects. Following a single oral administration, the strain B. longum ssp. longum AH1206 persisted in the human gut of 30% of trial subjects for the six-month duration of the study [10].

**Clinical Findings by Life Stage (from Gut Microbes, 2023):**

*Infants & Children:*
- **Necrotizing Enterocolitis (NEC):** A formulation including B. longum ssp. infantis BB02 was associated with a 54% reduction in NEC (Bell stage ≥2) in very preterm infants.
- **Diarrhea:** B. longum ssp. infantis CECT7210 significantly reduced diarrhea episodes by week 8. B. longum BORI combined with L. acidophilus reduced diarrhea duration by 1.2 days in rotavirus-hospitalized infants.
- **IBS:** A mixture of B. infantis M-63, B. breve M-16V, and B. longum BB536 resulted in complete resolution of abdominal pain in significantly more children (p=0.006).
- **Ulcerative Colitis:** The VSL#3® blend (containing B. longum) showed significant efficacy for inducing and maintaining remission in children with newly diagnosed UC (p<0.001).
- **Immunity:** B. longum BB536 significantly elevated IFN-γ secretion cells and the IFN-γ/IL-4 ratio in healthy newborns at 7 months. VSL#3® significantly reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines and increased anti-inflammatory cytokines in children with severe sepsis.
- **Respiratory Health:** B. longum BB536 significantly reduced sore throat duration in children aged 2-6 years. A multi-strain formulation reduced the number of children experiencing winter diseases by 25%.
- **Eczema:** Maternal supplementation with B. longum BL999 and L. rhamnosus LPR significantly reduced the risk of developing eczema in at-risk infants.

*Cardiovascular Health:* A combination of B. longum ssp. longum BL04 with other bifidobacteria significantly reduced total cholesterol and LDL-cholesterol in children with dyslipidemia [10].

B. longum and B. adolescentis are also reported to alleviate anxiety and depression, reduce stress, and enhance cognitive function, partly through production of neuroactive molecules like GABA [7].

### 5.3 Bifidobacterium bifidum

B. bifidum is one of the most prevalent species in the human gut alongside B. adolescentis, B. longum, B. breve, and others. It is abundant in breast-fed neonates and plays a key role in utilizing human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs) [6, 9]. B. bifidum, along with other Bifidobacterium species (B. infantis, B. breve), is important in infant gut for utilizing HMOs [6].

Bifidobacterium-based probiotics (including B. bifidum, B. longum, B. breve, B. lactis, B. adolescentis) are effective for gastrointestinal conditions such as constipation, antibiotic-associated diarrhea, acute gastroenteritis, IBS, IBD, H. pylori infections, and celiac disease. Benefits are achieved through modulating gut microbiota, boosting immune responses, strengthening the gut barrier, and producing metabolites (e.g., acetate, lactate, SCFAs, GABA) [7].

### 5.4 Bifidobacterium lactis (B. animalis subsp. lactis)

Probiotic efficacy has been best studied for strains of B. animalis subsp. lactis, B. breve, B. longum, and B. bifidum [9]. B. lactis and B. adolescentis are reported to reduce respiratory infections and asthma severity [7].

A 2019 study in Nutrients showed that the combination of B. animalis subsp. lactis and L. acidophilus showed the strongest anti-inflammatory activity in HT-29 cells, reducing IL-8 secretion, p-p65 NF-κB, p-p38 MAPK, VCAM-1, and COX-2, while increasing TLR2 expression. The authors concluded: "These results suggest that L. acidophilus and B. animalis subsp. lactis may exert a potent anti-inflammatory effect through modulating TLR2-mediated NF-κB and MAPK signaling pathways in inflammatory IECs" [36].

### 5.5 Bifidobacterium breve

Bifidobacterium breve is defined as a species within the Bifidobacterium genus, characterized as a Gram-positive microbe with potential health benefits, including immunoregulation and protection against infections, thus making it significant in the development of probiotic products. B. breve has been commonly isolated from the intestines of healthy breastfed infants and also from human milk [6].

**Health Benefits and Therapeutic Applications:**
- **Allergy Management:** B. breve strains in infant formulas with prebiotic oligosaccharides may help manage allergies, especially in non-breastfed infants. B. breve M-16V modulated cytokine expression and reduced allergic lung inflammation in mice exposed to prenatal air pollution.
- **Neuroprotection and Cognition:** B. breve appears neuroprotective for preterm neonates due to anti-inflammatory effects, though no significant neurodevelopmental effects were observed in children from RCTs. B. breve A1 showed potential in preventing cognitive impairment in Alzheimer's disease models and improving cognitive function in elderly humans with mild cognitive impairment. It also improved anxiety and depressive symptoms in schizophrenia patients.
- **Cardiovascular and Metabolic Health:** B. breve CECT7263 attenuated endothelial dysfunction and hypertension in animal models. B. breve B-3 showed anti-obesity effects and potential for increasing muscle mass (even heat-killed forms).
- **Necrotizing Enterocolitis:** A large study (1755 newborns) showed B. breve M-16V significantly reduced NEC, though another large study (1315 infants) found B. breve BBG-001 did not prevent NEC or late-onset sepsis.
- **Celiac Disease:** A trial in 49 children found B. breve reduced TNF-α levels after 3 months, though effects reversed after intervention ceased.

**Safety Considerations:** B. breve has been associated with rare adverse effects, including a case of septicemia in a neonate with omphalocele after administration of B. breve BBG-01, and reported cases of meningitis in neonates and infants (with strains showing resistance to penicillin and cephalosporins). Bifidobacterium isolates showed resistance to several antibiotics (cefoxitin, aztreonam, vancomycin, streptomycin, etc.) but susceptibility to penicillins and other specified antibiotics [6].

**Gut Microbiota and Immune Function:** Bifidobacteria produce acetate and lactate, which can be converted to butyrate by other bacteria, supporting colonocyte function and anti-inflammatory effects. Patients with gastrointestinal and metabolic diseases often have decreased Bifidobacterium levels [6].

### 5.6 Cross-Talk Interactions and Mechanisms

Bifidobacteria inhibit enteropathogens through organic acid production, antibacterial peptides, quorum-sensing inhibitors, and immune stimulation. They engage in cross-feeding mechanisms with other gut bacteria (e.g., Bacteroides, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Eubacterium rectale). Bifidobacterial exopolysaccharides and pili structures are important for gut colonization and are modulated by intestinal factors [9].

## 6. SACCHAROMYCES BOULARDII

### 6.1 Strain Background and Unique Advantages

Saccharomyces boulardii is currently the only probiotic yeast with established clinical validation for use in both humans and livestock. It is a non-colonizing, non-systemic yeast first isolated in 1923 by French scientist Henri Boulard from lychee fruit in Indonesia [14]. S. boulardii offers distinct advantages: (i) higher resistance to gastric acid and bile salts; (ii) intrinsic tolerance to multiple antibiotics; (iii) secretion of unique antimicrobial metabolites such as phenyllactic acid and 2-hydroxyisocaproic acid [11].

S. boulardii is genetically close to Saccharomyces cerevisiae but possesses distinct physiological traits. It cannot produce ascospores, use galactose as a carbon source, and is more resistant to temperature and acidic stress. Compared to S. cerevisiae, S. boulardii has gene copy number variations in stress response genes (HSP26, SSA3, SED1, etc.), pseudohyphal growth genes, and flocculation genes (FLO1). It lacks certain Ty elements and has a mutation in PGM2 associated with galactose utilization issues. S. boulardii grows optimally at 37°C (human body temperature), survives gastric pH (2-3), and resists digestive enzymes. It is more resistant to low pH than S. cerevisiae but less tolerant to bile salts. S. boulardii is also more resistant to very high temperatures keeping 65% viability after one hour at 52°C, while S. cerevisiae loses viability down to 45% [13].

### 6.2 Mechanisms of Action

**Antimicrobial Activity:** S. boulardii secretes enzymatic proteins, including a 54-kDa serine protease that degrades Clostridium difficile toxins A and B, and a 120-kDa phosphatase that dephosphorylates LPS endotoxins [11, 14]. It also produces a 63-kDa protein and acetic acid that inhibits E. coli [13]. It binds pathogens via mannose residues in its cell wall, acting as a decoy to flush them out. It adheres to mucus but not strongly to epithelial cells [13].

**Intestinal Barrier Repair:** S. boulardii upregulates MUC2, ZO-1, occludin, and claudin-1, strengthening intestinal tight junctions and promoting brush border enzyme production [11].

**Immunomodulation:** S. boulardii modulates inflammatory responses by decreasing pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-8, IL-1β, NF-κB, MAP kinases) and increasing anti-inflammatory cytokines (IL-4, IL-10). It also increases IgA and IgG levels. It acts via Dectin-1/Syk-CARD9/NF-κB signaling, promoting IL-10 and Treg differentiation [11, 13].

**Trophic Effects on Intestinal Mucosa:** S. boulardii stimulates brush border digestive enzymes (sucrase, lactase, maltase), nutrient transporters, and polyamine levels [13].

**Anticancer Activity:** S. boulardii demonstrates anticancer activity through apoptosis induction in Caco-2 colon cancer cells (62.23% apoptosis rate) [11].

### 6.3 Clinical Evidence

**Antibiotic-Associated Diarrhea (AAD):** Meta-analysis of 10 RCTs in adults found that S. boulardii was significantly protective for AAD with a pooled relative risk (RR) of 0.47 (95% CI 0.35–0.63, p<0.001). In children, AAD prevention improved by 7.6–30.1% [12]. The incidence of antibiotic-associated diarrhea (including C. difficile diarrhea) in the treatment group was only 3.4% compared to 17.3% in the controls (RR 0.2, 95% CI: 0.07-0.5) in a study by Kotowska et al. (2005, n=269 children) [14].

**C. difficile Infection:** Significant reduction in recurrent CDI (19–33.3% in two RCTs). Meta-analysis of probiotics showed RR=0.59 for preventing recurrences [12].

**Acute Infectious Diarrhea:** Meta-analysis of 7 RCTs (944 participants) showed ~1 day reduction in duration of childhood diarrhea [12]. A meta-analysis of 5 studies (619 children) found S. boulardii reduced diarrhea duration by a weighted mean difference of -1.1 days (95% CI: -1.3 to -0.8). A 2008 study of 100 Myanmar children showed mean diarrhea duration of 3.08 days with S. boulardii vs. 4.68 days in controls (p<0.05) [14].

**Persistent Diarrhea:** ~50% reduction in children [12].

**Enteral Nutrition-Related Diarrhea:** 5–8.2% reduction in three RCTs [12].

**Traveler's Diarrhea:** 5–11% reduction in two RCTs [12].

**H. pylori Infection:** Improved eradication rates from 71% to 80% with supplementation; reduced side effects of triple therapy. The incidence of adverse effects associated with triple therapy was significantly lower in the S. boulardii group compared to the controls (8.3% versus 30.9%, p=0.047) [12, 14].

**Crohn's Disease:** Two small RCTs showed improvement; reduced relapse (6% vs 38% in one study) [12].

**Ulcerative Colitis:** Limited evidence; small pilot studies showed promise [12].

**IBS:** Improved quality of life but inconsistent results on symptom improvement [12].

**Parasitic Infections:** Beneficial effects in amebiasis, giardiasis, and Blastocystis hominis [12].

**HIV-Related Diarrhea:** Higher doses (3g/day) showed benefit in limited data [12].

**Chronic Diarrhea in Children:** A randomized trial in 40 infants (6-36 months) found 65% of S. boulardii group achieved normal stool frequency vs. 15% of controls (p=0.006). In 19 infants with C. difficile, 95% improved within 1 week, with 85% clearing toxin B and 73% achieving eradication [14].

**Premature Infants:** One study (2003, n=87 infants 28-32 weeks gestation) showed S. boulardii supplementation improved stool flora patterns but did not improve nutrient absorption [14].

### 6.4 Safety

While no adverse effects were observed in clinical trials, nearly 100 cases of S. boulardii-associated fungemia have been reported (as of 2012), primarily in immunocompromised patients or those with indwelling catheters. Up to 30 cases of systemic fungal infection have been reported, including 10 in children. Risk factors include central venous catheters, immunocompromised states, and long-term hospitalization. Airborne yeast from opened packets can contaminate surfaces for up to 30 minutes. S. boulardii is safe for use in otherwise healthy populations and fungemia with S. boulardii has not been reported in immunocompetent patients [12, 14].

### 6.5 Dosing

Children over 2 months: 250 mg twice daily. Adults: 500 mg once daily (prevention) or twice daily (treatment). Treatment duration: 1-4 weeks. Not recommended for children under 2 years without healthcare provider supervision. Marketed as Florastor® (Biocodex). 250 mg capsules ($10.95 for 10, $43.95 for 50) or flavored powder packets ($12.95 for 10) [14].

### 6.6 Food Applications and Postbiotic Potential

A systematic review in Frontiers in Nutrition (July 2026) by researchers analyzing 91 peer-reviewed studies describes S. boulardii's food applications: Live cells are viable in yogurt (≥2×10⁷ CFU/g after 16 days at 4°C), ice cream (6.16 log CFU/g after 120 days), cheese, kefir. Limited by pasteurization, baking (>180°C depletes viability to <5%). As a fermentation biocatalyst, it secretes β-glucosidase, protease, lipase; increases antioxidant activity in fermented blueberry juice (42% DPPH improvement); degrades antinutritional factors in lupin (oligosaccharides 27.3-82.3%, phytic acid 61.9-67.0%, alkaloids 25.5-36.7%). The β-glucosidase activity of S. boulardii has been reported to be significantly higher than that of other probiotics, resulting in a 3.4-fold increase in the conversion rate of grape skin aglycone-type polyphenols [11].

As postbiotics/paraprobiotics: Heat-inactivated cells retain bioactivity through β-glucan/mannan epitopes; used in bread (GABA at 30 μg/g after baking), edible films, and meat coatings. CRISPR/Cas9 has been used to enhance S. boulardii for expressing vaccine antigens, anti-inflammatory factors, and antimicrobial peptides (e.g., recombinant lysozyme at 0.8 μg/mL) [11].

## 7. STREPTOCOCCUS THERMOPHILUS

### 7.1 Strain Background and Safety

Streptococcus thermophilus is a Gram-positive, homofermentative lactic acid bacterium classified within the Firmicutes phylum, recognized for its probiotic properties and significant role in promoting human health. With an estimated global consumption of 10²¹ colony-forming units (CFU) annually and a market value of approximately $40 billion, S. thermophilus is recognized as the second most economically significant LAB species, following Lactococcus lactis [22]. S. thermophilus is classified as GRAS (Generally Recognized as Safe) by the FDA and holds QPS (Qualified Presumption of Safety) status from the European Food Safety Authority, making it one of the most thoroughly reviewed microorganisms in the food and supplement industries [21].

S. thermophilus is a probiotic (good bacteria) naturally found in the digestive tract that produces lactic acid. It helps break down food, absorb nutrients, and fight off bad organisms that might cause diseases. It is commonly used to produce fermented dairy foods like yogurt and is also used in probiotic supplements. When taken by mouth, S. thermophilus is likely safe and has been used safely alone and together with other probiotics for up to one year. It is usually well-tolerated [15].

### 7.2 Metabolic Properties

S. thermophilus primarily ferments lactose via the Embden-Meyerhof-Parnas pathway, producing L(+)-lactic acid as the main end-product, along with secondary metabolites like acetic acid, formic acid, and pyruvate derivatives. Optimal growth occurs at 40-42°C, with a G+C content of ~37 mol%. It produces exopolysaccharides (EPS) with molecular weights ranging from 10-2000 kDa, composed of glucose, galactose, rhamnose, and N-acetylgalactosamine, contributing to textural and viscosity properties in fermented products [22].

### 7.3 Antimicrobial Activity

S. thermophilus produces bacteriocins called "thermophilins" (e.g., Thermophilin 13, 110) that exhibit antimicrobial activity against pathogens including Listeria monocytogenes, Bacillus cereus, and Staphylococcus aureus. These bacteriocins show stability under heat and pH variations, making them suitable for biopreservation. Aromatic compounds such as acetaldehyde and phenylacetic acid contribute to the sensory characteristics of dairy fermentations [22].

### 7.4 Health Benefits

**Lactose Intolerance Relief:** A pivotal study published in the New England Journal of Medicine by Kolars and colleagues established that yogurt cultures—particularly the beta-galactosidase produced by S. thermophilus—serve as an "autodigestive source of lactose" [21]. Clinical studies show S. thermophilus produces beta-galactosidase that pre-digests lactose, reducing breath hydrogen levels in lactase-deficient adults [21].

**Gut Barrier Integrity:** Its exopolysaccharides (EPS) support tight junction proteins and mucus production [21].

**IBS/Inflammatory Conditions:** S. thermophilus is included in VSL#3, which showed efficacy in inducing remission in mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis [21].

**H. pylori Support:** May aid in competitive exclusion of the pathogen [21].

**Colorectal Cancer Prevention:** Preliminary research suggests gut microbiota composition changes that favor reduced cancer risk [21].

**Immune Modulation:** A study published in PLOS ONE examined its direct impact on human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and found that exposure to S. thermophilus produced measurable changes in gene expression across multiple immune pathways, including upregulation of anti-inflammatory cytokine signaling. S. thermophilus also inhibits the activity of endocannabinoid-degrading enzymes FAAH and MAGL, effectively elevating endocannabinoid tone and reducing pain and inflammatory signaling through the endocannabinoid system [21].

**Exercise Recovery:** A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial found that combined supplementation with Streptococcus thermophilus FP4 and Bifidobacterium breve BR03 significantly attenuated the decline in peak force and range of motion following muscle-damaging eccentric exercise [21].

**Probiotic Applications:** Specific strains have been identified to mitigate lactose intolerance, antibiotic-related diarrhea, and inflammatory bowel diseases through the modulation of gut microbiota, the production of short-chain fatty acids, and the inhibition of Helicobacter pylori [22].

## 8. SHORT-CHAIN FATTY ACIDS (SCFAs) AND MECHANISTIC PATHWAYS

### 8.1 SCFA Production and Cross-Feeding

Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs)—primarily acetate, propionate, and butyrate—are produced by gut bacteria through fermentation of dietary fiber. The molar ratio in the colon is approximately 60:20:20 for acetate:propionate:butyrate [19, 31]. Main butyrate-producing bacteria include Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Clostridium leptum, Eubacterium rectale, and Roseburia spp. (Firmicutes phylum). Bacteroidetes mainly produce acetate and propionate [19].

Cross-feeding between probiotic bacteria enables butyrate production—Bifidobacterium species produce acetate that butyrate-producing bacteria convert to butyrate. Multi-strain probiotics show superior SCFA-boosting effects compared to single strains due to synergistic cross-feeding interactions [30]. Butyrate-producing bacteria (like F. prausnitzii and Roseburia species) cannot directly ferment complex fibers but depend on acetate from Bifidobacterium species and lactate from Lactobacillus species [30]. Specific probiotic strains noted for SCFA production: Bifidobacterium longum (acetate production, substrate release enabling butyrate production), Bifidobacterium infantis (cross-feeds with F. prausnitzii), Lactobacillus plantarum (increases butyrate-producing genera like Anaerostipes and Faecalibacterium), Lactobacillus paracasei, and Lactobacillus acidophilus (releases fructose during fermentation) [30].

### 8.2 Functions in Intestinal Mucosa

SCFAs strengthen the epithelial barrier (via tight junction proteins, HIF-1 stabilization), serve as the main energy source for colonocytes (butyrate provides >70% of oxygen consumption, providing up to 70% of the energy needs of colonocytes), regulate cell proliferation, and exert anti-inflammatory effects through HDAC inhibition and activation of G-protein coupled receptors (GPR41, GPR43, GPR109A) [19, 30].

SCFAs are absorbed via MCT1 (SLC16A1) and SMCT1 (SLC5A8) transporters. They signal through GPCRs GPR41/FFAR3, GPR43/FFAR2, and GPR109A/HCAR2, which activate anti-inflammatory signaling cascades. MCT1 expression is induced by butyrate and fermentable carbohydrates but reduced in inflamed IBD mucosa [19].

### 8.3 Anti-Inflammatory Mechanisms

Butyrate inhibits HDACs, suppresses NF-κB activation, promotes IL-10 production, and induces Treg differentiation. GPCR activation (especially GPR43 and GPR109A) mediates anti-inflammatory effects, barrier protection, and NLRP3 inflammasome/IL-18 activation. GPR43 and GPR109A knockout mice are more susceptible to chemically-induced colitis. High-fiber diets or acetate/GPR43 activation suppress colonic inflammation in WT but not in KO mice [19].

### 8.4 SCFAs in IBD

A review from the International Journal of Molecular Sciences (2025) on gut microbiota-derived SCFAs in IBD details: SCFAs—primarily acetate (60%), propionate (20%), and butyrate (20%)—are produced by gut bacteria through fermentation of dietary fiber. Butyrate serves as an essential energy source for colonocytes, strengthens epithelial integrity, modulates immune functions, suppresses pro-inflammatory cytokines, and enhances mucosal defense mechanisms. SCFAs signal through Free Fatty Acid Receptors 2 and 3 (FFAR2/FFAR3) and influence inflammation, metabolism, and neurological function via gut-organ axes [31].

In IBD, patients show altered SCFA levels due to gut microbiota disruption, leading to immune dysregulation and compromised barrier function. Butyrate strengthens the gastrointestinal epithelial barrier by stimulating mucus production, reinforcing tight junctions, promoting Treg differentiation, and inhibiting HDACs [31].

Clinical trials on SCFA administration (primarily enemas with sodium acetate, propionate, and butyrate) have yielded variable results since the first successful 1989 study by Harig et al. on diversion colitis. Key trials include: Breuer (1991) showing improvement in 9/10 distal UC patients; Senagore (1992) finding SCFA enemas equally efficacious as corticosteroids at lower cost; Vernia (1995) showing significant improvement in 14/20 SCFA-treated patients vs. 5/20 placebo; and a 1997 multicenter trial (n=103) finding no overall statistical significance but benefit in patients with flare-ups <6 months. Variability is attributed to differences in study design, patient characteristics, dosages, and notable placebo effects [31].

Oral butyrate studies show promise for remission maintenance. Vernero (2020) found 83.3% of UC patients maintained remission with oral microencapsulated sodium butyrate (BLM, 1g/day for 12 months) vs. 47.6% controls. Vernia (2000) showed that 4g/day oral butyrate-coated tablets combined with mesalazine improved efficacy over mesalazine alone. A pediatric study (n=72) found no significant difference between butyrate and placebo. Firoozi et al. demonstrated 600mg/day oral sodium butyrate reduced inflammatory biomarkers and improved sleep quality in active UC patients. Overall, while SCFAs show therapeutic potential, particularly butyrate for IBD, further well-designed research is needed to optimize therapy [31].

### 8.5 Mixed Probiotic Enhancement of Butyrate

A 2025 study in Food Bioscience evaluated the therapeutic effects of a mixed probiotic formulation (Lactobacillus rhamnosus, Lactobacillus plantarum, and Clostridium butyricum) on DSS-induced colitis in mice. Key findings: Mixed probiotics enhanced the conversion of lactate to butyrate by restoring the acetyl-CoA pathway in the colonic microbiota of mice with DSS-induced colitis. This restoration led to restored butyrate levels in the intestine and activation of the butyrate receptor PPAR-γ (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma), sustaining the energy supply of intestinal epithelial cells. The intervention reinforced intestinal barrier integrity and modulated intestinal immune responses. The study concludes that mixed probiotics alleviate colitis, providing a potential therapeutic strategy for IBD [34].

## 9. PROBIOTICS IN INTESTINAL INFLAMMATION AND IMMUNE MODULATION

### 9.1 Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Intestinal Barrier Function

A systematic review and meta-analysis published in Frontiers in Immunology (April 24, 2023) investigated the impact of probiotics on intestinal barrier function, analyzing 26 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 1,891 participants. Key findings: Probiotics significantly improved gut barrier function as measured by transepithelial resistance (TER): MD 5.27, 95% CI 3.82-6.72, P<0.00001; serum zonulin: SMD -1.58, 95% CI -2.49 to -0.66, P=0.0007; endotoxin: SMD -3.20, 95% CI -5.41 to -0.98, P=0.005; lipopolysaccharide (LPS): SMD -0.47, 95% CI -0.85 to -0.09, P=0.02. No significant changes were observed for fecal zonulin, L/M ratio, L/R ratio, DAO, or D-LA. Probiotics reduced inflammatory markers including CRP (SMD -1.76), TNF-α (SMD -0.68), and IL-6 (SMD -0.80), but showed no significant effect on IL-10 or hsCRP. Probiotics significantly boosted the enrichment of Bifidobacterium (SMD 1.85) and Lactobacillus (SMD 2.22), with no significant changes in Enterococcus or Enterobacteriaceae. The authors concluded: "Probiotics could improve intestinal barrier function, and alleviate inflammation and microbial dysbiosis" [19].

### 9.2 Anti-Inflammatory and Immunomodulatory Effects

A comprehensive review published in Frontiers in Immunology (February 2021) explores the anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects of probiotics in gut inflammation. Key findings: The immune system has evolved to sustain the host–microbiota symbiotic relationship. Western diets high in simple sugars, saturated fats, and processed foods, combined with reduced microbial exposure, contribute to chronic low-grade inflammation. The "hygiene hypothesis" suggests reduced early-life microbial contact increases risk of inflammatory diseases later in life. Probiotics exert anti-inflammatory effects through multiple pathways: modulation of T-cell differentiation toward Treg cells (anti-inflammatory); regulation of cytokine production (increasing IL-10, decreasing TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6); interaction with toll-like receptors (TLR2, TLR4, TLR6, TLR9); inhibition of NF-κB and MAPK signaling pathways; enhancement of mucosal barrier function and IgA production; and production of anti-inflammatory metabolites (SCFAs, histamine, tryptophan derivatives) [32].

### 9.3 Strain-Specific Immune Modulation

A 2026 review in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences (Szota et al., "Current Understanding of Probiotic Strains and Immune Function: From Gut Microbiota to Systemic Immunity") emphasizes that probiotic immunomodulation is fundamentally strain-specific rather than species-defined. Even within a single species such as Lactiplantibacillus plantarum, strains can differ by 14-fold in IL-10 induction and 16-fold in IL-12 induction. Key pathways include: innate immunity (TLR2/MyD88 signaling, macrophage polarization, NK-cell activation); adaptive immunity (regulatory T-cell (Treg) induction, Th1/Th2 balance modulation); anti-inflammatory pathways (IL-10 induction, NF-κB attenuation, epigenetic control via histone acetylation). The article emphasizes that the most meaningful immunological effects arise from precisely characterized strains acting in specific host contexts, whereas inconsistent trial design, small sample sizes, variable dosing, and poor strain resolution continue to limit translation. Overall, current data support a shift from generic probiotic use toward mechanism-based, strain-specific, and increasingly personalized strategies for immune modulation [17].

### 9.4 Probiotics in IBD

The review article "The role of Lactobacillus in inflammatory bowel disease: from actualities to prospects" (Cell Death Discovery, 2023) examines how Lactobacillus strains serve as probiotic-assisted therapy for IBD by strengthening three key intestinal barriers: the immunological barrier, epithelial cell barrier, and mucus barrier. Key mechanisms: immunological barrier—Lactobacillus strains (e.g., L. reuteri, L. rhamnosus) restore immune cell balance by increasing Treg frequency, decreasing Th17/Treg ratio via JAK-STAT signaling, promoting M2 macrophage polarization, and reducing pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α) while increasing anti-inflammatory mediators; epithelial cell barrier—Lactobacillus restores tight junction proteins (ZO-1, occludin, claudin-1, E-cadherin), upregulates heat shock proteins (HSP25, HSP70) via MAPK pathway, and enhances antioxidant enzymes (SOD, CAT, GSH-Px) to protect intestinal epithelial cells from oxidative injury; mucus barrier—Lactobacillus increases expression of protective mucins (Muc-2, Muc-4) and TFF3 [38].

The article notes that Lactobacillus accounts for ~0.3% of human colon bacteria and up to 6% in the duodenum. The combination of Lactobacillus and other probiotics or prebiotics is widely used in treating IBD in clinical trial stages, and some of them have apparent therapeutic effects [38].

### 9.5 Evidence-Based Summary for GI Conditions (American Family Physician, 2017)

High-quality evidence (Grade A) supports probiotics for: acute infectious diarrhea (reduces duration by ~25 hours), antibiotic-associated diarrhea (NNT=10-13), ulcerative colitis remission (NNT=8), and necrotizing enterocolitis (reduces risk by 57% and mortality). Moderate evidence (Grade B) supports probiotics for: C. difficile-associated diarrhea (NNT=29-30), hepatic encephalopathy (NNT=7), IBS (NNT=7), and functional abdominal pain. Probiotics are INEFFECTIVE for acute pancreatitis and Crohn disease. Dosing of ≥5 billion CFUs/day is significantly more effective than lower doses. Probiotics are generally safe for infants, children, adults, and older patients, but caution is advised in immunologically vulnerable populations [8].

## 10. PROBIOTICS IN COLORECTAL CANCER

### 10.1 Comprehensive Review of Mechanisms

A review published in Biomolecules (2025) by Ahmad et al. presents a comprehensive review of how probiotics modulate the gut microbiome to impact various cancers, including oesophageal, lung, liver, and colorectal cancer. Key mechanisms discussed include modulation of the gastrointestinal microbiota (e.g., inhibiting pathogenic bacteria, enhancing gut barrier integrity, and regulating bile acid metabolism), inhibition of carcinogen metabolism (e.g., reducing bacterial enzyme activity that converts compounds into carcinogens, upregulating phase II detoxification enzymes), and production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) like butyrate that inhibit cancer development. The review also highlights the importance of baseline gut microbiota composition in influencing probiotic efficacy, notes that the genus Lactobacillus has been most extensively researched (with recent taxonomic revisions splitting it into 25 genera), and discusses the potential for probiotics as a complementary approach in cancer management. The article covers protective effects against chemotherapy-induced toxicity and emphasizes that while probiotics show promise, further clinical trials are needed to fully understand the relationships between cancer and probiotics [26].

### 10.2 Probiotics as Oral Vaccines Against Colon Cancer

A review article in Frontiers in Immunology (October 2022) by Singh, Singh, and Gaur explores the potential of probiotics as oral vaccines for colon cancer therapy. Key mechanisms: Probiotics exert immunomodulatory effects through three main mechanisms: (1) secretion of metabolites that modulate systemic effects including wound healing and immune response initiation; (2) activation of pattern recognition receptors on dendritic cells, macrophages, and APCs; and (3) cross-reaction with tumor cell antigens and T cells. Probiotics also produce short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) like butyrate and conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) that exhibit anti-carcinogenic properties. The authors used the "PROBIO" database to screen 20 probiotic strains with immunomodulatory potential. Among these, 12 strains are marketed, 6 are in clinical trials, and 2 are under research evaluation. Notable strains include various Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus species. Multiple probiotic strains demonstrated anti-tumor effects in animal models, including reduced expression of anti-apoptotic proteins and inflammatory markers, increased pro-apoptotic protein expression, reduced tumor incidence and multiplicity, and modulation of gut microbiota composition toward health-promoting bacteria. The authors conclude that probiotic-based oral vaccines represent a promising non-invasive approach for colon cancer management, but further clinical trials are needed to fully determine their anti-cancer efficacy [25].

### 10.3 Probiotics in CRC Prevention and Therapy (Discover Oncology, 2025)

A review by Morsli et al. (Discover Oncology, March 2025) examines probiotics in colorectal cancer prevention and therapy. Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most diagnosed cancer and second leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide. Poor lifestyle factors (low-fiber diet, insufficient physical activity, tobacco use, alcohol) are strongly associated with increased CRC risk. Probiotics (defined by FAO/WHO as "Live microorganisms that, when administered in adequate amounts, confer health benefits on the host") include Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, and Saccharomyces. CRC patients show gut dysbiosis characterized by reduced SCFA-producing bacteria, lower Lactobacillus/Bifidobacterium, and increased pathogenic species (Fusobacterium, E. coli, Bacteroides fragilis). Key mechanisms: inhibition of TLR4/NF-κB signaling, upregulation of pro-apoptotic genes (BAX, caspase 3), downregulation of anti-apoptotic Bcl-2, modulation of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway, and promotion of apoptosis via JNK-DDIT3 ER stress response. The WHO and European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) have recognized their safety and effectiveness, classifying them as Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) and Qualified Presumption of Safety (QPS), respectively. The evidence for their clinical efficacy is inadequate, and additional research is requisite to establish them as therapeutic agents rather than simply as dietary supplements. Although probiotics are, in most cases, safe, high-risk patients should exercise caution due to the potential risk of infection [27].

### 10.4 Probiotics and Postbiotics in CRC (World J Gastroenterol, 2022)

A review by Kvakova et al. (World J Gastroenterol, 2022) examines the roles of traditional probiotics, next-generation probiotics (NGP), and postbiotics in the prevention and complementary treatment of CRC. Traditional probiotics (live microorganisms, mainly Lactobacillus spp., Bifidobacterium spp.) can stabilize gut microbiota, enhance intestinal barrier function, and produce anti-carcinogenic compounds like SCFAs. Multiple clinical trials show perioperative probiotic administration reduces postoperative complications, inflammatory responses, and hospital stays in CRC patients. Next-generation probiotics (NGP) include SCFA-producing bacteria like Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Akkermansia muciniphila, and Clostridium butyricum. Animal studies demonstrate NGP can inhibit tumor development through mechanisms involving SCFAs, modulation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling, and immune regulation. Postbiotics (inactivated microbial cells, cell components, or secreted metabolites) can induce apoptosis in CRC cells, exhibit anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activities, and demonstrate selective cytotoxicity against tumor cells while sparing normal cells. The review concludes that traditional probiotics are useful as adjuvant therapy, especially combinations of specific strains. However, further research on strain and dose specificity is needed to ensure efficacy and safety of these approaches in CRC prevention and treatment [28].

### 10.5 Clinical Trial Evidence

A completed clinical trial (NCT07194954, "Dietary Fiber and Probiotics in Advanced Colorectal Cancer") sponsored by The First Hospital of Hebei Medical University, with a status of "Completed" as of October 1, 2025, has investigated the effects of dietary fiber and probiotics in advanced colorectal cancer [29].

Another completed Phase 4 trial (NCT07144475, "Comparison of Probiotic Effects on the Outcomes of Patients After Colorectal Cancer Surgery") by Dharmais National Cancer Center Hospital, Indonesia, compared Lactobacillus casei Shirota vs. Lactobacillus acidophilus in 90 adult CRC surgery patients, assessing gastrointestinal function (I-FEED score), sepsis (NEWS2), CRP, IL-6, and length of stay [40, 41].

## 11. PATHOGEN COMPETITION AND ANTIMICROBIAL MECHANISMS

### 11.1 Meta-Analysis of Competitive Exclusion

A meta-analysis published in Nutrients (2026) by Alshatari and Ziarno systematically evaluated the effectiveness of probiotics in reducing pathogen colonization in the human gut through competitive exclusion. A literature search across PubMed and Scopus (October 2018 to August 2023) identified 30 studies for qualitative synthesis, with 4 providing quantitative data for meta-analysis. The pooled odds ratio for probiotics' impact on pathogen exclusion was 1.68 [1.13–2.51], demonstrating a statistically significant benefit (p<0.01), with minimal heterogeneity (I²=0%). Probiotic strains from Lacticaseibacillus, Limosilactobacillus, and Bifidobacterium showed efficacy in competitive exclusion. Subgroup analyses found stronger effects in antibiotic-associated dysbiosis (OR=1.96 [1.03–3.72]) compared to inflammatory conditions (OR=1.54 [0.93–2.55]). Publication bias assessments (funnel plot, Egger's test, trim-and-fill) showed no substantial asymmetry. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of findings. Of the 30 studies reviewed, 24 reported increased microbial diversity with probiotic use, and 18 documented reduced pathogen colonization. The paper concludes that probiotics support competitive exclusion of pathogens and recommends integrating probiotics into therapeutic strategies for gastrointestinal infections, while calling for more research on strain-specific effects and optimal dosing [50, 52].

### 12.2 Molecular Mechanisms

A review article in Gut Microbes (2020) by van Zyl, Deane, and Dicks from Stellenbosch University, South Africa, provides molecular insights into the mechanisms of action employed by probiotic lactic acid bacteria (LAB) against intestinal pathogenic bacteria. Key findings: GI diseases caused by bacterial infections are a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, and treatment is complicated by rising antibiotic resistance. Strains that colonize the GIT have a greater beneficial effect on the host than strains passing through the GIT. Adhesion to mucus and epithelial cells provides competitive advantage and stimulates immune response. The review covers pharmacokinetics of various probiotic strains (e.g., B. longum SB T2928 persisted >30 days, L. rhamnosus DR20 persisted 60 days). Probiotics prevent pathogen adhesion by competing for receptor sites, producing steric hindrance, and utilizing specific adhesion proteins (e.g., Msa protein in L. plantarum, MapA, S-layer proteins, sortase-dependent proteins). Bacteriocins (ribosomally produced antimicrobial peptides, 2-10 kDa) are key mechanisms, including nisin, plantaricin, mundticin, and bifidocin B. Bacteriocins act by permeabilizing membranes, inhibiting DNA/RNA synthesis, or forming pores. Several in vivo studies demonstrate efficacy against pathogens like Listeria monocytogenes, Salmonella, VRE, and MRSA. Despite their powerful anti-infective therapeutic potential and a large selection of isolated and characterized bacteriocins, these peptides have not yet entered into clinical use [51].

### 12.3 General Mechanisms

The NIH Office of Dietary Supplements fact sheet states that probiotics exert health effects through nonspecific mechanisms (inhibiting pathogen growth, producing antimicrobial substances, reducing colonic luminal pH), species-specific mechanisms (vitamin synthesis, gut barrier reinforcement, bile salt metabolism), and strain-specific mechanisms (cytokine production, immunomodulatory activities, effects on endocrine/nervous systems). Effects can be specific to particular strains, so clinical recommendations need to be strain-specific [23].

The comprehensive review in Frontiers in Microbiology (2025) by Sarita et al. notes that the most commonly used probiotic genera include Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, Enterococcus, Lactococcus, Streptococcus, Bacillus, and Saccharomyces. Key health benefits include treatment of diabetes, obesity, inflammatory diseases, cardiovascular conditions, respiratory issues, CNS disorders, and digestive problems. The effectiveness of probiotics can be enhanced by formulating them with prebiotics (synbiotics). Complete efficiency of any probiotic can be achieved only if the number of viable organisms is either higher or is equal to 10⁷ CFU/mL [24].

## 12. SYSTEMATIC REVIEWS AND META-ANALYSES SUMMARIES

### 12.1 NIH ODS Fact Sheet Key Evidence

The NIH Office of Dietary Supplements Probiotics Fact Sheet for Health Professionals summarizes:

- **Atopic Dermatitis:** Probiotics during pregnancy and early infancy may reduce risk of developing atopic dermatitis in children. A 2018 meta-analysis (27 RCTs, 6,907 infants) found probiotics reduced risk from 34.7% to 28.5%. L. rhamnosus or L. paracasei significantly reduced incidence; L. reuteri or L. acidophilus did not.
- **Pediatric Acute Infectious Diarrhea:** A 2020 Cochrane Review (82 RCTs, 12,127 participants) reported 36% reduction in risk of diarrhea lasting ≥48 hours and 21.3-hour reduction in mean diarrhea duration. LGG (at ≥10¹⁰ CFU/day) and S. boulardii (10⁹-10¹⁰ CFU/day for 5-10 days) reduce duration by ~1 day. However, two subsequent U.S. trials found LGG no better than placebo in emergency department settings. ESPGHAN (2023) weakly recommends LGG, S. boulardii, L. reuteri for acute gastroenteritis in children. AGA (2020) recommended against probiotics for this use in the U.S. and Canada.
- **Antibiotic-Associated Diarrhea (AAD):** Up to 30% of antibiotic users experience AAD. Meta-analyses indicate probiotics may reduce AAD risk by 51%. Benefits depend on antibiotic type, probiotic strain, life stage, and inpatient vs. outpatient care. LGG (4×10⁸ to 12×10¹⁰ CFU for 10 days to 3 months) reduced AAD risk from 22.4% to 12.3%. S. boulardii reduced AAD risk from 17.4% to 8.2% in adults and 20.9% to 8.8% in children. Starting probiotics within 2 days of first antibiotic dose is more effective.
- **Necrotizing Enterocolitis (NEC):** Life-threatening GI illness mainly affecting preterm infants with very low birth weight (<1,500 g). Researchers have evaluated specific probiotic combinations to reduce severe inflammatory responses, but the FDA has raised concerns about adverse effects when administering probiotics to preterm infants [23].

### 12.2 Overview of Probiotic Clinical Evidence by Condition

The American Family Physician (2017) article provides a comprehensive evidence-based review:

- High-quality evidence (Grade A): acute infectious diarrhea (reduces duration by ~25 hours), antibiotic-associated diarrhea (NNT=10-13), ulcerative colitis remission (NNT=8), necrotizing enterocolitis (reduces risk by 57% and mortality)
- Moderate evidence (Grade B): C. difficile-associated diarrhea (NNT=29-30), hepatic encephalopathy (NNT=7), IBS (NNT=7), functional abdominal pain
- Probiotics are INEFFECTIVE for acute pancreatitis and Crohn disease
- Dosing of ≥5 billion CFUs/day is significantly more effective than lower doses
- Probiotics are generally safe for infants, children, adults, and older patients, but caution is advised in immunologically vulnerable populations [8]

## 13. OTHER NOTABLE PROBIOTIC STRAINS AND GENERAL INFORMATION

### 13.1 Definition and Regulation

The International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics defines probiotics as "live microorganisms that, when administered in adequate amounts, confer a health benefit on the host" [23]. The World Health Organization (WHO) defines probiotics as "Live microbes which confer a health benefit to their host when administered in adequate amounts" [24]. Probiotics are identified by genus, species, and strain designation. Common genera include Bifidobacterium, Saccharomyces, Streptococcus, Enterococcus, Escherichia, Bacillus, and the family Lactobacillaceae. The Lactobacillus genus was restructured in 2020 [23].

### 13.2 Safety Considerations

Probiotics are generally safe for infants, children, adults, and older patients, but caution is advised in immunologically vulnerable populations [8]. The WHO and EFSA have recognized probiotics as Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) and Qualified Presumption of Safety (QPS), respectively. However, high-risk patients should exercise caution due to the potential risk of infection [27]. Probiotics may transiently colonize the human gut mucosa in highly individualized patterns, depending on the baseline microbiota, probiotic strain, and gastrointestinal tract region [23].

### 13.3 Market and Global Context

The global probiotics market reached USD 54.77 billion in 2020, projected to exceed USD 96 billion by 2030 (CAGR 7.5%). Yeast-derived probiotics are expected to grow at 12.4% CAGR [11]. The human GI tract contains approximately 100 trillion microorganisms, of which ~20 trillion are probiotics, primarily located in the ileum and colon [53].
